TUESDAY, 26 MAY 2015
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
Prayers.
KiwiSaver—Government Contributions
1. METIRIA TUREI (Co -Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister: Does he stand
by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does he stand by his reported statement that no one had been
disadvantaged by the move to scrap the $1,000 KiwiSaver kick-start payment?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member might want to table the source for that because I
cannot recall it.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Has the Prime Minister seen that New Zealand ranks 22 nd out of 24
countries in the OECD for savings, and will his removal of the $1,000 KiwiSaver kick -
start contribution make this poor savings record better or worse?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, savings records have improved under this
Government. Secondly, there are multiple ways of measuring those things. And, thirdly,
the removal of the $1,000 kick -start contribution will not make a blind bit of difference
to the number of people who join KiwiSaver.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: What evidence does the Prime Minister have that the sign -up rates
for KiwiSaver will not be affected?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: That is t he formal advice from the Inland Revenue
Department, and it is supported by the view that the people who are joining KiwiSaver
are essentially doing so because it is now well organised within the workplace. Some of
the big scheme providers are extremely we ll organised. We have got about 15,000 to
20,000 people joining in a month. I would be very, very surprised if it changes at all as a
result of this.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Prime Minister agree with the Service and Food Workers
Union, which said that low -paid workers said that they would be the hardest hit by his
decision to axe the kick-start?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Definitely not. The lowest -paid workers will be supported by
the fact that the Government increased the Working for Families contribution by $12.50
a week. They will also be supported if they were ever on a benefit by the increase of
$25. But, overall, I  do not think the removal of $1,000 that people would get in 40
years’ time will be that material.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Has the Prime Minister seen that savings in New Zealand are
currently concentrated in the top one-fifth of all income earners, and will his removal of
the $1,000 KiwiSaver kick -start make saving for those in the bottom four -fifths of
income earners easier or harder?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, it is logical, actually —and, I suspect, consistent around
pretty much eve ry OECD country —that those who earn the most technically save the
most, because savings, of course, is for gone consumption. It is one of the very reasons
why this political party will never be means testing New Zealand superannuation, as
Labour is now promoting.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Prime Minister understand that wealth inequality in New
Zealand is twice as large as income inequality, and will his removal of the $1,000
3934 Oral Questions  26 May 2015
KiwiSaver kick -start strengthen or weaken the incentives for all New Zealanders to
build wealth through savings?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think it is important to remember that KiwiSaver is a scheme
where after you put in your 3 percent contribution, employers put in 3 percent and the
Government puts in the memb er’s tax credit. If you look at all of those numbers over
the normal sort of 45-year working period for most people, $1,000 is immaterial.
Budget 2015—Support for Vulnerable New Zealanders
2. TIM MACINDOE (National —Hamilton West)  to the Minister of Finance :
How does Budget 2015 continue the Government’s plan to manage the public finances
while supporting the most vulnerable?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government has continued its
plan to be careful with spending and to choose carefully where it allocates new
spending. As a result of that, despite fiscal constraints, we have continued an ongoing
programme of supporting New Zealand families to get ahead. This has resulted in a
number of changes. From 1 April this year paid parental leave increased by 2 weeks to
16 weeks. It will increase by another 2 weeks next April. On 1 April the adult minimum
wage increased to $14.75. New Zealand superannuation increased by another 2 percent.
From 1 July this year children under 13 will have access to free GP visits and free
prescriptions. From 1 April next year the benefit rates for beneficiary families with
children will go up by $25 a week.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: How will Budget 2015 support more jobs and higher wages for New
Zealand families?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: One of the most important things we can do for vulnerable
families is to assist the parents into work. When they are in work, of course, it is
important for them to see the prospect of steadily rising incomes. This is occurring. The
Budget forecast shows 194,000 extra jobs since late 2010, and another 150,000 jobs are
expected by 2019. Average annual wages have increased by $5,700 in the last 4 years
and are forecast to rise by a further $7,000 to where the annual average wage will be
$63,000 a year in 4 years’ time. We can assist more people into work because there are
more jobs, and when they are in jobs both the minimum wage and the average wage will
continue to rise.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: How will the Government’s $790 million child hardship pa ckage
deliver more support for the families who need it most?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The evidence shows that those families who are most in
need are those who are persistently on low incomes, for a long time on benefit, where
there are children. Therefore, the Government’s package is targeted at lifting the benefit
rates for families with children. This is the first time that core benefit rates have been
increased, apart from inflation adjustments, since 1972. We also recognise that low -
income working families are under pressure, and so there are increases in the minimum
family tax credit and in the base rate of the in -work tax credit. And, in addition to that,
childcare assistance will be increased. The package targets around 160,000 families,
with 300,000 children, on incomes of less than $36,350 per year.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What other measures were progressed as part of Budget 2015 to
support vulnerable New Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government is continuing to advance its social
investment approach, which is aimed at resolving some of the most complex social and
family problems that there are in our community. Outside of the child hardship package,
the Budget also provides over $100 million for these further initiatives, and they are
initiatives aimed at breaking the cycles that lock fam ilies into long-term dependency—
that is, the cycles of drug and alcohol addiction, criminal offending, persistently low
26 May 2015 Oral Questions  3935
incomes, low educational achievement, and domestic viole nce. This Government is not
afraid to try to address those issues directly, because, in a sense, it does not matter how
much income those families have, they have got more serious long -term problems that
need sustained support in order to resolve them.
Prime Minister—Statements
3. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister: Why
has he reneged on his commitment made in 2011 that “the $1,000 kick -start for new
KiwiSaver members will remain as it is now” by removing the kick -start in this year’s
Budget, and did he renege on any other commitments in the Budget?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Those comments were made with re gard to
KiwiSaver changes in Budget 2011—when Labour’s policy was from about four leaders
ago—raising the retirement age at the time. As I said, the Government intends to reduce
the amount of money it has to borrow from overseas to put into KiwiSaver, and increase
the amount of genuine savings from the private sector. That is precisely what we have
done. The only reneging I have seen since the Budget has actually been from the Labour
leader, who spent Friday talking about means testing, then sort of reneged, then went—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why has he broken his promise made last year to invest $212
million in regional highways, with Budget 2015 allocating less than half that amount
over 3 years?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Sorry, could you just repeat the question? I could not hear one
word—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I will ask Andrew Little to repeat the question.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why has he broken his promise made last year to invest $212
million in regional highways, with Budget 2015 allocating less than half that amount
over 3 years?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: You really need to direct that question to the Minister of
Transport, because there will be a log ical explanation. We are totally committed to
those roads, but they will be accounted for in a certain way.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why has he broken his promise made in September last year to
create 150,000 jobs in 2 years, given that the Budget sh ows him missing that target by

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member is wrong, again.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why has he broken his promise made in September last year to
increase the average wage by $7,000 in 3 years, given tha t the Budget shows the
average wage will rise only half that much?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think the Budget showed that wage growth over the next 3
will be about $7,000. Prior to that it was $5,600. But what is true is that average wages
are g rowing faster than inflation under this Government, something that the previous
Government could not achieve.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What reports has the Prime Minister received on other approaches
to managing retirement savings policy?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Provided it is within the prime ministerial responsibility, I call the
Rt Hon Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have seen a number of conflicting reports on other
approaches to retirement savings policy. One included a questio n about means testing

items.speaker: New Zealander superannuation. The answer was
items.text: “Yep, I don’t think we can avoid
looking at that.” and “You’ve got people over 65 able to keep on working, earning a
good income, working alongside people who are doing the same or similar  work not
3936 Oral Questions  26 May 2015
getting it. Is it right that the person over 65 on a full -time income should also get this
income supplement?”.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! Would the Prime Minister resume his
seat. This answer is only going to lead to disorder.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why has he broken his promise made last year not to impose new
taxes, by putting a new levy on people entering and leaving the country and hiking the
levy on broadband users, bearing in mind the Oxford Dictionary says a levy is “a tax
raised by levying”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: We have not broken our promise. What we have done is
ensure that there will be more money for biosecurity. Mr Little can spend all his time in
question time asking these questions if he wants, but the real question is: will he get
back on side with his caucus , who now hate him because he is polling 25 percent
because he wants to means test New Zealand superannuation? It ain’t going well,
Andrew.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Before I call the honourable member Tim Macindoe
[Interruption] Order! Before I call him I will need him to be aware of Speaker’s ruling
154/2A: “It is not reasonable to use questions from the governing party or its support
parties to attack other members of the House.”

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What measures has the Government taken to ensure its retirement
savings policies are sustainable over the long term?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What an excellent question. We have set out a responsible
path for overall Government spending so that current settings for New Zealand
superannuation are both affordable and fully factored into our long -term forecast. As
Treasury notes, New Zealand’s current superannuation costs are quite low by world
standards, at less than 5 percent of GDP, compared with over 9 percent, on average,
across the OECD. By 2060 —that is 45 years from now —New Zealand’s annual
superannuation costs are forecast to be 8 percent of GDP. That is lower than the current
OECD average. If one was reall y worried about this issue, as one political party in
Parliament says it is, there are only three ways of resolving this issue: raise the age of
superannuation, means test, or make it less generous to everybody. Mr Little has ruled
out two; it must be No. 3. No wonder your caucus—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why has he broken his promise to stop Kiwis becoming tenants in
their own country, by failing in this Budget to stop foreign buyers who are purchasing
one in every 10 h ouses sold in Auckland, and instead announcing a range of measures,
none of which will make a difference to the Auckland house price crisis?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member would be a lot more credible if he did not make
up numbers. It is not  one in 10. He has no evidence to support that. Actually, nobody
knows. In fact, if he stopped making up policy on the hoof, like the means testing of
superannuation, he would do a bit better as well.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Speaking about the primary question, which was “renege
on any other commitments”—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can I just have the supplementary question without the
preamble, please.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: You are getting it right now. I a m relating it to the primary
question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will resume his seat. There is simply no need to
relate it to the primary question. The Standing Orders require that the supplementary
question is related to the primary quest ion. I call on the member to simply ask his
supplementary question.
26 May 2015 Oral Questions  3937

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am asking a
supplementary question. I have used five words, and you have stopped me.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am very tempted to not allow the member to ask a supplementary
question. When he wants to ask a supplementary question, I give the member the call.
He rises and asks the question. There is no need for an introduction about relating it to
the primary question. I do not want to have to repeat this for the member. We will be
moving to somebody else if I need to.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. With the greatest of
respect, and I have been here longer than you—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It is a point of order. I intend to listen in silence.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If I intend there to be some relativity to the primary
question in what I am about to ask, that is  up to my discretion. With the greatest of
respect, this is the first time I have had someone make the ruling you have just made
from that Chair.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Well, then, I suggest the member needs to listen more often in
question time. You are required to—[Interruption] Order! The member will stand and
withdraw that remark immediately.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I withdraw.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Supplementary question, Andrew Little.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Supplementary question, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, supplementary question, Andrew Little.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will also be very familiar with the Standing
Orders. I have the right to decide where I will take a supplementary question. I warned
the member that he would not get a sec ond chance. I am going to hear a supplementary
question from Andrew Little. I may change my mind and then let the member ask a
supplementary question. I may do so.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. You did not tell me
that I would not get a supplementary question. You have—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] The member will immediately —
[Interruption] The member will now leave the Chamber.
Rt Hon Winston Peters withdrew from the Chamber.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why does he not just keep his promises rather than inventing new
excuses for breaking them?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: This Government keeps its promises, and that is why it keeps
getting re -elected. I f the member wants to recreate history he is welcome to it, but,
actually, he knows, like I know, that the most popular thing on Thursday and Friday
was our Budget, and the least popular thing was his decision to means test New Zealand
superannuation.
Budget 2015—Water Management
4. BARBARA KURIGER (National—Taranaki - King Country) to the Minister
for Primary Industries : How will Budget 2015 help develop more water storage and
irrigation projects?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: As part of Budget 2015,
irrigation projects will now receive through the Irrigation Acceleration Fund a kick-start
of $25 million in operating funding for 5 years from 2016 -17. The Irrigation
Acceleration Fund helps support the development of irrigation infrastructure proposals
to the stage where they are investment -ready, which means that they  must be
commercially robust and demonstrate a high level of user and community support.
3938 Oral Questions  26 May 2015
Around 100,000 hectares of new irrigated areas are expected from the Irrigation
Acceleration Fund - funded projects to date, with around 36,000 hectares of that
commissioned or currently being constructed.

items.speaker: Barbara Kuriger
items.text: Why is this funding boost so important for our regions?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: That is a good question. The need for water storage projects
is obvious, given that nearly e very part of the country has suffered through droughts at
some stage over the last 3 or so years. We do not have a water shortage issue in New
Zealand; we have a water storage issue. It just does not rain in the right place at the right
time. Providing a consistent, reliable water supply for farmers and growers has massive
potential to boost growth, create jobs, and grow our exports from provincial regions.

items.speaker: Barbara Kuriger
items.text: What other ways does the Government help support water storage
in irrigation projects?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: The Government also supports water storage projects through
Crown Irrigation Investments Ltd., which acts as a bridging investor for regional water
infrastructure development. Over the last 2 years, $12 0 million has been allocated to
Crown Irrigation Investments Ltd, with the potential to provide a further 125,000
hectares of new irrigation. Work is under way to enable greater collaboration between
Crown Irrigation Investments Ltd and the Irrigation Acceleration Fund. This will help to
ensure that more of these critical regional water storage projects get to the construction
stage. This is hugely exciting for rural New Zealand.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: Will the Government’s funding initiatives in the Budget assist in
the promotion of the Ruataniwha Dam scheme?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: I could not hear him. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It was difficult to hear. I did hear the question but I suspect
some members did not. The mike might not have been on. I will ask Richard Prosser to
repeat the question.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: Will the Government’s irrigation initiatives in the Budget assist in
the promotion of the Ruataniwha Dam project?

items.speaker: Hon NA THAN GUY
items.text: Currently  the Irrigation Acceleration Fund has invested
almost $6 million in Ruataniwha, and that is now working through a process of getting a
consent. Then it will need to prove to Crown Irrigation Investments Ltd that it is indeed
investment-ready for them to have a look at it.
Iraq, Military Deployment—Iraqi Army
5. RON MARK (NZ First)  to the Prime Minister : Does he stand by all his
statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: When he said in the House “Get some guts”, was he talking to the
Opposition parties or to the Iraqi Army, which has been in retreat for the last 2 months
and was routed at Ramadi by a force that it outnumbered ten to one?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, really specifically, I was speaking to the Leader of the
Opposition, who I think, in his heart of hearts, knows that the right thing for this country
to do on a bipartisan bas is is to actually stand up to the people who undertake these
atrocities, and I hope that he will eventually see it our way, because we are right on this
side of the House.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Does he stand by his statement “If Iraq is to gain control of i ts cities, it
will need strong and well-trained forces.”; if so, does he not realise that you cannot train
cowards to fight?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In terms of the first part of the question, yes, you do need
strong forces; in terms of the latt er part of the question, I think that the member should
26 May 2015 Oral Questions  3939
really probably reflect on that. To put that generalisation across a whole country’s
population is either foolhardy or harsh. He can choose which one he prefers.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: When he received his most recent briefing from the Defence Force on
Iraq, did that briefing state that there was a possibility that our troops would be
surrounded at Camp Taji?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am not going to go into the individual briefings I get,
because I think that it would not be in the national interest to do so, but what I am quite
prepared to say is that the safety and security of our men and women who are in Taji
airbase is our No. 1 priority. There is obviously work done to make sure we contin ually
assess that situation. There is a variety of trigger points that we would look at if we
thought that it was appropriate to bring our people home, and we have always said that
we would do that. But I am quite comfortable in the advice I have at the mo ment that,
notwithstanding it is obviously a dangerous environment in Iraq, our people are in the
safest position they can be in, actually—in Taji airbase.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Does the Prime Minister agree with the US Chairman of the Joint Chiefs
of Staff, General Martin Dempsey, who said that the Iraqi security force “was not driven
out of Ramadi. They drove out of Ramadi.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am not going to be a Monday morning quarterback on what
happened in Ramadi, but I have seen the comments from Prime Minister al -Abadi, who
said that they are keen to retake that ground. Certainly, the advice that we have had is
that some ground was lost and some ground was gained. But if you take a step back on
the overall thing, if the member’s logic is followed to the obvious conclusion, what he is
basically saying is that Iraq should surrender itself to the Islamic State of Iraq and the
Levant (ISIL). I simply say to the member that if he thinks that is not going to increase
the risks to New Zealan ders, then it is really unbelievable. If the member wants to go
out there and tell New Zealanders that he is quite prepared, through his own inactions,
to put them at greater risk, then he is welcome to go and campaign on doing that. But he
will run a million miles from that when I start pointing it out publicly, and that is what I
intend to do.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Does he think that troops who flee and leave tanks and artillery worth
millions of dollars behind and troops who flee when they outnumber the en emy ten to
one are able and capable of being trained to fight?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: In so far as there is prime ministerial responsibility, the right
honourable Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: All I can say is that if you listen to the Chief of Defence
Force, he is very confident of the training capability that our people have. He has seen
that demonstrated in places like Afghanistan, where we have made a difference, and I
am confident, actually, that in time we will make a difference in improving the skills of
the Iraqis.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: What is the Prime Minister’s view of Ash Carter, the United States
Secretary of Defense, who said “What apparently happened was that the Iraqi forces just
showed no will to fight. They were not outnumbered. In fact, they vastly outnumbered
the opposing force … that says to me, and I think to most of us, that we have an issue
with the will of Iraqis to fight ISIL and defend themselves.”? What is the Prime
Minister’s view of that statement?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am the Prime Minister of New Zealand, not a commentator
on what other politicians around the world say.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Does he not realise that he sent our brave New Zealand soldiers t o Iraq
on a fool’s errand and the training the Iraqi Army to stand and fight is literally Mission:
Impossible?
3940 Oral Questions  26 May 2015

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No. What I do think is that ISIL presents a threat not only in
the region but also presents a regional threat to countries that New Zealanders travel to,
and I think it presents a domestic threat. The member can sit there all he likes and say
that we should abdicate our responsibilities and do nothing, but I simply say to the
member that that would put them at gre ater risk. I think that if you look at the public
polling that has been undertaken on this matter, the most recent poll that we saw in the
New Zealand Herald indicated that on a ratio of 3:1 New Zealanders actually do think
we should do something to protec t ourselves from people who are abhorrent. If the
member does not believe in doing that, I am quite surprised, because he is a former
military man and I would have thought he would understand that.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: When the Prime Minister said  the trigger for changing his stance on
deployment to Iraq was if the New Zealand Defence Force thought there was “an
absolute threat” to New Zealand troops, how does he define “absolute threat”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: That is the very point —I do not. They decide that. T hey are
the ones who tell us, through their advice. On the back of our advice, we will decide
whether they come or no, but they define the risks.
Finance, Minister—Tax Revenue
6. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Finance
items.text: Does he agree with National Party finance spokesperson Bill English: “We
don’t believe in new and more taxes. We think we can manage with the tax revenue we
have”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, I do agree with my party’s
finance spokesman, which is more than I can say for Andrew Little, who does not agree
with his party’s finance spokesman. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am having trouble hearing because of the yelling from my
left here. [Interruption] Well, no, it was this one who was distracting me.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In lig ht of that answer, why, then, did he and John Key promise
New Zealanders in the 2014 election campaign that there would be no new taxes when
he has introduced a property tax, an arrivals and departures tax, and extended the
broadband tax?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The extension of broadband was certainly discussed prior to
the election. As we have discussed, the tax measures are an extension of existing taxes,
which the member may not have known about in his case. The levy at the airports is a
user charge, and we would expect to be able to continue to expand the use of user
charges.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: What is the difference between a levy and a tax?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The levy is a user charge, and that is different  from an
income test on national superannuation.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Will every dollar collected under the regime brought into place
by the Border Processing (Arrivals and Departures) Levy Bill go towards the cost of
border processing?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, and I would imagine that every dollar of expenditure on
those services is going to be heavily scrutinised by passengers, airlines, airports, and
anyone else who is interested in getting those levies down, as we are.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does he stand by his statement: “Further extension of the current
tax on capital gains is likely to have high compliance costs, and that is a conclusion that
three tax inquiries and several Governments have come to over the last 20 years. If it
excludes the family home,”—like it does—“it will not [make] much difference, … ”; if
so, why has he now introduced a tax that he says that he does not know the impact of,
does not know how much revenue it will raise, and that has such high compliance costs?
26 May 2015 Oral Questions  3941

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I do stand by the statement, and part of the point of
introducing a brightline test is to avoid excessive compliance costs. We have yet to see
how much impact the introduction of that test will have on the housing market.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Can he confirm his statement in the weekend that he does not
know whether this tax that he has introduced on property speculators will work?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The question has be en about what impact we expect it will
have on the Auckland housing market. The member will be familiar with the discussion.
If the Auckland house prices are driven significantly by speculators turning over
properties within 2 years, then the tax may have an impact. If the prices are not driven
primarily by that but are driven by other factors such as restricted supply of land or
costs of construction, then it will not make much difference.
Budget 2015—Benefit-dependent Households
7. TODD MULLER (Nation al—Bay of Plenty)  to the Minister for Social

items.speaker: Development
items.text: How does Budget 2015 help parents who receive a benefit?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Last week we
announced a $790 million child hardship package as part of Budget 2015. The package
includes increased work obligations for sole parents on a benefit, more childcare
support, a $25 -a-week increase in benefit rates for families with children —the first
increase above inflation in 43 years—and an increase in Working for Families payments
to low-income families who are not on a benefit. Alongside the successes that we have
seen with our reforms to the welfare system, which have resulted in 38,000 fewer
people on benefits compared with 3 years ago, the number of children in benefit -
dependent households has fallen by almost 42,000 over the same period.

items.speaker: Todd Muller
items.text: What feedback has she received on how Budget 2015 will support
children in benefit-dependent households?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I was encouraged to read that the Southland Beneficiaries
and Community Rights Centre supports the pack age. It welcomed the package as
“overall, a step in the right direction”. Its press r elease also said that a policy of
withholding State support for beneficiaries unless they are enrolled to vote, as was
proposed by Labour, was hardly inclusive or progressive. This National Government is
making considered and appropriate changes to support children in families in hardship.

items.speaker: Todd Muller
items.text: How will changes to part -time work obligations help children in
benefit-dependent households?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: This Government believes that the best way out of poverty is
through work. The package announced last week will see sole parents more intensively
supported into part-time work when their youngest child turns 3. I was delighted that Dr
Lance O’Sullivan supported this change, saying that we should expose children in
benefit-dependent homes “to positive environments, keep them warm, safe and dry and
give them a learning opportunity that will prepare them for school, because I don’t
believe we should wait till age 5.” The number of sole parents is the lowest since 1988.
The more sole parents we can get into work, the fewer children we will have dependent
on a benefit.
Animal Welfare—Live Sheep Exports to Saudi Arabia
8. JAMES SHAW (Green)  to the Minister of Foreign Affairs : How many of the
900 ewes that flew to Saudi Arabia on Singapore Airlines in October 2014 at the
taxpayers’ expense are still alive?

items.speaker: Hon MURRAY McCULLY
items.text: Officials confirm that
all of the 900 ewes arrived in Saudi Arabia in good condition. The nature of the project
being undertaken in Saudi Arabia makes it impossible for me to provide a specific
3942 Oral Questions  26 May 2015
answer to the questions that h e asks. However, officials advise that according to the
most recent reports the answer is approximately 850.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Did he remove the provisions guaranteeing the welfare of the sheep
once they arrived in Saudi Arabia because  he knew that Suffolk sheep, br ed for cold
climates, will not survive the 40 degree heat, or because the sheep just happened to get
there the same month as the haj, a religious pilgrimage that involves the ritual sacrifice
of over 700,000 sheep?

items.speaker: Hon MURRAY McCULLY
items.text: There were three reasons for agreeing to remove the
provision that the member refers to. The first was that as a matter of principle the Saudi
Arabian Government found it offensive that we should seek to extend the jurisdiction of
New Zealand law on to Saudi Arabian soil. Secondly, it was probably unenforceable,
legally, anyway. But, thirdly, the Animal Welfare Act 1999 requires the Director -
General of the Ministry for Primary Industries to have regard to such matters as the
previous history  of the exporter, the provisions for the animals’ welfare during the
journey, and all the relevant Ministry for Primary Industries animal welfare standards
and guidelines. That seemed to me and the New Zealand Government to provide the
protection that New Zealand wanted.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Why do recent satellite pictures of New Zealand Trade and
Enterprise’s $7.5 million agri-hub in Saudi Arabia to which the sheep were flown show
no visible livestock farming in the middle of the desert?

items.speaker: Hon MURRAY McCULLY
items.text: I have received recent reports from officials and from
those who are superintending the project who tell me that what is a partially completed
project is proceeding well. I do not know what images the member refers to, but what I
will say is that the Green Party members are difficult to please on this matter. They
wanted us to ban the export of live sheep for slaughter and the Government has renewed
that export prohibition. They wanted us to have regard for animal welfare matters  and
so the Government flew the sheep for the pilot on Singapore Airlines. If the member is
telling us that he wants us to fly them business class next time, that is something we will
give consideration to!

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Does he think it is susp icious that the New Zealand company that won
the tender to fly sheep over to Saudi Arabia is, in part, owned by Mr al -Khalaf, the
influential Saudi businessman who was blocking the free -trade deal with Saudi Arabia;
and is it not also suspicious that only he was kept up to date with the tender process
while other tenderers such as Deloitte and GG Wrightson were not?

items.speaker: Hon MURRAY McCULLY
items.text: The contract for the lead provider’s position, which is
what the member is referring to, was awarded th rough a tender process that was
overseen by officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, New Zealand Trade and
Enterprise, and an expert who was formerly the chief executive of Landcorp. I am
satisfied that the New Zealand Government procurement require ments were met in that
respect.
Housing, Auckland—Housing Developments on Crown Land
9. PHIL TWYFORD (Labour —Te Atatū)  to the Minister for Building and

items.speaker: Housing
items.text: Does he stand by his statement that the 500 hectares of surplus Crown land he
has identified “has already been zoned as residential, but with no existing buildings or
tenants to manage – meaning houses will be able to be brought to market faster”?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I stand by my full
statement, and it said: “It is estimated that the Crown, through various agencies, owns
approximately 500 hectares of land with the potential for residential development.” The
work is at an early stage, but on Friday I will be able to confirm a number of sites that
will assist us with housing.
26 May 2015 Oral Questions  3943

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Will he confirm that, before the announcement, offic ials told him he
would be lucky if only one-quarter of the 500 hectares could be built on?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: No, I certainly cannot confirm that. There are 150,000
hectares of Crown land in Auckland. Officials have been sifting through  thousands and
thousands of titles, and on Friday I will be able to identify the first blocks of land that
will have potential, albeit it is not until you actually test sites with the private sector as
to where it is economical to develop such areas that will bring houses on stream.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Will he at least admit that his officials questioned the economic
viability of building on much of the 500 hectares; if so, why did he ignore their
concerns?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Qu ite the opposite. Officials have been very enthusiastic
about this programme. They brought it to me and the Minister of Finance. I invite the
member to have a look at Christchurch, at sites like Awatea, like the partnership we
have with the Christchurch Ci ty Council at Colombo Street and Welles Street, like the
new houses that have been built at Rangers Park, the developments at Hobsonville, and
the developments at Weymouth, to see the progress the Government has been able to
make, where the previous Government did nothing.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Did his officials carry out proper site inspections on each property
prior to his announcement; if not, why did he refuse to allow them sufficient time to
check whether each parcel of land is suitable for buil ding before he rushed out his
announcement?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: We made a Budget announcement of $53 million to support
this programme, as well as $2 million of operational funding. If the member actually
reads the release, it makes plain that the work is to go ahead around the identification of
these sites. What I can confirm for the member is that the previous Government
announced the Hobsonville housing development in 2002, and by 2008 not a single sod
of soil had been turned. We now have hundreds of houses built on that site, showing the
progress that is possible under this National Government.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Can he confirm that no parcel of land in his 500 hectares has any of
the following on it: power substations, pylon s, a cemetery, a fire station, or school
playing fields; if he cannot confirm that, is his refusal to release the full list of sites
down to his embarrassment or his incompetence?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: There are thousands of sites, and I k now Mr Twyford
yesterday claimed—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Answer the question.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I will, if the member gives me half a chance. The member
identified a site yesterday in Hepburn Road. It is a site on which he  said there could be
no houses because there was a substation on it. The problem is the substation is only in
one corner, and there are 3 hectares of vacant land. Why would we not consider a
housing development on the remainder of the vacant land? I seek t he leave of the House
to table the title to the site, showing the substation in one corner of the 5 hectares.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The document has been described. I will put the leave and
the House can decide. Leave is sought to table that parti cular document. Is there any
objection? There is none. It can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. If the member is in his previous
answers quoting an official document that is the list of sites he is talking about, can I
ask whether he would table it?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is easily resolved. Is the member quoting—

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Point of order.
3944 Oral Questions  26 May 2015

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I just need to know whether the member was quoting from a
legal—

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: No, just a search of the titles—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Then there is no need to add any more.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Is this  not yet another overcooked, poorly -thought-through stunt to
look like he is doing something about the Auckland housing crisis, which will simply
end up as another list of broken promises?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: When we came into Government  we were building 200
houses per month in Auckland. Last month we built 750 in Auckland. That shows the
progress that we are making. We have more work to do, and that is why we have
committed additional funds in the Budget.
Question No. 8 to Minister

items.speaker: Hon MURRAY McCULLY
items.text: I apologise for not
doing so at the end of question No. 8, but I want to seek leave to table a Cabinet paper
dated 13 February 2013, entitled Saudi Arabia Food Security Partnership.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that particular Cabinet document. Is there
any objection? There is none. It can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
Health Targets—Progress
10. SCOTT SIMPSON (National—Coromandel) to the Minister of Health: What
progress has been made towards achieving the Government’s national health target?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Today the Ministry of
Health published the health target results for quarter three, 2014 -15. They show good
progress overall, with the highlight being that the Government’s target of reducing
emergency department waiting times has been achieved for the very first time. Across
New Zealand, 95 percent of patients were admitted, transferred, or discharged  within 6
hours. I would like to congratulate all the emergency department staff across our district
health boards on this outstanding result. The other stand -out result is that district health
boards achieved 107 percent of the national target for electiv e surgery, delivering 7,997
more elective surgeries than planned for the year to date.

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: What impact will Budget 2015 have on the national health targets?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: New Zealand’s health  budget will reach a
record $15.9 billion in the coming year, and includes new funding to provide more New
Zealanders with timely elective surgery. There is $92 million being committed to
continue the Government’s effort to increase elective surgeries, del ivering 5,000 extra
elective surgeries each year. On top of that, $6 million has been committed to create
community-based early intervention teams for diagnosis in management of orthopaedic
conditions. Budget 2015 supports the Government’s clear plan for d elivering the health
services that our communities need.
Iraq, Military Deployment—Iraqi Army
11. Hon PHIL GOFF (Labour—Mt Roskill) to the Minister of Defence: Does the
New Zealand Defence Force training of Iraqi Army troops include giving them the will
to fight?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The New Zealand Government
has made a decision to assist the Iraqi defence forces in their training because we assess
that there is a threat to New Zealanders from Daesh. It is, therefore, appropriate that we
assist the Iraqis to try to defeat Daesh. This question, I think, cheapens the desire of so
many Iraqis to overcom e that evil. We would not be there if the Iraqi Government had
26 May 2015 Oral Questions  3945
not made that request. We can only assume that that is a commitment from the Iraqi
Government to defeat the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL). Might I also say
that the New Zealand Defence Force has a very proud record of training in these sorts of
conflicts—it goes right back to Malaya in the 1950s, through to Afghanistan most
recently. These sorts of loaded and facetious questions are, I think, very disrespectful to
the New Zealand Defence Force.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Would your office have allowed
a question as the primary question that you judged to be facetious?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I would not have used those words myself but in the  answer that
was given, Mr Brownlee certainly addressed the question that was asked. If the member
wants to take it further with a supplementary question, I invite him to do so.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Does he accept that the lack of will to fight, which the United States’
defence secretary, Ash Carter, blamed for the failure of the Iraqi army, results
predominantly from the abysmal leadership of the Iraqi army and from the absolutely
extensive corruption that undermines the will of the ordinary sold ier to fight? And does
he accept that neither of those things can be altered by the professional work of the New
Zealand Army?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I am certainly not going to make any comments about
the views of the United States Secretary of Defence. I will be meeting him shortly, and I
will have a further discussion with him. The rest of that question was based on Mr
Goff’s own opinion of Iraqi forces. Although he is entitled to that opinion, I am not
making a comment on it. My view is  that the New Zealand Defence Force is very, very
capable and professional. It has engaged, in this exercise, with some very specific
aspects of the training mission that it will deliver —we think, in the best interests of
New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: When people like Dr Ron Smith from Waikato University, who was
a fervent supporter of deployment to Iraq, now believe that it was a bad idea to go there,
what will it take to persuade the Government that the benefits of the training that we
provide are too little and the risks too great to pay the price for being in the club?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I very much doubt that the analysis that the professor
has relied on would be as good as the analysis that the New Zealand Governme nt has
made its decision based on and continues to support.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: What assessment has he given of the risks now facing the New
Zealand Defence Force approximately 100 kilometres away from Islamic State (IS)
forces in Ramadi, and is that assessment such that if the risk is regarded as considerable,
he would reverse his position and bring those troops home?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Answering the first part of the question: considerably
better information than the member has.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Somebody with the temerity to
accuse a questioner of being facetious then gives an answer that can be described only
in exactly the same way—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No, no, no—I listened, again, quite carefully to the question.
In fact, there were two questions asked. The Minister has chosen to address the first
one. It may not be to the satisfaction of the member but it was certainly addressed.
Housing, Christchurch—Government Initiatives
12. Dr PARMJEET PARMAR (National)  to the Minister for Building and

items.speaker: Housing
items.text: What progress has the Government made in increasing the supply of housing
in Christchurch and what lessons can be learnt in addressing Auckland’s issues?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The housing market
in Christc hurch became very constrained following the loss of 10,000 homes in the
3946 Oral Questions  26 May 2015
2010 and 2011 earthquakes. There have been over a dozen Government initiatives to
tackle this, from emergency repairs to interventions in the planning and building
consent system, as w ell as facilitating new housing on unused public land. The house
build rate in Christchurch has quadrupled from 80 per month to over 360 per month.
House price increases have dropped from 12 percent per year to just 2 percent in the last
year. Rents, which  were soaring in 2012 and 2013, have now stabilised, to the point
where rents in the last year have declined by 5 percent. The lesson for Auckland is that
increased supply is the main solution. That is why the Government has put so much
focus on increasing  the rate of house builds. It was 200 per month when we came to
Government; last month we got to over 750 new homes.

items.speaker: Dr Parmjeet Parmar
items.text: What initiatives does the Government have under way on
public land for housing, and how are these to be expanded?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: We have initiatives well under way in areas like
Hobsonville, Weymouth, Tāmaki, and Papakura in Auckland; and at Ranges Park,
Awatea, Colombo Street, Welles Street, and Riccarton  Racecourse in Christchurch.
Budget 2015 expands this work with a programme to investigate and identify public
land holdings in Auckland for housing. This Friday I will be launching the programme
with developers from both New Zealand and Australia, and pub licly naming the first
potential blocks of land.

items.speaker: Dr Parmjeet Parmar
items.text: When will the first houses be completed from this initiative?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Our objective is to have the first partnership agreements
with de velopers agreed within 6 months. We may also need to use the streamlined
special housing area process to be able to appropriately zone the areas, and also to get
the resource consents for the infrastructure. There will then be the timetable for the
construction of that infrastructure, the consenting of the homes, and their building. My
expectation is that the first homes from this initiative will come on stream and be
available for families in 2017.
Relationships Aotearoa—Government Funding
Skycity Convention Centre—Design
Iraq, Military Deployment—Iraqi Army

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received a letter from the Hon Annette King seeking to
debate under Standing Order 389 the failure of the negotiations between Government
agencies and Relationships Aotearoa. This is a  particular case of recent occurrence
involving ministerial responsibility. The failure of the negotiations with Government
agencies was reported by Relationships Aotearoa yesterday. The negotiations concerned
the level of future Government funding for the service. The House this week is debating
the 2015 -16 Budget and the departmental estimates are currently before select
committees for examination. The Budget debate will provide the opportunity to discuss
the matter today, and the estimates examinations w ill provide the opportunity to
consider it in detail and debate it further when select committee reports on the estimates
are considered in the Committee of the whole House. On this basis the matter raised
does not meet the test for me to set aside the bus iness of the House today. The
application is therefore declined.
I have also received a letter from Dr David Clark seeking to debate under Standing
Order 389 the announcement today that the Skycity Auckland Convention Centre
design will be downsized. This is a particular case of recent occurrence involving
ministerial responsibility. The revised design was announced today by the Minister for
Economic Development, and the Government is party to the agreement to build the
26 May 2015 Urgent Debates Declined 3947
convention centre. However, the busin ess of the House should not be set aside just
because a ministerial announcement has been made, even though it may be important.
There must be such an element of urgency that the matter must take precedence over
other business. In this instance I am not pe rsuaded that there is an element of urgency
that warrants the setting aside of the business of the House. The application is therefore
declined.
I have further received a letter from Ron Mark seeking to debate under Standing
Order 389 the advance of the Is lamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) to within an hour’s
range of the Taji base, and the Iraqis’ lack of will to fight. The matter outlined in Mr
Mark’s letter does not constitute a particular case of recent occurrence, and does not
involve ministerial res ponsibility. The advance of ISIS and the state of the Iraqi army
are not matters for which there is ministerial responsibility. The Government decision to
deploy troops to Iraq was announced in February of this year, and was debated in the
House at that ti me. Because the application does not meet any of the criteria for an
urgent debate set out in Standing Order 389, it is declined.
Debate resumed from 21 May on the Appropriation (2015/16 Estimates) Bill.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am very happy to
rise and take a call on the Budget. I would like to commence by congratulating Bill
English on his seventh Budget for this Government, and a fine Budget it is. But there is
a problem, because last year it was pointed out that Mr English had come up with six
Budgets, which was exactly the same number as he had children. So I need to check —
Bill, have there been further children in the intervening 12 months? No, there have not.
So Bill has had to move on to nephews and nieces in 2015. The good news is that Bill
has, roughly, at last count, 60 nephews and nieces —so that is many Budgets to come
from the current Minister of Finance.
Bill, of course, is not flashy. He is not a flashy finance Minister. He is solid. He is
dependable. As one of the commentators pointed out, he is not flash in any way, and his
Budget last week was not flash. It was solid. It w as dependable. It was conservative —
all except for his tie. A lot of work went into the Budget, and it is fair to say that a lot of
work went into choosing Bill’s tie this year. The caucus would like to congratulate
Mary English on choosing Bill’s tie for the first time, in Budget 2015.
This Budget is a Budget from a Government that is working hard, and for a plan that
is working. It is a Budget that provides for continued falling unemployment. It is a
Budget that provides for wages continuing to grow faste r than inflation, and for
reducing hardship. It is a Budget that delivers solid economic growth. It constrains
spending. It controls inflation. It balances the books. It keeps debt under control. It
provides significant ACC reductions. It delivers better p ublic services—$1.7 billion for
health, and nearly $700 million for schools and early childhood services.
It is a Budget that invests in a growing economy. It invests in business research and
development. It invests in tertiary education. It invests in ar eas like agriculture, science,
pharmacy, and Māori and Pasifika trade training. It is a Budget that invests in New
Zealand’s assets. It invests in ultra -fast broadband. It invests in the rail system, in rural
broadband, in the Canterbury rebuild, and in regional science institutes.
It is a Budget that encourages the building of more houses in Auckland; a Budget
that increases investment in social housing. It is a Budget that strengthens property
income taxes, amongst many other things. It is an excellent B udget for New Zealand,
and I congratulate Bill English on delivering a fine Budget last week—
I would also like to congratulate the Leader of the Opposition.
3948 Budget Debate 26 May 2015

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Really?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —yes, I think we should —on a  superb Budget reply
speech. [Interruption] Hear me out —hear me out. That speech hit all the right buttons.
It hit all the right buttons. We got the seven veils. We got the roosters on heat—that was
a goody; that got them thinking. It is not often you see roosters on heat, to be fair. It had
Gene Simmons—that was an absolute stroke of genius, the old Gene Simmons. And, of
course, it had gender reassignment as well.
You can just imagine those members sitting in the war room of the Labour Party with
their copy of the Budget, which they had been given at 1 p.m. last Thursday afternoon,
and between 1 p.m. and 2 p.m. last Thursday they realised that Bill English had stolen
all of their attack. He had stolen all their lines. Their only approach was: “Oh, I don’t
know. How about a series of massive distractions?”. First, they thought of doing a little
more poetry, as Andrew Little said yesterday. Let us face it, Andrew Little’s poetry was
brilliant. Chris Hipkins popped up and said: “Why don’t you do that ‘Enrol fo r the
Dole’ poem that Tim Barnett taught you?”. But no, no, Andrew Little pulled out Gene
Simmons. That is leadership.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Oh, it really is too early in the day for Horlicks.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Then Grant Ro bertson pipes up, just like he is now, and
says: “I know what, leader. Let’s give that gender reassignment thing a go again. It will
go down well with the party.”, and he was serious. He did take Grant’s advice, because
every other leader has, and let us f ace it, where would the Labour Party be without
Grant Robertson’s advice?

items.speaker: Hon Bill English
items.text: 20 points higher in the polls.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, 20 points higher in the polls, maybe, for a start. But
let us face it—you take Grant’s advice and you run with gender reassignment, but you
draw the line at two dead fish. You draw the line at two dead fish. You snap out of that
one. You say to yourself—

items.speaker: Hon Bill English
items.text: The leader doesn’t listen to him.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, he did. He listened to the gender reassignment story.
And then what do you do on Friday? Well, there you are on Friday morning and you
have not got any of the team behind you. You are up the front, you are on yo ur own,
you are king of your domain, and you are out there, angry—but controlled, to be fair.
So it is a Friday morning speech in Wellington, and Andrew Little, angry —but
controlled—says: “I know. What am I going to go on about? How will I distract them
today? I know. Superannuation is too expensive. It is way too expensive. What about all
these people who are working past 65 supplementing their superannuation? Where do
these people get off? Outrageous! Look at people like Winston Peters, acting like the
Leader of the Opposition when he’s on a pension. He should be at home. He shouldn’t
be trying to take my job. So let’s get into that. There’s a platform right there —it’s time
to man up and deal with people who sit in Parliament and collect superannuation. I ,
Andrew Little, am going to deal with that.”

items.speaker: He goes on
items.text: “What is that, Sue? Oh, I’m not going to deal with it. OK, fair enough.
You’re right, Sue; I’m not. So no manning up this time. Sue Moroney is in charge and
we’ll put out a press release, because I  didn’t mean it. I didn’t mean anything about
means testing superannuation. We could lift the age, though. We could lift the age
because people work for ages these days. We could lift the age; that would work. Oh,
we’ve said that already. No, no, I didn’t say that. That bit about means testing your
income—that wasn’t me.”—that wasn’t Andrew Little; that was the media —“the media
made stuff up. You have got the footage? Well, no, I didn’t say it that way. Don’t go
putting words into my mouth, Paddy.” That is Andrew Little’s favourite line: “Don’t go
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3949
putting words into my mouth, Paddy. Even if I’ve said them already, I don’t say them
now, and I hope you’ve got that. Kindly stop questioning me on the subject.”
That is Andrew Little’s approach to the Budget, and  I think he should be
congratulated. But, not to be outdone in the policy -on-the-hoof division, we have the
newly minted fiscal conservative —one Grant Robertson, the newly minted fiscal
conservative. The man who spent his entire first 6 years in Parliament as the big spender
is suddenly reconstructed as Labour’s new fiscal conservative. The man who could not
see a spending programme that did not need to be expanded has suddenly become
“Balance the Budget Grant”. He is the one who says that there should be l ots of savings
and there should be balancing of the Budget. He is the one who says that ACC should
be cut back, despite the fact that Labour extended ACC. Grant’s new version of life is
that we should be fiscally conservative, until the Budget is delivered.
Then suddenly the Budget is delivered and, actually, no, you should not be taking
away the KiwiSaver kick -start, and, on the hoof, he declares: “Yep. I will reinstate it.”
That is the power of being the Opposition’s newly minted conservative spokesperson on
finance. He can say: “Yep, I will reinstate it. Forget the fact that I put out a press release
not half an hour ago that said I would not necessarily put it back.” Half an hour to an
hour before, he puts out a press release, but then he goes out and s ays: “Yep, I’d put it
back.” Feel the power! This is Grant Robertson, who is not just the finance
spokesperson; he is now contemplating his fifth, or sixth, attempt at the leadership of
the Labour Party following that brilliant speech he wrote for Andrew L ittle last week.
But that is all right. On Saturday it was back to the empty rhetoric of soulless
Opposition politics, calling for more innovation, except we are delivering it; calling for
more skills, except we are delivering them; and calling for a bette r Budget, except we
are delivering it.
This Government has secured a Budget with a relentless focus on a strong economy
and jobs, a Budget that is continuing to invest to support families in need, a Budget that
is responsibly managing spending and revenue , and a Budget that is increasing our
resilience to global risk. This is a Budget that delivers a plan that is working, and the
Opposition is just delivering a mess.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBER TSON
items.text: What a pathetic bid for
the leadership of the ACT Party that was. I mean if you are going to do it, do it how
Maurice Williamson does it. There was only one person laughing after that: Judith
Collins. No one else over there was laughing, after that pathetic attempt.
Today I want to talk about a Budget that has two deficits in it —a deficit of money
and a deficit of ideas. Be very clear: Bill English being the Dipton version of Rip Van
Winkle and waking from his 7 -year slumber to suddenly decide that there is a problem
with poverty and there is a problem with the housing crisis does not make for a plan. It
does not make for a real plan to grow the New Zealand economy. There is a complete
deficit of ideas in here and, indeed, a deficit of money.
It is interesting because when the Government was challenged about the extent of its
support, in this case, for working families or for beneficiary families, Bill English was
heard to say: “Well, something’s better than nothing.” That is it now. That is the extent
of the aspiration of this National Government—something is better than nothing. That is
as good as it gets for New Zealanders from now on with the National Government —
something is better than nothing. The party that used to sa y it was ambitious for New
Zealand has now resigned itself to the level of the micro-managing and the tinkering.
Where are the opportunities for young New Zealanders to look at this Budget and
say: “There’s the chance for me to be a success. There’s the c hance for me to grow up
in a regional town in New Zealand, get a job, raise my family there, and buy a house.”?
Where is that in this Budget? All we saw was a Budget with its eye firmly on one thing:
3950 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
the 2017 election and promising tax cuts. Mark my words,  that is what this Budget is
about. Throw out $25 a week that, by all means, will be welcome in those households,
but that is the build -up to 2017. It is the build -up to once again —just as this National
Government did in 2010 —putting forward a package of t ax cuts designed to bribe and
win National an election, rather than dealing with the social and economic problems that
are in front of New Zealand today. It is irresponsible. It is a politician’s Budget; it is not
a Budget for the people of New Zealand.
But if we take a look at the deficit of money in this Budget, let us be clear. Yes,
National promised surpluses to New Zealand for 2014 -15. It promised that at two
elections. It promised that right throughout the last 4 or 5 years and it has completely
failed to deliver on that promise. But it is much worse than that, because what this
Budget does is kick the fiscal can down the road. Even in the optimistic scenario that
Treasury put up for New Zealand, we will see growth halved on an annual basis from
now through until 2019. That growth today is built on the shaky foundations of milk, of
selling houses in Auckland, and of recovering from disaster, but even that, in the
optimistic scenario, halves over the next period.
Debt as a percentage of GDP peaks in 20 16, but get this clear. Not a single cent of
the current $88 billion worth of debt will be paid off until 2019. That is the real casualty
of failing to post a surplus. It is the fact that future generations of New Zealanders are
again being saddled by a Na tional Government with huge levels of debt, and that is in
the optimistic scenario that Treasury is putting forward. We see exports remaining
stagnant at about 27 percent of GDP in the most optimistic scenario, and then today we
hear that dairy exports are  now down 27 percent compared with where they were last
April. We have got the largest current account deficit in 6 years.
These are the scenarios in which National would say good times are ahead for New
Zealand. But if we look into the detail of the Budg et, look at what is called the
downside scenario, included in the downside scenario is falling commodity prices. Let
us be realistic here. Everyone in the world is telling the National Government that dairy
prices will continue to fall. Last year Goldman S achs put out a report that said there is a
5-year glut in milk products being supplied into the global market, and commodity
prices will keep falling. It also says that there will be higher inflation. We have seen no
evidence of that. The Reserve Bank Governor cannot guarantee that.
In that scenario there will be no surplus next year. There will not be a surplus until
2018 in that scenario. There will not be any debt paid back before 2019 in that scenario.
In fact, the percentage of debt as a percentage of  GDP will be 26 percent —miles away
from where those members are now. The current account deficit hits 7.7 percent of GDP
in 2016-17 under that scenario.

items.speaker: The numbers in this Budget are clear
items.text: the economy is standing still in the best
scenario and going backwards in the worst scenario. That is the economic legacy of Bill
English and John Key kicking the fiscal can down the road. They made promises to
New Zealand that wages would go up by $7,000 and that there would be 140,000 more
jobs. They made that promis e last year. It was to happen in 2017. What they do in this
Budget, in the most optimistic of scenarios, is kick the can down the road to 2019. It is
always jam tomorrow, with Bill English. We are always on the cusp of something
special. The only something special in the National Government is Nick Smith and he is
very special indeed. We are always on the cusp of something special with Bill English,
and it never comes.
Government members like to crow about being the great economic managers. Well,
the reality is seven Budgets, seven deficits, no debt being paid back, and exports flat -
lining. There is no real growth, sustainable growth, in this economy going forward for
New Zealand under the settings of this Government and it is all done in a sacrifice at the
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3951
altar of tax cuts in 2017. That is irresponsible Government. That is irresponsible
management of the New Zealand economy.
So what should the Government have been doing in this Budget? Well, it should
have been investing in the regions of New Zealand. No doubt someone on the

items.speaker: Government side will get up and tell us
items.text: “No, there’s a great initiative in there. There
are the regional research institutes.” Well, to start with, there are only three of them and
it may have escaped members on the other side, but th ere are more than three regions.
The other thing is that the amount of money for them is pitiful. What it typifies is an
approach to economic development driven by Steven Joyce. We do not want to see
more money going to Steven Joyce’s mates, whom he talks to in the Koru Club. What
we want to see is real investment in the regions, making sure that we get alongside all of
regional New Zealand, and build on the strengths.
I was in Gisborne last week. There are people there doing amazing, innovative things
in engineering, in adding value to wood products. They need to be backed by a
Government, and that is what the Labour Government will do after 2017 —not pick
winners out of Steven Joyce’s rolodex, and not put Steven Joyce, who thinks a big night
out is at Skyc ity on the pokies, in charge of economic development. We need real
economic development in our regions. That was shockingly absent from this Budget.
Also shockingly absent from this Budget was a proper plan to diversify the New
Zealand economy. How long w ill this Government go on believing that it can simply
supply one product to one big customer and think that that is a proper strategy for the
New Zealand economy? We must have real initiatives to add value, but they were
absent from this Budget.
Then there is the housing crisis, where Bill English’s solution is to come up with a
tax that will not work —which he has acknowledged himself —and a housing
programme that Nick Smith has admitted today will not build even a fraction of the
houses that have been pro mised in Auckland. The failure of this Government to deal
with the housing crisis in New Zealand was emphasised by the fact that the Budget
documents did not even contain most of the housing initiatives because it was such a
panicked, last-minute reaction to being told off by the Reserve Bank Governor.
The biggest deficit in this Budget is not actually the deficit in the finances; it is the
deficit of ideas, the deficit of hope, and the deficit of opportunity for New Zealanders. A
young New Zealander today, with the world at their feet, will be looking at this Budget
and asking themselves: “What is here in New Zealand for me? What future is here?”.
New Zealanders deserve far, far better than a Budget that focuses so much on micro -
issues, that is so much abou t political management, and that breaks every promise that
has been made. New Zealanders deserve far better than this Budget, and they will get it
after 2017 with a Labour Government.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: It is great to be
participating in this Budget debate and to be part of a Government that is getting on and
addressing the issues that are important for New Zealanders. And it is even more of a
special privilege to be following Mr Grant Robertson. I have got a simple challenge for

items.speaker: Mr Robertson
items.text: tell me a single economic statistic that today is not better than when we
became the Government. Let us go through the list. How about we take—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Oh, an interruption.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I would like to respond to Dr Smith’s question. We can start with
debt—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: No, be seated. You cannot do that.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Let us look at inflation. At 0.1 percent it is the lowest figure
in over 17 years. Let us look at job growth. We have a Budget with 150,000 new jobs
3952 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
over the next 3 years. Unemployment has  come down from 5.8 percent to 4.5 percent
over the Budget period. Let us look at interest rates. When we came into Government,
they were 11 percent. Today, they are about 5.5 percent, and that matters for businesses
that are creating jobs and that matters  to New Zealanders wanting to own their own
home.
A Budget is about making choices, and this Government is making choices to back
children who are in hardship, and we say that that is the right response for New Zealand
at this time. This is a Budget that puts more money into important services like health
and education, whether it be for cancer treatment, or improving educational standards in
early childhood centres, in our schools, and in our tertiary institutions.
I was appalled—appalled—to hear Mr Grant Robertson say that there was nothing in
this Budget for the regions. Well, let us do a test. For most of us who represent
regions—and there is a good number of those members in the House today —we know
that irrigation offers opportunities for areas like t hat of my colleague the MP for
Kaikōura, in Hurunui, and for my area, on the Waimea Plains. And what has the Labour
Party said about irrigation? Every step of the way it has opposed the Government
providing support for rural communities to grow their irrig ation, and it has opposed the
reforms to the Resource Management Act that will enable those irrigation schemes to
come on stream. Was it not interesting listening to the Mayor of Westport? If there was
ever a region that was in difficulty, it is that one. What did the Mayor of Westport say
was the most important thing for his community in Buller? It was increased
communications, broadband, and cellphone services, which we provided for in this
Budget, and members opposite had the audacity to vote against the  bill that would
enable us to deliver for a community that is having a difficult time.
The part that I just find so shallow about Opposition contributions to this Budget
debate is that those members complain that there is not enough money for this, that, and
everything. The Labour members oppose any steps in the Budget to generate additional
revenue, and then they whinge about the surplus. Those members obviously did not get
to year 1 mathematics and learn how a Budget makes up those choices. Then we had the
clangers—the clangers —from Andrew Little. The big priority for Labour —the issue
that has got to make the difference —is gender reassignment surgery. I do not know
about my colleagues on this side of the House, but all the time we get bailed up in the
corner and asked: “What’s the Government doing about gender reassignment surgery.”!
That is the No. 1 priority for members opposite, and they wonder why they are down in
the polls.
But the clanger—the real clanger—for Labour came the day after the Budget. Th ose
members will look back on the career of Mr Little and identify his post -Budget speech
as the beginning of the end for his period as leader. With just a few words he has
undermined the security of 600,000 retirees in our country. Let me quote what he sa id:
“I cannot commit to New Zealand superannuation being universal.” That is, word for
word, what he said. Does Jacinda Ardern agree with Mr Little’s statement? Does
Annette King agree with their leader’s statement? As the Prime Minister said, there are
only three options for Labour in respect of its statements about superannuation: is it
going to raise the age, is it going to means test, or is it going to reduce the level of the
entitlement? I challenge the next member from Labour on their feet to give bac k to
those New Zealand superannuitants some idea of what their entitlements are to be if we
are to ever have a Labour Government again. I had a call from my electorate chairman
at the weekend. He said that with Mr Little’s comments on superannuation, he wa s
feeling more optimistic than ever about National’s prospects of winning a fourth term.
Let me come to the issue of good fiscal management. Let me give the numbers. Five
Budgets ago, there was a deficit of $18 billion. In the Budget after that, Bill Engl ish got
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3953
it down to $9 billion. In the Budget after that, it was down to $5 billion. In the one after
that, it was down to $3 billion, and the latest estimate for this year is for a deficit of only
$0.6 billion, or 1.3 percent of Government expenditure.
Last week I tried to table in Parliament the official figures from the Parliamentary
Library on the record of different Governments in terms of comparing their Budgets
with the actual results. I am not surprised that the Labour Party objected to the
document being tabled. So let me explain to the House what it says. How accurate was
the previous Labour Government in its predictions of surpluses and deficits? Well, the
numbers are that over its nine Budgets it was, on average, out by 4 percent. Well, Mr
English was out by 1.4 percent. If we take the very last Labour Budget, Labour
members stood on their feet and promised a surplus of $1.3 billion. Do you know what
we actually got? We got a deficit of $3.9 billion. Labour was out by $5 billion. How
dare members opposite get to their feet and criticise Bill English, our Minister of
Finance, for being out by only 1 percent? They know in their hearts that this is a good
outcome.
