Let us talk about some of the initiatives and the way in which they benefit my own
home community in Nelson. This Budget means $4 million more going to the families
on the lowest incomes in my Nelson constituency. There are 1,300 people on benefits in
Nelson who are going to benefit by $25 per week. There are another 2,200 families on
low incomes in my electorate who are going to benefit by $25 per week.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: When?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: There are 6,000 children in the lowest -income families in
my electorate who are going to benefit from this Bu dget. The member asks when. I say
to the member that it is 43 years since a Government increased the base level of
benefits, and I am proud to be part of a National Government that has delivered it and
delivered alongside it increasing—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: —requirements for work, and alongside that this Budget
provides for 150,000 additional jobs over coming years. There have been comments
about levies. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Take a breath.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Let me give an example of one. This Budget provides for a
$200 per car reduction in ACC levies—a $200 reduction in ACC levies.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Who put them up?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: That is a good question. Mr Mallard asks who put them up.
I will tell you who. In July 2008 the Labour Government put the ACC levy on cars up
by 50 bucks, and we are a Government that is reducing it b y $200 per car, and that will
be welcome relief for the 2.4 million car owners across our country.
I could talk of the very constructive measures in this Budget to improve New
Zealand’s management of water and to improve our management of the Resource
Management Act. I could talk at length about so many initiatives in this Budget that
provide for the issues that matter to New Zealand, and that is why members on this side
of the House have been so strongly supporting the best Budget I have seen in my 25 -
year career.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Before I call the next member, can I just encourage
members to take a breath. It is going to be a long debate. It will be robust, no doubt, and
it is a lot easier if people make their interje ctions rare and reasonable, and, hopefully,
witty, as a previous Labour Speaker indicated should be the case. I call Dr Russel
Norman—sorry; the Hon Nick Smith has a point of order.
3954 Budget Debate 26 May 2015

items.text: I apologise to Russel
Norman. I seek leave of the House to table a document covering the last 20 Budgets,
prepared by Grant Cleland from the Parliamentary Library—

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: I rise to speak on the Budget.
Before I begin, I would just like to say to National Party members and Labour Party
members that the jokes about gender reassignment surgery are pretty disgusting. They
are ugly, and I think they should stop.
I would like to start by acknowledging the positive dimensions of the Budget. I
would like to identify four particular parts of it. The first is the benefit increases above
inflation. I think that they are important. I think th at they are real. There is no question
that they are not enough. There is no question that they have been abated and partially
taken back by the changes forcing parents to go to work when their children are only
3—that is appalling. But it is also true tha t the benefit increases are good. Breaking the
ground and saying that benefits should increase ahead of inflation because of the terrible
poverty in our country  is, I think, a good thing. I acknowledge the work of Child
Poverty Action Group and all those w ho have campaigned on poverty for so many
years.
The second area that I would like to acknowledge is the introduction of a capital
gains tax and the foreign buyers tax identity changes. The introduction of a capital gains
tax, I think, is a very positive m ove. Obviously, 2 years is too short, as are the other
limitations around it. I would particularly like to congratulate David Cunliffe and David
Parker, who  provided, along with the Green Party, the momentum to actually get a
capital gains tax introduced, and over time it will be regularised and made more
sensible, as it should be. I think that those two initiatives —the increase in benefits and
the capital gains tax —are ones that the Green Party has also campaigned on for many
years, and we are very pleased to see them, as limited as they are.
Thirdly, I would like to identify the user -pays airport charges. I think that they are
important. Biosecurity is an important issue for New Zealand, and this is a good way to
fund it.
Fourthly, I would like to congratu late National on abandoning the fetish around the
surplus that characterised its election campaign. It was always ridiculous the way that
National characterised the surplus as the defining feature of prudent economic
management, and I think Bill English ha s now acknowledged that. I wish that he had
done so during the election campaign.
Aside from the good elements of the Budget —and there are some —there are,
unfortunately, many other elements of the Budget that are quite bad. Let me start with
climate change. We now have about 421 billion tonnes of ice being lost each year from
the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets as a result of climate change. We are losing
about 421 billion tonnes as the planet warms. The south Antarctic Peninsula ice sheet is
starting to  break up. This is the greatest challenge on the face of the planet facing
humanity right now, and, unfortunately, this Government is accelerating New Zealand’s
emissions rather than cutting them. When we look at an economy like New Zealand’s,
which is dep endent on a stable climate, and when we look at the floods in Wellington
and the drought in Canterbury—the 2013 drought, which had such a big impact on New
Zealand—we can see that New Zealand should be at the forefront of taking action to
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3955
reduce emissions and taking action on climate change. An economy like ours is
particularly susceptible to extreme weather events like floods and droughts and the
changes that are coming our way as a result of our increased greenhouse gas emissions
globally.
When we look at what New Zealand is doing, it is actually shameful. New Zealand’s
gross emissions increased 20 percent from 1990 to 2013. New Zealand’s net greenhouse
gas emissions increased by 42 percent from 1990 to 2013. I think it is worth dwelling on
how amazingly i rresponsible we have been as a country. Increasing our net emissions
by 42 percent from 1990 to 2013 is an incredibly irresponsible thing to do, and there is
no getting away from that. The Ministry for the Environment has produced forward
projections that say that New Zealand plans to increase its net emissions by a further 50
percent in the next 10 years. So not only have we increased our net emissions by 42
percent over this period but, looking forward, the Ministry for the Environment’s
projections say t hat New Zealand’s net greenhouse gas emissions will increase by a
further 50 percent in just one decade. That is an incredibly, grossly irresponsible thing
to do, and future generations will curse us for it, as they rightly should.
The reason why these emi ssions are increasing is that we have policy settings
designed to increase emissions. Since this Government got into office, it has gutted the
emissions trading scheme, which was meant to put a price on greenhouse emissions in
order to be an effective econ omic instrument to drive down greenhouse emissions.
Every economic report you read tells you very clearly that the most effective way to do
this is to put a price on emissions. That has an effect right across an economy and
reduces emissions. Unfortunately , when this Government got in, it gutted the key
elements of the emissions trading scheme. We now have the emissions trading scheme
as a major liability for the New Zealand Government. It is projected in the
Government’s papers that the cost of the emissio ns trading scheme to the Government,
because the subsidies to pollution are now so large, is $684 million of taxpayer
spending over 2 years. So we plan to subsidise greenhouse pollution via the emissions
trading scheme —the system that is supposed to cut po llution—to the tune of $684
million in just 2 years. That is the subsidy that taxpayers are giving to climate polluters
in New Zealand. The subsidy since the scheme started now totals $859 million of
taxpayers’ money that has been given to polluters via th e emissions trading scheme.
That is not a scheme designed to cut emissions; that is a scheme designed to increase
emissions.
Treasury has tried to estimate what the cost of the failure to cut greenhouse gas
emissions will be to the New Zealand public. Its estimate is that our failure to cut
greenhouse gas emissions means that we are going to have to buy carbon credits
offshore. Depending on the cost of those carbon credits, Treasury says that it could cost
us up to $52 billion to buy offshore  carbon credits  to cover the big increases in
emissions coming out of the New Zealand economy, because all the policy settings are
set up to increase emissions. We are going to have to buy carbon credits offshore.
Treasury says that it could cost up to $52 billion of tax payers’ money to buy those
offshore carbon credits because we have increased our emissions so radically over this
period. Do we really want to spend $52 billion buying offshore carbon credits that may
be worthless—but, you know, they make the grade for acc ounting purposes—or would
we rather spend that money in New Zealand to reduce our own emissions? The
Government’s answer to that is very clear. It would prefer to buy offshore carbon
credits because its plan is to increase emissions. I think that is incred ibly irresponsible
and stupid. It is hard, really, to characterise how stupid it is for a Government to have a
whole bunch of policy settings to increase emissions and then to spend $50 billion
buying worthless hot air offshore. That is an amazingly short-sighted and stupid policy.
3956 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
The thing is, it is not just the emissions trading scheme. Of course, there are
subsidies in many sectors in New Zealand to increase emissions. Just think of the dairy
sector. If you are in the dairy sector, you do not pay for yo ur methane emissions  or
nitrous oxide emissions. The taxpayer covers the cost of those for you. They are free to
the dairy sector. Plus, you get free fresh water. You do not have to pay any charge for
the water. You get free water pollution. There is no ch arge when you pollute a stream.
You do not have to pay anything to dispose of that polluted water. As the Government
crowed about in question time today, there are very large  subsidies to expand the dairy
sector—the irrigation subsidies, which is $400 mill ion of subsidies going directly into
the dairy sector in order to expand it so that its emissions will increase and water quality
will decline. It is an amazingly short -sighted policy to spend that much money to
increase pollution.
Then, of course, beyond that, we have the poor old forestry sector —the forestry
sector sequesters our carbon and actually reduces our net emissions. Because the price
of carbon emissions is so low in New Zealand now, the forestry sector is cutting down a
larger area of trees than  it is replanting. As a result of the Government’s policies, the
forestry sector is now a net emitter in New Zealand.
Then we have the subsidies for road freight and road transport. Literally tens of
billions of dollars are given to motorways and road freight companies for free so that we
can increase emissions coming out of the roading sector.
Then we have the subsidies  for fossil fuel exploration. The Government is very keen
on, and very proud of, the high level of subsidies that  it provides to oil explor ation
companies in order to look for fossil fuels. So we are subsidising that as well. Is it any
wonder that Fonterra is literally building coal-fired boilers right now, in the 21st century,
when we should be cutting emissions? Fonterra, which does not see m to care in the
slightest about its global brand, is building coal -fired boilers in New Zealand. Is it any
wonder that the rail network is talking about removing electrification from the main
trunk line? Could anything signify more how backward and mid - 20th century we have
become at the beginning of the 21 st century than the rail industry talking not about
electrifying the rail network but about de -electrifying the rail network in New Zealand?
We are so out of the loop about what is going on in the world , in terms of the smart
green economic revolution that is taking the whole of the rest of the world by storm. In
New Zealand we are determined to drive back to the mid - 20th century. We are going to
have coal. We are going to have motorways. We are going to subsidise oil exploration.
We are going to get rid of electrification on rail because “Oh, who wants that
electrification stuff?”.
That is the reality of where climate policy has got to in our country, and it is a total,
total disaster. New Zealand can embrace the smart Green economic revolution, we can
be part of this global change, we can do the right thing by our kids, but we need the
Government to change direction.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Just before I begin the substance
of my contribution, can I just pick up on a comment that Dr Nick Smith made. He said
that a budget is about choice, and I would agree with him. Every budget is about choice.
One prioritises what is important —whether it be  for a company, a family’s household
budget, or a Government’s Budget, for example. So it is worthy of note that this
Government chose to prioritise $25 million for a flag referendum that nobody actually
wants, but chose—

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Speak for yourself.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: —to make orphans and unsupported children wait until 2018 ,
Mr Macindoe, for the clothing allowance. So that is the choice that this Government
made. It decided that a $25 million flag referendum that 84 to 90 p ercent of New
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3957
Zealand does not want —but it is their money —was more important than providing a
clothing allowance for orphans and unsupported children being raised by kin carers . So
I agree with Dr Nick Smith. The Government made choices and it will be judg ed by
those choices.
Now—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: “Ne-ow.”

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: —I think probably the first thing we have got here—obviously
Mr Finlayson does not like my contribution, either. You are getting snark y there, Mr
Finlayson. If one wants to put this Budget into context, one actually has to look at the
last six Budgets. I am going to hedge some bets here and say that National has actually
had a really clever strategy over the last 6 years, coming into thi s year’s Budget. I think
we can see it by the cuts that were made between 2009 and 2012. Just one example
would be the choices that were made way back in 2009. Back in 2009 this Government
wiped $400 million out of early childhood education. It wiped it out in a Budget back in
2009—$400 million out of early childhood education. In this Budget it has provided
$75 million over the next 4 years. How lovely —that is great. But it does not go
anywhere near the amounts that it withdrew.
Let us talk about the trai ning incentive allowance that this Government removed
from single-parent students. That had a value of approximately $4,500 a year. In this
Budget single-parent - family students will get $25 a week. That is lovely. That is about
$1,000. The Government jus t takes away and lets the people stay out there under
hardship just long enough so that when it throws them some crumbs, they are incredibly
grateful. It is a brilliant plan and this Government has done it very, very well over the
last 6 years. It keeps announcing these incremental positives, hoping all the time that the
New Zealand public will not remember the negatives. Thank goodness New Zealand
First is here to actually remind them.
The other thing that we have seen in recent days is, again, around edu cation and
some new schools that are being built. That is wonderful. You have to build new
schools when you have got a huge number of people coming into the country in net
migration numbers. Their children deserve an education like everybody else’s childre n,
and so, therefore, you have to increase the education budget to build new schools. It
seems sensible. It is unfortunate when one member of the Government does not know
that a school in his own electorate is going to be shifted and actually has to go and  ask a
Minister in his own Government —and he is a member outside Cabinet himself —but
nobody bothered to tell him that under this Budget a kura in his electorate was going to
be shifted from where it is now to a camping ground in his electorate. So he has t o go
public and actually ask, in a public fashion, whether he can know, please, what his own
Government and party are doing. I think that shows that the left hand does not quite
know what the right hand is doing. There are obviously some people who are on the
inside, and some people who are on the outside.
Perhaps that is punishment for that particular Minister for the advice he gave around
Novopay. It was that Minister who gave advice to Hekia Parata, saying: “It’s fine. Go
with Novopay. No, they didn’t me et their key performance indicators. No, they didn’t.
And, yes, there are about 147 glitches still in it and, no, we have not run a trial, but I’m
advising you, go ahead. Go ahead, Minister. Let’s roll it out.” So, now, let us take a
look at Novopay. There is $53 million in this Budget for the continuation of trying to fix
that lemon called Novopay. The increase in this Budget to the operations grant for State
schools over the next 4 years is $42 million. That equates to about $10.7 million per
year for the  next 4 years for the operations grant increase for State schools —around
about 1 percent. Power bills have increased by 3.6 percent in the same time frame, but
that grant increase is about 1 percent. Novopay is going to get $53 million from this
3958 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
Budget; State schools will get $42 million. You do not have to be very bright to figure
out the maths, and that is probably why it works over there for the Government. So this
is an interesting, interesting Budget, because you have to drill down past the spin and
the rhetoric and the marketing dollars that have been put here and actually have a look
across the last 6 years to see what this Budget does.
Here is another thing. This is from another press release from the Minister of
Education. There is about $62.9 mill ion of operating funding over the next 4 years. Of
that, $39.5 million is going to go to provide ongoing resourcing scheme support for
about 500 extra students. That is lovely. There are more students, of course. There are
more students in our schools. Tha t is why we are building two more schools. So,
actually, it is not more support for current students; it is actually an increase in budget
because we have got more students.
The next thing we have got is that this is going to pay for specialists such as s peech
language therapists, psychologists, physiotherapists, and occupational therapists. That
would be brilliant—brilliant—except we have not got enough of them. We have not got
enough of them because support has been withdrawn from our student body, from our
tertiary education provision, and these are not target areas. We now have a shortage
through that withdrawal of support and bad workforce planning, so we do not have
enough speech language therapists when schools call for them. We do not have enough
psychologists. So now when schools reach out trying to help the young people in their
schools—because now we have got a wraparound service and the resource teachers of
learning and behaviour have all been shifted off to goodness knows where —and they
reach ou t for psychologists, for example, you cannot get one to show up. You have
organisations like Marinoto—and I am not being flippant —telling schools that unless a
child has a rope around their neck, do not call it. That is how bad it is out there. That is
how bad it is. That is how short-staffed we are.
Supposedly, however, this Budget is going to fix it. There is $23.3 million for extra
in-class teacher aide support for 1,500 students in special needs education, such as those
with dyslexia. The Dyslexia Foun dation tells us that there are up to 70,000
schoolchildren who actually are affected by dyslexia —one in 10 New Zealanders —and
this funding is going to help 1,500 students. This once -over-lightly sprinkle of
assistance devalues the need that is out there. I t is crumbs from a quite well -laden table
when you have a look at the priorities that this Government has decided. There is
absolutely nothing in this Budget for professional development for the early recognition
of dyslexia, dyspraxia, or Asperger’s syndr ome when those students show up at school.
There is absolutely nothing in this Budget to provide extra support for early childhood
education, early identification, and professional development.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Special needs and early childhood are up.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: There is absolutely nothing in this Budget. In 2009, the gifted
and talented funding was taken away, Mr Macindoe . In 2009 the advisory groups were
disbanded. In 2009 targeting funding for innovative programmes around talent
development initiatives was abandoned. There is nothing in this report for gifted and
talented children. Where is the tagged funding for gifted and talented children? This
Government, which came in saying it had aspirational goals for our students, removed
the category “well above” from national standards. I do not even like national standards,
but how aspirational is it that apparently no longer is anybody going to be “well
above”? You are either “well below”, “below”, “at”, or “above”, but there is nothing for
gifted and talented children. Again, there is nothing for gifted and talented children in
this Budget.
I could go on. I have got a few mo re minutes; I will go on. The reality of this Budget
and 6 years’ worth of work by this Government is a shift of the cost around our free to
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3959
the end-user primary and secondary education. It is now being passed on to our parents.
This is the reality of this  Government’s Budgets over the last 6 years. If parents want to
go and have a look, they will see that at the same time they freeze the parental threshold
allowance where students can actually get some assistance so they can eat. It is a very
interesting Budget, people—drill down into it. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: The previous speaker, Tracey
Martin, said she was going to do some intro, then she was g oing to get into the
substance. Well, I am standing here still waiting for her to come to the substance of that
particular commentary on the Budget. But I guess we will still be waiting. Before I
begin, I just note that this morning I went to the Memorial Day service, noting those
who have fallen in service for the United States. It is a public holiday there today, like
with our recent Anzac and Gallipoli reflections in New Zealand. Actually, it was a very
good reminder of the friendship we have, and those we stand side by side with around
the world to protect the values that we all cherish and the price that has been paid over
many, many years for the freedoms and the values that we have in New Zealand and
that allow us to have free and open debate in forum s such as this. I think it is very
important never to forget—lest we forget.
Budget No. 7 —Bill English’s Budget No. 7. I did not think it would get better than
the last one, but I said that the last time as well. Actually, it is. Budget No. 7 continues
the core part of managing our finances prudently—a fiscally responsible Budget making
the hard calls for medium and long -term sustainability, if you want, or vibrancy for our
economy, rather than the short -term inclinations that some members in the House kee p
wanting us to go back to. Actually, I did mean to say when Mr Norman was speaking
earlier that if it is really as bad as he seemed to make out and if life is so terrible and
everything is as tragic as he seemed to be implying that it was, well, actually,  step out
into the real world, because any indicator, be it well -being, the happiness index,
confidence, or an economic -type matrix, is actually very, very good and solid, trending
in the right way. A little bit of a word to the Opposition —if you like, a w ord of advice.
Those members do not have to take it, but if you stay negative and you will stay
negative polling. Be positive, be aspirational, as we are with New Zealanders, for New
Zealanders, and perhaps their prospects will improve somewhat.
There has been a change. There has been a shift in our economy. Yes, it has been
gradual and incremental, but there has been a fundamental shift in the public’s
expectation of how we run the Crown finances and the environment that we are dealing
with today. For exa mple, there has been quite a bit of discussion about the fact that we
have almost zero percent inflation —zero point something. It is as good as zero percent
inflation. It is phenomenally good for consumers, it is good for our economy with
inflation not bei ng corrosive on wealth, but we also have about 2.83 percent growth
forecast. In fact we had 3.8 percent last year. I just say that right now we have near zero
percent inflation, last year we had about 3.8 percent growth, I think we have about 2.8
percent forecast through this Budget, and floating mortgage rates are around 5.5 to 6
percent. That is the real world passing judgment, if you like, on how we are managing
its finances and its balance sheets, and on how we are managing the economy.
Our only test o f another regime running our economy —say, the last Labour Budget
or the financials or the economic matrix when it was last in Government in 2008. It is
an interesting contrast. For some of it I still cannot work out how it managed to achieve
it. It is worth reminding us what happens with ill -disciplined, endless spending, endless
revenue-gathering, with productivity disappearing through the economy and inflation
absolutely—by theft almost —taking wealth from New Zealanders. For example, in
2008 the Consumers  Price Index was nudging 5 percent. The Consumers Price Index
was 5 percent. It seems unheard of now, because now it is around zero percent. It was 5
3960 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
percent, and that was pumped up by the revenue gathering, borrowing, and spending of
the previous administ ration. That is not a number I have made up. That is the number
that it was. I think most people in the House would agree that ongoing inflation is not
good for our economy or for our families. But anyway that is what it was —5 percent—
and it is now about zero percent.
And yet another metric —actually when National came into Government, New
Zealand had been in recession for about 1 year, which was 1 year earlier than the global
financial crisis and of course that hit at around the same time. But right now we  have
had over 3 percent growth. We have zero percent inflation and about 3 -plus percent
growth, versus 5 percent inflation and a recession under Labour. It is interesting how
those can be true. How does that play out for our families? Well, the simple mea sure or
comparison is their mortgage. For most families, the highest and largest expense in their
household budget is, in fact, funding their mortgages. Well, a mortgage is now around
5.5 to 6 percent, yet at the time when inflation was around 5 percent, t he country was in
recession and mortgages were around double figures, at 10 percent. I say to those
listeners on the radio or watching on TV, or members in the House, imagine if your own
mortgage was now 10 percent. You would probably be paying out almost double on a
mortgage what you do now, because it is now 5.5 to 6 percent. That is very interesting.
Even though many members opposite talk about the housing situation in Auckland —
and that has been well canvassed, I guess —actually, the horror thought is if a Labour
Government were running the show at the moment and it continued where it left off.
Remember, inflation was near 5 percent, mortgages were in double digits—at near 10
percent—and the country was in recession. In fact the export sector had been in
recession for about 4 or 5 years.
There is much in this Budget for small business. I could talk about the framework or
the cost. I could talk about the cost of working capital, for example, or cash -flow
management. You see, under a Labour Government, when floor inflation is around 5
percent, and when mortgage interest rates are around 10 percent, the cost of working
capital for our businesses is so much higher. Yet when we have near zero percent
inflation and mortgages at around 5 or 6 percent, the cost of running a business, of
being an entrepreneur, and of taking a risk under the National Government is
diametrically, totally, absolutely opposite and more beneficial to those business owners
and to New Zealand than it would be under a Labour Government. Ther e is nothing
subjective about those numbers.
For example, low inflation and stable interest rates all impact on and help our
families and our businesses, of course. The $500 million in ACC levy cuts benefits our
small businesses. In fact, that is on top o f the $1.5 billion in levy cuts already locked in
over previous Budgets. The tax cuts we had a few years ago —lowering company tax,
adjusting personal taxes, and rebalancing —all benefit our small businesses, particularly
our small -business families who are,  of course, those who are funding the small
businesses. The tyranny of distance has been smashed —not only international distance
but domestically the tyranny of domestic distance has been smashed. For example,
Kiwibank is now operating one of its back offi ces in Hastings in the Hawke’s Bay. The
150 to 200 new jobs in Hastings in the Hawke’s Bay would not have been possible
unless there was an ultra -fast broadband fibre roll -out across New Zealand. That is the
magic of empowering companies to have another lo ok at the regions, making an
economic analysis and evaluation themselves, and creating jobs in the regions. We are
going to see more and more like that. The New Zealand Business Number continues to
be rolled out, and there is money in the Budget to help facilitate that.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Ha, ha! More red tape.
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3961

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: The member may laugh. I would be interested to know whether
it is Labour policy to stop the New Zealand Business Number. If the member laughs at
the New  Zealand Business Number, he is laughing at the 1.1 million businesses that
already have it. The member is laughing at about 500,000 businesses that are looking to
take it up. I would be interested to hear from other speakers whether in fact it is now
Labour policy to cancel the New Zealand Business Number, which will be fully
implemented for Government agencies by 2017.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: You’re just making stuff up.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: No, I am not making it up. I am asking the question because the
member laughs—he laughs loudly—at the New Zealand Business Number and disputes
it. I ask whether the Labour Opposition supports and endorses the New Zealand
Business Number and all the benefits it creates, such as productivity, or othe r, for New
Zealand businesses, families, and our economy. It would be interesting to get that
clarification. I would welcome it if it does come. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: I would be delighted to provide
some of the clarification that that member, the Hon Craig Foss, asked for. He asked
about the New Zealand Business Number. We have supported that legislation to the
select committee, but we do have so me reservations. We know that his own
Government departments have been squabbling over whether it is really possible and
whether it is not just another overhead on small business. His Government has been
responsible for so many overheads on small business that it is not funny. Even his own
Government departments, which he likes to beat up on, want fewer overheads on small
business. They are suspicious that this Government is introducing another overhead and
one that it cannot even deliver on properly with t he New Zealand Business Number.
Time will tell. We will see what small businesses think about it. We will ask the Inland
Revenue Department why it does not think businesses can use their Inland Revenue
Department number, which would be a much simpler and m ore cost-effective way of
solving the same problem. But I am sure that member will have a reason.
He always has a reason. He has a reason for his overcharging on ACC levies. He has
a reason for why the Rural Broadband Initiative has reached only 8,500 hou seholds,
despite costing over $60 million —that is $7,000 per connection. He will have a reason
for the Government not reaching surplus, for the seventh year in a row. He will have a
reason for why exchange rates are much higher and say that the Government can do
nothing about it. He will have a reason for the flag being the top priority for New
Zealand. He will have a reason and an excuse —members on that side of the House
always do. They always have excuses. We heard plenty of them in the Budget. We
heard plenty of excuses. That member has gone surprisingly silent. I will listen for any
further interjections from him. There are none from that member over there. In fact, it is
difficult to even pick him out. He seems to have crawled under his desk.
This is a  Government of broken promises. This is a Budget of broken promises. I
guess, at least, it is in theme. Let us have a look at some of the ones that the
Government has delivered recently. National told us that its central campaign promise,
going into this recent election, was reaching Budget surplus. Has it delivered on that? It
has not—it has not. It has failed again for the seventh Budget in a row. National said it
would not put up GST. John Key himself said he would never put up GST. Where is it
now? It i s at 15 percent —a broken promise. He said that the Government would
increase wages by $7,000 by the end of next year. Now it is saying it will be 2019. The
Government said it would increase the number of jobs. Now it is saying that is being
pushed out to 2019 as well. This is a Government of broken promises.
In this Budget we have seen the Government give with one hand and take with
another. We have seen some sensible steps towards making sure that beneficiaries have
3962 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
a little more money in their pockets—making sure some beneficiaries will. We have got
to remember that income-related rents will be offset against it. I would not be surprised
if the next trick is to try to look at them, so that there is a zero -sum game in the next
Budget. We will see. We will see where it goes with that.
These things that the Government has introduced have come at the expense of New
Zealanders just a couple of rungs further up the ladder. It is robbing Peter to pay Paul. It
has told us that 500,000 New Zealanders will miss out  on the $1,000 KiwiSaver kick -
start payment. That is what it told us in this Budget. That is how it is trying to get to
surplus, and it is failing, by the way. That is how it is trying to get closer, to make it
look not as bad as it otherwise would look —by robbing the future savings of young
New Zealanders.
This is a Government that is looking at the here and now, and not at New Zealand’s
savings future. We on this side of the House know that it is so important to have money
for investment—for investment i n new ideas, for investment in small business, and for
savings so that we can grow our economy over time. The Australian scheme, which it
started after the Kirk Government’s superannuation savings scheme, now has A$1.3
trillion in it. The Muldoon Governmen t canned ours. Now we see the exact same
behaviour from John Key’s Government. It has made seven cuts to KiwiSaver in its
time—seven cuts. It is going down the same track as Muldoon’s Government.
In fact, when it comes to borrowing, it is doing worse. We learnt from the Budget
that we are $88 billion in debt under this Government. New Zealanders now pay
through their taxes about $10 million a day just in interest payments.

items.speaker: Hon Nanaia Mahuta
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: It is $10 million a day in interest payments. That is where this
Government has taken us with debt. It is a Government with no vision for the future,
which is borrowing for today. The Financial Services Council said of the KiwiSaver
cuts that this is like rob bing the kid’s piggy bank to head down to the pub for a beer.
That is the kind of vision we have from this Government. It is out of ideas, it is tired,
and, not just that, it is starting to hurt New Zealanders. That is starting to hurt kids in the
future.
Not one of the Government members was prepared to get up in the debate on
KiwiSaver and say that they had not taken the $1,000 for themselves and that they had
not arranged for the savings to be gathered by their children or their families. I hear the
member David Bennett grunting over there. I read somewhere, and he may like to verify
it himself, that he did not take the payment. I read this actually on Twitter. Somebody
was saying that that might be true. Maybe the member David Bennett is principled —he
is either principled or stupid, I think was the allegation in the Twitter sphere.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I request that the member
apologise for that last comment. I take offence at it.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: No, I think the member is a
robust member, and there was nothing in the suggestions that were being made that
offended the Standing Orders. I think that quotations from Twitter —and even if the
comment was made by the member—do not come close. I think that saying a member is
stupid is not a breach of the Standing Orders.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: So this is a Government that is breaking promises —promise
after promise after promise. Gover nment members might worry that somebody has
reported somewhere else that they are stupid. They should be more worried about
broken promises. That is what they should really be worried about.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! There are quite a
number of rulings that I think date back to the 19 th century that indicate that the
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3963
members do not go back to points of order once they have been ruled on. The member
just did that.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: This Government across from us has broken promises.
National, as a Government, needs to face the voters of New Zealand and answer the
question why it is that it has broken its central campaign promise —its central campaign
promise—to bring this Gover nment into surplus. It has promised it before in a
campaign. It is the seventh deficit in a row. If we contrast that with the last Labour
Government, which delivered nine surpluses in a row —nine surpluses in a row, not like
National’s seven deficits—we can see who might be the better manager of the economy.
Of course, in terms of economic development, the Government promised to diversify
the economy —well, it has not promised to do that. It has said that it will grow the
exports as a percentage of our overa ll economy. The Government said it would get that
figure to 40 percent. Well, it is now below 30 percent and it is going backwards —it is
around 27 percent. It is due to drop again next year, according to the Government’s own
forecast. The Government has failed to diversify the economy. This is a Government of
broken promises.
It is also interesting to note in this Budget Steven Joyce’s waning influence. We have
seen him over recent years play a significant role in negotiating many of the economic
development initiatives of this Government. In the 2013 Budget, he had six press
releases and $470 million worth of new spending. In last year’s Budget it went down to
four press releases and just $363 million worth of new spending —a cut of over $100
million on the  previous Budget. And in this one there is another $100 million cut. He
has only three press releases and $259 million in new spending. He is a Minister on the
wane.
The Government has seen the way in which he has handled the Skycity deal. We
have learnt again today that there is a 10 percent cut in the overall capacity of the centre.
We have seen a downsized Skycity convention centre. That is not what was promised. It
is another broken promise from this Government, a Government that said it would
deliver on a convention centre that was world class and iconic. Its own independent
report, which it commissioned, said the convention centre would create a net 18 full -
time equivalent jobs in New Zealand once it was built —18. That was with an
international, world-class, iconic one. The members for Hamilton should have answered
to their own constituents as to why it is sucking hundreds of jobs out of Hamilton, out
of Rotorua, and out of Taupō. This is a convention centre deal that will hurt the regions
and is not the world-class, iconic deal that was promised. The Government has put itself
over a barrel of its own making and Steven Joyce was right there in the midst of it.
This is a Government that is failing to deliver on its promises, on almost every
promise that it makes. It is a Government that is out of ideas, that is tired, and that is so
arrogant it does not think it needs to answer to the public any more on its decisions, and
it is a Government whose day of reckoning will come when New Zealanders stand up in
the next election and say: “We do not want to hear your broken promises any more.”

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: It gives me great pleasure to rise
in this debate and also t o follow that last speaker, David Clark, who came to Hamilton
some months ago and tried to debate economic policy in the Hamilton community. He
left with robust articles in the paper really just destroying his credibility and showing
the inane comments tha t come from that side of the House. They showed that that
member, who is supposed to be talking about economic development, actually has no
idea of what economic development is. Next time he comes to Hamilton, he will be
driving on those beautiful, new hig hways that we have built, he will be visiting those
beautiful, new schools that we have built, and he will be seeing that lovely, new hospital
3964 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
that we have built. He will see a university that has gone into Tauranga. He will see
broadband being delivered first of all in that city, and around the country.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I feel like I have entered into a
battle of wits with an unarmed opponent.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will
take a seat, and now he will apologise for that comment. If he has really got a point of
order, he will make it.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: I withdraw and apologise.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker, and a very good Assistant
Speaker we have as well in doing that, because that member has got—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It was not 5 minutes
ago when I told the member who raised the point of order that he was not allowed to
comment on rulings. It does not matter whether it is a positive or a negative comment —
the member is not to comment.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: That member came to Hamilton and tried out the Labour
economic policy and was resoundingly told where to go, just like the Labour Party
members are resoundingly told where to go all the time when they come into this House
with their economic policy.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Arrogant, out of touch.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: They are saying “out of touch”. Well, let us have a look at
being out of touch. I remember that member’s speech last weekend when we were
talking about KiwiSaver. He s aid: “Let’s give $1,000 to everybody who signs up to
KiwiSaver.” His exact words were: “The reason to do that is because it will make
people feel better.” Those were his exact words. That is the economic policy from
somebody on that side. Why do we not jus t make it $10,000, if it will make people feel
better? What about those people out there who stand and work for 60 years in hard
labour, working in hard jobs, who will be made to feel better when they sign up but who
will actually lose money because the Labour Opposition wants to means test them when
they come to get their superannuation, and it wants to make sure they do not get their
superannuation until they are 70? Go out there and tell somebody working on the farms
and in the factories of New Zealand t oday that when you are 18, we are going to put
$1,000 into some account to make you feel better, but you are going to have to work
until you are 70. You are going to have to stay in that job, when you have done 50 or 60
years of hard labour in that work. G o and see how that goes down with those people.
That is the reality of what you are saying.
Look at the statistics around KiwiSaver. The Inland Revenue Department put out a
report on Saturday and it showed that 38 percent of people who signed up for
KiwiSaver never make another contribution —38 percent of people who sign up for
KiwiSaver just take the 1,000 bucks because they know it is a gift from the
Government. That is the kind of thing we do not need to do as a country. Those are the
statistics. Read th e report. It also says that two -thirds of the people who should be in
KiwiSaver—the bottom income earners —are not in KiwiSaver. The people who are in
KiwiSaver are the upper and middle income earners, and 38 percent of them are just
taking the $1,000.
That is the great economic policy of the Labour Party —make them feel good, make
them happy, we will give them another $1,000. Well, that is $500 million you have to
find in the next election campaign, and that is $500 million that Grant Robertson
promised without going through his caucus. That is $500 million that we could spend on
vulnerable children and vulnerable families. That is $500 million that we could spend
on infrastructure to make sure the people of Hamilton get what they deserve and what
they want.  They know what they want, and they want that infrastructure so they can
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3965
grow. They want to have that ability to look after the people in their communities who
are in the most need. For 43 years —43 years—the Labour Party has been in this House
and not delivered for those people.
The Labour members will talk about Muldoon. They go back to Muldoon. Well,
there has been a Labour Government or two between now and Muldoon, and they did
not do anything in that time. They did not bring in a savings plan.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: It’s called KiwiSaver, you idiot.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: They did not bring it in to the same extent that you were
talking about here, as a compulsory savings scheme —that is what David Clark was
talking about. That was not bro ught in. There was no compulsory savings scheme. So
they can go back to Muldoon, but that is not the reality. When they had a chance they
did not do anything.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: What do you call the Cullen fund? What do you think the Cullen
fund was?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: There is Mr Goff there now —he is another economic genius.
He would know all about these things, would he not? He is still trying to work out
things about foreign affairs, let alone economics, so we would like to hear h is opinion
on this.
But 2 weeks ago there was a Budget delivered in Australia. In the country right
beside us, called the Lucky Country, guess what its deficit was? It was A$41.1 billion.
Guess what New Zealand’s deficit is? It is NZ$684 million. GDP grow th in Australia is
under 3 percent; in New Zealand it is over 3 percent —under 3 percent there, over 3
percent here. In 2014 we grew faster than the US, the UK, and Japan. Net migration is
positive in New Zealand for the first time. People are staying. Peop le are coming here
because they believe in this country, they believe in this Government, and they believe
in what we stand for. The unemployment rate in Australia is over 6 percent; in New
Zealand it is under 6 percent. All the economic statistics stack up in our favour—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: What about the latest ones?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: —because we have come through the recession, we have come
through rebuilding Christchurch, and we have delivered the best for New Zealanders.
That member there will talk about economic policy and he will go back to the Muldoon
days. I say to those members—and do not let anybody in New Zealand forget this —that
the Labour Government put New Zealand into recession before the rest of the world.
Before the global financial crisis even came along, the Labour Government had New
Zealand in a recession. It had 10 years of huge deficits ahead for this country. It
destroyed this country’s economic potential 10 years ago. We have taken 6 years to get
it back, and it is back now at a stage where it is better than our biggest competitor and
our biggest neighbour, which typically has done better than us.
It is really rich of Labour Party members to come into this House and pretend that
they look after people, preten d that they want to look after the vulnerable people in our
communities, and pretend that they actually care about economic growth when they
have no interest in that. The Labour Party always has been and always will be about
power, because that is all Labo ur stands for. Labour is about the union -dominated
power of the workers. That is what the Labour Party’s core fundamental beliefs are. It
sees itself as some kind of privileged elite whose members can sit in here and make
judgments for other people. It does not believe in giving people the chance to get a good
education, to have health care, and to have the infrastructure to grow. That is what this
Budget does. This Budget delivers that for New Zealanders. That is why New
Zealanders out there understand this Budget and actually believe in it.
I remember when we had the Budget speech. Bill English delivered a very competent
speech about the Budget, as you would expect, and the Labour members’ heads sank.
3966 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
They absolutely sank. They did not want to look up. They were looking at their papers,
trying to work out what was happening. They were embarrassed for their own party. I
give credit to one member of the Labour Party, though, who was not embarrassed.
There was one member on the front bench who actually looked at the Minister of
Finance, and she s miled. She is here today —Nanaia. She knew every one of those
policies were good policies for her people, for the people of Waikato, and for the people
of New Zealand. I did not see her head go down. She was smiling, nodding, and saying:
“Yes, this is good stuff—this is the stuff we should have done 9 years ago. This is the
stuff we should have done 12 years ago.” She knew that it was good. And then the
Labour leader stood up. He was stunned. He was a stunned mullet. He had no idea what
was going on. Then th e Prime Minister stood up and absolutely carved him up —
destroyed him, shredded him to pieces.
That was the story of Budget day 2015. What a great Budget day that was. So New
Zealanders will not forget that. They will not forget that this is a Government t hat has
delivered to all New Zealanders. It has delivered not just to the ideological elite that the
Labour Party preaches to—it actually has delivered to not just one core set of voters —it
has delivered to all New Zealanders, as it should and as it needs to do, to keep people
engaged and progressing in this country. I ask you, members of the community and
members of this House, to remember that. We are not going out there making fickle
promises about spending $1,000 just to make you feel good. We are not g oing out there
and attacking your superannuation after all those years of hard work that you have put
in. We are not going out there and doing silly policy things on the hoof, like the Labour
Party did this weekend. The Labour Party will not retract those policies. It has had 2
days to say that it made a mistake. It will not. We know that going into the next
election, this is what it will do.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: What policies? You’re making things up.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: And then w e have got Jacinda Ardern there. I tell you what,
Jacinda, I remember that great policy of capital gains tax that you had at the last
election. Then the Labour Party retracted it —the Opposition members and their leader
said there would be no capital gains tax under Andrew Little. They said there would be
no capital gains tax under Labour. Then we brought in a tax on people selling properties
within 2 years, and the Labour Party cannot do anything because it has said no to that
policy. It has said no to that  policy because it does not want to have any taxes. That is
the Labour Party that will say one thing, do another, and does not actually deliver for
New Zealanders. This is a great Budget.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: Talofa lava. Can I just
take a brief moment to acknowledge the families of the Pike River miners who are in
the gallery today and who are listening to this particular debate. They could be forgiven
for thinking that we were on a whole different planet and that Budget 2015 is delivering
to the many regions across New Zealand in positive ways.
Well, Mr Bennett, it gives me great pleasure to follow you. You mentioned Waikato
University, but you failed to  recognise what the vice -chancellor himself said. He said
that the change in tertiary policy has had a huge effect on new enrolments to Waikato
University and that the change in postgraduate policies also had a huge implication for
enrolments at that parti cular university. I am proud of our university, I am proud of
what it does, and I am proud of what it is trying to do to ensure that more young people
come to Waikato University to study. But the Budget did not actually deliver to many
young people who see  their prospects in education, and it certainly did not deliver in
tertiary education.
There have been many things that have been said through this Budget debate that I
am very, very concerned about. In fact, you could be forgiven for thinking that the
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3967
Government wants to roll through this very quickly. When one listens to Minister
Steven Joyce’s contribution, one might almost think that the Ministry of Business,
Innovation and Employment was becoming irrelevant to the aspirations of the regions.
Just the  other day I was in Manukau, and it is glaring where the priorities of the
Government are. We hear a lot about National’s economic plan and the benefits for the
country. If you look on one side of the road, you see that the Ministry of Business,
Innovation and Employment office is in a very dimly lit building, with no signage
whatsoever. It is in a small building on the one side, and just across the road in the
biggest building, the flashiest building on the street, is Housing New Zealand. However,
people in Manukau have to ring an 0800 number to try to get a house. If they are lucky,
they might be rated as priority B, but they more than likely will not get a house. There is
hardship in the regions. This Budget has not delivered to a whole lot of families th at I
think it could have.
Mr Bennett, you made the comment that the $25 increase to base benefits will make
a difference. It will make a slight difference, but when you yourself know that the
Children’s Commissioner said that it is a start but that it is not a plan to tackle child
poverty, how can you look members on this side of the House in the face and say:
“We’re doing a whole lot to address child poverty.”?

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: My apologies, Mr Assistant Speaker. In fact, the
Government refuses to set targets for a comprehensive, whole -of-Government strategy
to reduce child poverty. The Opposition has continued to push for targets that are
possible to measure by every Government department that has an ability to influence
outcomes for children and set some simple measures in place.
Coming back to the Budget, there are a number of litmus tests that members might
want to put across the Budget t o ensure that it is achieving something. Mine is simple:
regional development and regional opportunity. I have had a lot of opportunities to visit
several regions. I just want to comment on a few things that have come up through the
regions and then ask whether or not this Budget addresses issues for them.
We were in Gisborne, and one of the visits that we had was with an entrepreneur. He
said: “Look at those ports out there. We want to be able to do more than export raw logs
from our particular region, bu t the rail link is a problem.” The Government has done
nothing there. We are still exporting raw logs. There is a huge health and safety risk in
the industry itself, but there is huge potential to diversify what is happening in
Gisborne. Did the Budget del iver for that region? I think not. I do not think any of the
investment in research and innovation will go into the Gisborne area.
I will take a look at some of the other areas. Yes, the net migration to New Zealand is
significantly positive. However, ove r 50 percent of those people choose to live in
Auckland, and that compounds the housing pressure in Auckland. In regions like
Invercargill and Gisborne, people are saying: “We want to attract skilled migrants into
our region. It is cheaper to get a house h ere than in Auckland. However, we need a
whole plan for regional growth and development, where central government and local
government and the business community can work together and collaborate around firm
plans to ensure opportunity exists here.” Did th e Budget deliver against that priority? I
think not.
In Pukekohe, we have just got a new milk factory, built by the Chinese down the
road in Pōkeno. Again, the people there are saying it is more than likely, under the
current growth limits for the city of  Auckland, that Tuakau and Pukekohe are prime
areas to attract population into. But, again, there are the regulations around housing and
some of the challenges around infrastructure and the investment required, and the public
transport needs create certain  pressures for places like Pukekohe and Tuakau. They
3968 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
themselves would say that they have got huge challenges in both cutting through the red
tape of local government and getting central government onside to recognise that there
is more to Pukekohe than horticulture and the Glenbrook steel mill just down the road at
Waiuku. Did the Budget deliver for them? Well, perhaps in time, but not immediately.
In the area of education and skills training, one of the things that continues to come
up more and more as I travel around the country is the cost that occurs when you try to
ensure that young people have opportunities beyond school, not only in apprenticeships
but also in going and studying at their nearest tertiary institution, whether it is to secure
a trade or a professional degree. Many parents, teachers, and, indeed, mayors identified
that one of the significant barriers to getting their young people into training is the cost
of travel from rural areas into the city. The cost of tertiary fees alone is a sign ificant
barrier, as is the cost of accommodation if they have to find accommodation in the area
where they are going to study. Has the Budget delivered for them? Is there hope and
opportunity for the young people who are wanting to do more and be more? Wel l, it is
hard to see—it is very hard to see.
This is a serious debate and it requires serious attention, but one of the things that I
am most concerned about is the lack of a plan for young New Zealanders. We were in
urgency debating the removal of the $1 ,000 kick-start payment. If you were to believe
the member for Hamilton East, David Bennett, you would think that just because 38
percent of people take up the $1,000 and make no contribution, it is a justification for
removing it. I totally reject that debate. I totally reject that proposition. In fact, the kick -
start payment enabled families to be able to open up an account and create a savings
history.
When KiwiSaver started, it was really clear that New Zealanders were not good
savers, but KiwiSaver provided an opportunity for people to start to put a little bit away
in the hope of having a nest egg. Taking away the kick -start payment will not help the
next generation. It robs from the future and it creates no hope that people can have
security in retirement.
Coming back to the point that I really want to make about child poverty measures, it
is time now. If the Government  makes the decision to give an extra $25 to those
families who most need it in order to give them a little bit of support, then it is now time
for the Government to set some targets to reduce child poverty . We need a whole-of-
Government target that it consistently reports against to ensure that all the policies —a
comprehensive set of policies —can reduce poverty and inequality and improve the
outcomes for children and young people.  We just cannot have a country where
inequality gets bigger. Budget 2015 was a major flop, in my perspective, for children
whose lives really require our attention and who should be put at the centre of a whole-
of-Government approach, to improve opportunities for the future. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to speak this afternoon.
At the heart of this Budget is  the concept of fairness. I was in Japan when the Budget
was delivered, and one of the things that struck me was the number of people from
countries within the Asia -Pacific region who said this to me: New Zealand is the
comeback country. It is really impor tant, when we have this Budget debate, to
understand the history here. In 2011 we said there would be 170,000 jobs created, and 3
months before that deadline we have done it. When we came in from Opposition we
were faced with a decade of deficits. We have seen an incredible comeback as a nation.
We are within reach of surplus.
But what we have also said, and what has been a hallmark of this Budget, is that we
will not get to surplus at the expense of our most vulnerable. So with all due respect to
all of those Opposition members who stand up in this House and talk about the surplus,
they know, actually, that when you are in Government it is about the hard choices. I am
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3969
proud to be a member on this side of the House, to not only be delivering at a fiscal
level—to be responsibly managing the books; we have got 150,000 jobs forecast in the
next 4 years and we have got 2.8 percent growth forecast —but also to have delivered
over a long period and to now be focusing on some of the harder issues for New
Zealand. We have had public sector reform, but we have to do more. What you can see
in this Budget is a concerted effort to tackle the hard issues. But this is on the back of
years of hard work, in areas like some of our most vulnerable children. So let us walk
through it.
We have, under our Government, insulated more houses than ever for vulnerable
children. We have, in the last year’s Budget, really focused on those children having
access to good health-care. That is why we announced free GP visits for under -13s. We
have also done a range of other things, so you can see that on the back of that there is an
investment in the vulnerable children’s action plan. And then, on top of that, $790
million in this Budget is targeted at those children who are in hardship. This  has been a
concerted effort over a range of years to help our most vulnerable children.
Secondly, if you actually look at what we are trying to do from the education
perspective, part of our legacy is significant reform in terms of ensuring where those
kids who need basic numeracy and literacy  are. Through national standards we are
targeting those schools more than ever in terms of numeracy and literacy, and we are
seeing those results, particularly around Māori and Pacific Island students. You can see
in this Budget another round in terms of investment in those young people, and you can
also see that we are fixing those schools that have for years been in a state of disrepair.
Over successive Budgets we have done more than ever. I think we have spent abo ut
$80 million on weathertightness and earthquake strengthening, and another $240
million is in this Budget package around not only ensuring those schools are fixed and
earthquake strengthened but also so that we can expand where we need to expand, and
build for growth. It is not a model whereby communities have been left in the cold
because they have not had the planning for growth that we need. So we have got another
area in this Budget, building on all of the good work that we have done before, to invest
in young people, on top of a targeted package of $790 million targeted towards our most
vulnerable children.
If you take the area of science and innovation —again, we have had sustained
investment. But if you look at this Budget alone, there is funding of  $25 million for
regional research institutes. The Budget will give an $80 million boost over 4 years to
research and development growth grants. We have got a $113 million boost for tertiary
education and skills. This is very significant, and it is very si gnificant particularly in the
investment in terms of Māori and Pacific students in trades academies.
So for those members opposite who say that we are not investing in young people,
they need to have a really good look at the line items in the Budget. We are investing
more than ever before. In fact, $2.4 billion in this Budget is in education and health
services. But this is 6½ years of concerted effort around our most vulnerable and young
New Zealanders. I am very proud of this Budget.
The second area we have been really tackling is housing affordability. Again, let us
look back and see what we have done. So, firstly, we have increased subsidies for the
HomeStart grants. Secondly, we have had one phase of Resource Management Act
reform. Thirdly, we have invested more than ever to really tackle those issues of
productivity in the construction sector. But, also, we have really got a focus in this
Budget on ensuring that those people who are trading, effectively, or speculating in
terms of houses are penalised for that. Again, this is a very targeted policy focusing on
penalising those people who may be shutting young New Zealanders out of the housing
market, while also respecting the fact that we do not want to be taxing those people in
3970 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
terms of the family home. That is building on an existing policy that we think needs to
be enforced properly. That is about tackling the hard issues and having dedicated policy
focused on housing affordability.
In my area of ACC, again, we were left with a $4 .8 billion hole. Again, I heard
Andrew Little. Andrew Little went out there when I made these announcements—

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Just not true.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: No, I think it is time the member Mr Cunliffe listened for  a
second. Andrew Little went out there when I announced $500 million of ACC
reductions and when I announced a new piece of legislation aimed at transparency. I do
not have his exact quote, but it went something like this. He said that it was dishonest
and manipulative.
This is a piece of legislation based on transparency of the ACC accounts, after we
have come back from a $4.8 billion hole, to actually be able to give another round of
levy reductions, and this is after we have already given back $1.5 billion. He is so out of
touch. He is so emotional that he does not actually have any policy that exists behind
what he says. We saw it with the means testing of superannuation. We saw it when he
commented on ACC. We are seeing it all over the place, and that is because those
members do not have targeted policy on the other side, they do not have the grunt
within their caucus, and then they have got a leader who, effectively, just goes out there,
says what he thinks, and then has the caucus pulling him into lin e. That is compared
with a Government that has continually developed good policy that is targeted and has
invested where it matters.
Another area where we have invested where it matters is the Future Investment Fund.
Again, we had ideological opposition from members on the other side of the House, but
I think the total capital investment in New Zealand is about $939 million. This includes
a contingency of up to $210 million for additional investment to bring ultra -fast
broadband to 80 percent of New Zealan ders. We have got the telecommunications
development levy extended to provide $150 million for major improvements in rural
broadband. I represent Great Barrier Island, actually, and we have a whole lot of young
people there who have not done as well as the y could have but who are now getting
access to learning resources that they have never had before. For members opposite,
again, who talk about this Budget not delivering for young New Zealanders, these are
very tangible things that make a difference to iso lated communities and to young New
Zealanders.
We are also seeing KiwiRail receive $210 million in new capital investment and a
further $190 million as a pre -commitment against Budget 2016. In the area of the
Resource Management Act and freshwater reforms , we have got $37 million of
operating funding for 4 years to provide greater national direction and support to
councils. Again, this is on the back of a whole lot of other money that we have invested
over successive Budgets around fresh water.
So there i s a lot of hot air and rhetoric that comes from the Opposition, but, at the
end of the day, what it knows, and what I knew when I was in Japan —I was there when
this Budget was delivered by our Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister —is that
people there said to me that we are the comeback country. In my view, the numbers
show that. We have created over 170,000 jobs. We are on track for 2.8 percent growth.
We are in reach of surplus. But we are a Government that has done more than that. At
the heart of our Government is fairness and you saw that with this targeted $790 million
package for some of our most vulnerable children. That is on the back of so much
investment, whether it is education reform, whether it is free GP visits for under -13s,
whether it is  insulating houses, or whether it is an investment in fresh water. We have
managed to do that in very difficult fiscal times, balancing the books but looking after
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3971
New Zealanders and providing fairness at the heart of this Budget. This is a great
Budget. This is a fair Budget. This is in contrast to an Opposition that is bereft of ideas.
I support this Budget.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: Like many Aucklanders, I am an immigrant to
Aotearoa New Ze aland. I chose to make my home here because I love this country. I
love the mountains, I love the beaches, I love the old -growth forest, and I love the
people of New Zealand, whom I have found very warm, welcoming, practical, and,
above all, fair-minded.
I had a successful career as a transportation analyst, and I did that because I wanted
to have a job that allowed me to find creative solutions to some of the biggest, most
pressing challenges of the 21 st century. So I did a lot of work in the areas of
transportation planning and economics because I wanted to be part of the solution. I
ended up joining the Green Party, firstly, because it is the party that shares my values —
looking after the environment; ensuring that we have a fair society and democracy, th at
decisions are made at the lowest level at which they affect people—but, most important,
because the Green Party in Aotearoa was the only political party that was really
championing the proven, practical policies that should be mainstream but are not bei ng
implemented here in New Zealand.
We know they have been proven overseas in very successful northern European
countries that are managing to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions and reduce
pollution, and that do not have the levels of increasing inequal ity that we see here in
New Zealand. I think that we could follow that path —we do not have to reinvent the
wheel. Unfortunately, neither of the two larger parties has grasped the opportunities that
are provided by understanding all the interconnections bet ween our environment, our
economy, and our society. It is common sense to respond to climate change as soon as
possible, because we have to respond sooner or later. The sooner we take action, the less
it will cost us. It is common sense to reduce the growi ng gap between the rich and the
poor, because it is better for everyone in society. It ensures that we are all better off. It
ensures that we build a much more successful society and economy in the future if we
invest in our poorest kids.
The National Government members—and in particular I heard the previous speaker,
the Hon Nikki Kaye—claim some of these values. They want to say that they care about
the economy, they care about fairness, they care about the environment, and they are
doing all these things.  But when you get down to it and you look at the numbers and
you look at the policies they are implementing, they are simply not taking us in a
smarter, greener, and fairer direction. They are taking us in a direction of greater
inequality and more polluti on. I would say the Green Party is the only party that is
really prepared to stand up for younger New Zealanders, who are being let down by this
National Government.
I think the National Government is deeply out of touch if it says the economy is
working for everyone. We have got a younger generation that is drowning in student
debt, and is unable to afford a home in Auckland and unlikely to afford one any time
soon, even if those people get a job and work hard. Wages are actually stagnating for at
least half of the people in this country, and a quarter of all children are still living in
poverty. So I would say National has really lost touch with everyday New Zealanders. It
is choosing to build an economy that relies on increasing pollution in the extractio n of
natural resources. It only really works for the New Zealanders who already have a lot. It
works very well for them. They have got tax cuts and were able to buy shares in our
State-owned energy companies. They are doing quite well. They are not paying any tax
on the capital gains they have seen in Auckland over the last few years.
3972 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
There is an alternative to this. There is an alternative to just tinkering around the
edges, which is what this Government has done. The Green Party has a costed plan to
retool the economy to get a better, cleaner future that provides opportunity and
prosperity for everyone.
I want to speak specifically about two issues —firstly, environmental protection and
the Resource Management Act, and, secondly, transport —because those are  two areas
in particular where this Government is missing huge opportunities.  John Key admitted
last week after the Budget that National cannot get support for its most radical proposed
changes to the Resource Management Act. These are the changes to secti on 6 and
section 7, which would fundamentally gut our world -leading environmental protection
law. The reason it cannot get support for these changes is that they are very radical and
cut to the heart of our national identity. I know New Zealanders love the ir natural
environment. They are proud of it. They know there is huge value in protecting it —
immeasurable value. We set environmental bottom lines to protect the things that we
value. If you really believe in the ingenuity of people, as I believe the Green  Party does,
we know that people can adapt. Any economic activity must respect those bottom lines.
As we know, the economy is a wholly -owned subsidiary of the natural environment,
and once something is gone it is gone for good. When a developer in Auckland
proposed to cut down a 500 -year-old kauri tree to build a house, 93 percent of New
Zealanders agreed that the tree should be protected. That is where the rubber hits the
road, because National’s changes to the Resource Management Act have already made
it more difficult for communities to protect trees, to protect the places they love, and to
have a say on the development that is happening. Changing the purpose and principles
of the Act would fundamentally change the balance in a way that means no
environmental bottom lines —communities cannot protect trees, they cannot protect the
things they really care about.
Giving up environmental protection does not make us richer. You only need to look
at China to see where this trade -off has occurred. It has managed t o achieve huge GDP
growth, but it has been at the cost of clean air, clean water, and healthy communities. I
know that is not what New Zealanders want here. We do not need growth of an
economy that is reliant on increasing pollution and the extraction of n on-renewable
resources. That is just going to end up costing us in the long run.
National has used the housing crisis in Auckland as a Trojan Horse for these reforms
to the Resource Management Act. It is claiming that we cannot have affordable housing
and protect our environment. I know that is not true. There is no evidence to support
Nick Smith’s claims that planning rules are entirely responsible for the housing crisis.
In fact, if you look at the research, you can see that pretty clearly. We have got re search
here in New Zealand from 2014 -15 from the New Zealand Institute of Economic
Research, Arthur Grimes, and Ian Mitchell. In this graph, we have got estimates of what
the impact of planning rules has been on development in Auckland. If you believe the
Government, which likes to listen to a pro - urban sprawl thinktank called
Demographia, you would guess that the whole difference in the increase in house price
costs is due to planning regulations, when the actual research in New Zealand shows
