that they h ave a much smaller impact. Maybe 20 to 30 percent of the price can be
explained by planning regulations, but most of the cost is actually on apartments or
medium-rise density—you know, the development not just of apartments but of town
houses, character flats.
These are all things that the Green Party has been saying for a long time we should
be developing, because it is better for the environment and it means people can live
where they want to live in compact, walkable neighbourhoods where they can access
goods, services, and jobs through public transport or by walking and cycling.  That is
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3973
what people really want. Land values are highest on the isthmus, not out on the fringe,
because people want to be on the isthmus. They want to be close to where things ar e.
The reason they cannot afford it is that the planning rules do not allow that high-quality
mid-rise intensification, which is what we have been arguing for and are quite happy to
work on with the Government.
Of course, that is just the supply side. I wo uld say that on the supply side the Greens
have got it right. We have got a smart solution that not only reduces housing costs but
reduces transport costs, reduces pollution, and enables people to live where they want to
live. On the demand side it is clea r that the tax treatment of income has fuelled
speculation in residential property. The Green Party has long called for smart measures
like a capital gains tax, limiting the amount of capital coming in from overseas —
limiting the purchase of land and proper ty to citizens and residents here in New
Zealand—and also having minimum standards for rental accommodation. All of that
would help take the heat out of the housing market. And on the supply side we would
welcome central government leadership, with a natio nal policy statement and
environmental standards on good-quality mid -rise development  in the central city,
because that is where the evidence says people want to be.
The other side of the coin is, of course, transport. There is no point in building cheap
houses on the fringe, where people just have to spend more on cars and transport to
access education and jobs. A smart, green approach enables people to live closer to jobs
and closer to public transport, but we need that investment in public transport
infrastructure first. This is where National is really failing Auckland and future New
Zealanders, because there is no money in this Budget for new public transport
infrastructure in Auckland. In fact, since National came to power there has been no new
money announced for rail projects in Auckland. All of it was committed under Labour,
thanks to the pressure of the Green Party, 8 years ago.  If you look at the next 10 years,
this chart shows what the National Party is planning to spend the transport budget on —
mostly on a bunch of motorways that have no business case when growth in rail in
Auckland is at 20 percent a year and there has been no growth in vehicle kilometres
travelled. So this is where the investment should go, because it is smart, it reduces
pollution, it increases people’s quality of life, it reduces costs for Government, and it
reduces costs for households.
We can have this smart, green revolution here in New Zealand. We can have a fair
society and we can respond to climate change, but we need a Government that is willing
to actually take on the evidence and take us in a better direction. The Green Party would
do that. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I am very much
looking forward to an overview of the Budget and, in particular, of the votes in my
responsibility, but I cannot let the final comments by Ms Genter go unchallenged in
respect of public commitment to public transport and, in particular, rail. I would say two
things about that. Firstly, wild commitments that are unfunded are not commitments.
They are just promises of the future. It was this Government that found the funding to
meet the need for the electrification of Auckland.  I will also say this. This Government
has committed—I am not sure of the exact number, but I am sure this is pretty close —
$3.4 billion investment into KiwiRail and another $0.25 billion in this Budget just to
help KiwiRail stay afloat. So let there be no question about this Government’s
commitment financially to rail, but it needs to be smarter than that. Big, grand plans for
rail and rail links and things like that neglect the way in which the vast majority of
people do go about their business —that is, on  roads—and let us just remember most
public transport goes on roads. The significant investment of, I think, about $100
million that Minister Bridges has announced for cycleways means that this Government
3974 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
can hold its head high in respect of its commitment  to both public transport and
cycleways.
Budgets are hard, and the longer Governments are in office, the harder it can be to
put together packages that in straitened times continue to fund the programmes that are
existing while looking and finding the fun ding for those new programmes that are
invested in. So I was extremely proud to be part of a Cabinet that came up with the
package for families in hardship. I must say it was a surprise to most, but not to this side
of the House. I think the description from my colleague and friend from Taranaki - King
Country, Barbara Kuriger —I do not know whether this has been publicly said, Ms
Kuriger—that I heard recently of the reaction from the Labour Opposition, when that
part of the Budget was being read, was that i t was like seeing a child reach out for a
balloon that burst in front of its eyes before the child could grab it. That, I think, was the
best metaphor for the reaction and the surprise that Labour —having banged on about
how heartless this Government is —had to this Government being the first Government
since 1972 to increase support for families in hardship over and above the cost of
inflation.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: You’ve taken it away from KiwiSaver.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Well, the member is quite right. My offer to the
member—and my chequebook is still in my pocket —is I will pay that $1,000 back
when just one member says that they did not take the tax cut. That is all I am asking. It
is not a big ask, but not one member has knocked on my door yet.
I think that package reflects this Government’s compassion towards those in most
need, while at the same time acknowledging —and I heard Mrs Tolley  in question time
say—that the best pathway out of poverty is work. Well, I would suggest, actually, that
the only pathway out of poverty and the constant battle and the resilience that one needs
to be able to pay the first bill, then the next bill, then t he next, and not live fortnight to
fortnight, is to find work and work that can be sustained. I know, as the Minister of
Immigration, that that work is there. It is a fact that we do have a skill mismatch and a
geographic mismatch, and the challenges for m any of our young in particular, in terms
of their ability to be able to get and sustained work, are ones that this Government will
overcome. But let there be no doubt that with the support comes an expectation that
working-age beneficiaries will seek work.  I think that is what the taxpayer, who invests
in their support, would expect.
We have had a focus on exports and growing exports through these straitened times.
One thing we have failed to do —one export that seemed to be going gangbusters under
the previous Labour Government and that this Government has singularly failed to do—
is export its people. We could have filled Westpac Stadium with the people who were
leaving these shores every year. The Prime Minister, when Leader of the Opposition,
made a commi tment to turn that round. We turned it into a bus, then a phone box, and
now they are coming back. They are coming back, not only in positive numbers for the
first time but Australians are now looking to this country for the job opportunities that a
strong, growing economy will have.
I was at the Brisbane job fair, one of four job fairs that the Government initiated in
Perth, Brisbane, Sydney, and Melbourne, and the level of interest in, and applications
for, the jobs that were available with the employers that went over to those fairs was
very, very high. There is a nervousness across the Ditch about their economy. I think
last year’s Budget by the Australian Government was an example of where slashing and
burning and not sticking to a plan can have political ramifications. This Government has
not done that, and there would have been a temptation, I suspect, to cut just to get to
surplus. I would much rather suffer the slings and arrows of that Opposition about the
Government’s failure —albeit by a wafer -thin margin—to achieve surplus than to cut
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3975
important programmes just to get there. Not only did this Government not do that but it
invested very heavily in its most vulnerable.
With that flow of people, and a significant increase in the number of people wanti ng
to visit New Zealand, our tourism industry —our single largest service export earner —
has gone very, very strongly over the last couple of years from emerging markets.
Immigration officers in Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou are very, very busy with a
significant increase —40 or 50 percent year -on-year interest —in that growing middle
class in China wanting to come and visit New Zealand. It is not just China; it is India, it
is the rest of Asia, and it is the United States. New Zealand is a desirable destina tion,
but with that comes risk. The important challenge for immigration is to ensure that we
let the right people in and we keep the wrong people out, and so I was very pleased to
be able to announce a $33 million increase in Budget 2014 over the next 4 ye ars to
ensure that those growing passenger arrival numbers do have a commensurate increase
in the risk management—in the advanced passenger processing—that we have for them.
Indeed, as Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety , I announced another $32
million, because many of those people coming to work or study here have work rights
attached to them. It is very important to me, as Minister, that they are well looked after,
and that the people who are helping us to rebuild Christchurch following the
earthquakes can do so on the back of supportive employers and not exploitative
employers. I think that the incidence and prevalence of that is quite low, but it is very
important that we keep it that way, and so the extra investment in the labour
inspectorate—which has now increased that team by 40 percent since we came to
office—is a significant reflection of this Government’s priority to make sure that our
migrants who are working are made welcome and are well looked after. The task is
prevention and then pro secution for those who fall below. I must say, it is very
disappointing that Labour and the Greens did not support my Immigration Amendment
Bill, which significantly increased the punishments for employers who knowingly
exploit legal workers in this country.
I just want to touch on Vote Police. An extra $164 million is going into the baseline
to consolidate the police’s funding, to continue the excellent work that they have done
in reducing reported crime in this country to its lowest level in 30 years —a more than
20 percent reduction. That has been done in a number of very, very smart ways, using
technologies that this Government has enabled the police to get, to get police out from
behind their desks and their cars and to be out on the beat, visible, and supporting their
communities. IPads and iPhone technology is just one example of the hardware that
police have been given to support their communities, but it is also an example of very
clever tools that are being developed by their software providers to e nsure that the
process of infringements and prosecutions is a much more efficient one. The Policing

items.speaker: Excellence
items.text: The Future programme, I think, will continue to deliver excellent results in
enabling the police to have, and maintain, the very high levels of trust and confidence—
probably world leading for a law enforcement organisation —that the public have had in
them, despite the fact that they work in extremely difficult parts of our community. I
want to commend them for the work that they do and I certainly will continue to support
them in their efforts.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: It gives me some pleasure and also some sadness,
actually, to rise to speak in this debate on the Government’s 2015 Budget. I was
reminded before I came down here that there was an interesting documentary on the
former Australian Prime Minister Paul Keating, who provided a warning to members of
his Government that they had better give heed. This Government had better give heed
too, given the chest-beating that we have seen over this “I Can See Red, I Can See Red,
I See Red Budget”, because that is all we see in New Zealand First. It is a red Budget,
3976 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
but not because it is a Labour Party Budget. It is red because it is a deficit —again, a
deficit—despite all the promises and all the assurances.
I have got to say to anybody listening, when you are talking about the police budget,
there is only one fact that one can actually bank on when looking at this Budget, and it
is not the fact that there is  in the Budget a $164 million increase for the police over the
next 4 years—you cannot bank on that. We cannot bank on that. What we can bank on
is a $41 million increase for this year—this first year. The rest of it is pie in the sky. The
rest of it is al l doctored and fudged to create the illusion of the potential of a surplus
and, maybe, a tax cut. It is all designed to appease and appeal to New Zealanders who
are driven by greed and driven by keeping their own money, no matter what cost that
actually has on the rest of New Zealand in terms of delivering services. The services I
am talking about are services delivered by our police force.
I do actually want to digress a little bit because the Minister raised the question of
transport funding in saying how much money this Government is spending on transport.
Well, let us be very clear about this. Rural provincial New Zealand —go to the New
Zealand Transport Agency website, I say for the benefit of all the new backbench
members of the National Party, pull do wn the New Zealand Transport Agency table,
and look at how much funding is being cut from rural roading by your vote in this
House. For Carterton, Masterton, and South Wairarapa that cut is 1 percent each year
for the next 4 years. That will result in a 1 percent increase in rates for all of those
farmers and all of those rural people, if those councils want to keep pace with the same
level of maintenance. That is a cut that the Government members are voting for. Let us
be clear about that. All the prattlin g on about how much money they are spending in
Auckland—actually, in the Wairarapa we do not give a stuff about how much money
you spend in Auckland. We want to know how much money this Government is cutting
from the funding that goes to our councils, beca use that shortfall will be met by a rates
increase, which is the very thing that young Nick Smith used to bleat on about when he
was chastising local government.
So let us look at the police budget. Looking at the estimates appropriations, on page
129 it says that the total appropriation is $15 million less than it was in 2014. Output
expenses are $5 million less than in Budget 2014, and the capital budget is a staggering
$13 million less. That is not an increase; they are all reductions.
It is so sad, I have been reliably informed, that on Saturday, 21 March, on the night
of the Cricket World Cup match in Wellington, there were only 18 police officers on
duty in the city that night at 11 p.m.—18 police officers in the whole of Wellington city.
Why do the police numbers concern New Zealand First? Well, I am sorry, folks, beat
your chests all you like over on the Government benches, but there is only one party,
and one party alone, that has consistently stood by the police when it comes to numbers,
and that is New Zealand First. Nobody else in history has ever produced 1,000 extra
police in one Budget. Nobody in their short time in Government has ever increased the
police establishment by 2,500. New Zealand First did that.
So when we look at the shrinking si ze of the police force and the shrinking budget —
and let us be clear: $41 million is not an increase in the police budget. It is simply
marking time, treading water. It is keeping things where they are, and what does that
mean? Well, it means no extra capac ity and no extra equipment. There is no extra
capital works in there. There is certainly no pay rise, and there is certainly no increase in
the establishment.
In fact, what do we see? No matter where we go, there is the closing of police
stations in rural New Zealand. My colleague sitting beside me, Ria Bond, who is proud
and pleased to now be representing people in the Invercargill -Southland area—in fact,
the whole of the lower South Island —knows about this. We know the cutbacks that
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3977
have occurred down in the South Island in rural, provincial New Zealand. We know the
number of police stations in rural, provincial New Zealand that are being closed.
That is not improving capacity. That is not improving capability. That is not
improving the service to New Ze aland. That is not improving people’s safety and well -
being or improving the standard. Do not go bleating on at me, Government members,
about reported crime being down, because a large number of the police officers I talk to
say: “All we have done is chang e the way we collate the data.” How convenient. They
changed the way they collate and report the data to present information that satisfies the
Government and suits its political needs.
Crime is not down. Go and ask any police officer on the beat. Go and sit in a police
station, and go and talk to people who put in insurance claims. What do they complain
about now? Well, actually, they are resigned to it —they give up now. They say that
reporting to the police is simply a measure you have to do to get your insurance claim
accepted by a company. They have no belief whatsoever that a police officer is going to
turn up, take fingerprints, and interview them—

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: They still record them.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: Mr Woodhouse, do not even go there, because we will start to roll out
the numbers for the Minister. We will start to roll out the numbers for the Minister.
Now he is looking embarrassed. He has got that little look on his face, and I know that
when “Woodie”, the Minister, gets embarrassed that little smile comes on. I have seen it
enough on the rugby paddock. Look, Mr Woodhouse, you are the Minister of Police;
you know that crime is not down. The way it has been reported has changed. The way
the statistics are being presented has changed.
By the way, if we think that shutting down the services of Relationships Aotearoa is
going to help reduce crime, we in this House have got to be nuts. Relationships
Aotearoa is actually one of the front -line teams that are working to r educe domestic
violence and working to help the police indirectly by resolving those matters and
dealing with those people who are in that situation. So once Relationships Aotearoa has
closed down, what do we think is going to happen with domestic violence ? What do we
think is going to happen with the number of people being bashed in their homes? And
how many extra police officers are going to be needed to cater for that shortfall?
This is short -term thinking. This is not holistic policing. This is short -term, narrow-
minded, Budget -focused, numbers -focused thinking that is all orientated around
producing a Budget that gives a surplus next year, maybe. Well, it is not good enough.
New Zealand First opposes this Budget, and we will do so at the final vote.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: It is interesting following Ron Mark from
the New Zealand First Party. You would think it was single-handedly responsible for all
the good things that might hav e happened in the policing budget in New Zealand’s
history. In fact, the last time that police numbers were increased in this country, New
Zealand First was not even in Parliament. New Zealand First was not even in Parliament
because it got turfed out after its shoddy dealings in Parliament between 2005 and 2008.
This Government, I have to say to Mr Mark, is delivering for New Zealanders in the
law and order sector. Crime is down by 20 percent, Mr Mark. If you want to talk to
police officers, come to Count ies Manukau and I will put you in front of a whole lot of
police officers who will say that they are working hard every single day to get crime
down. The disrespect shown by members like Mr Mark who are saying that police
officers are not getting crime down, I think, is shameful. Our police do an excellent job.
Crime is down by 20 percent, and 600 extra police officers have been delivered by this
Government. Crime is at a 35 -year low. This Budget backs up the police through the
funding they require to do th eir job, and, on this side of the House, we are proud of the
things we are doing for police and for New Zealanders when it comes to law and order.
3978 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
I did not intend to start my speech by talking about law and order, but after listening to
the drivel from Ro n Mark I simply had to respond. He is wrong and New Zealanders
know it.
I want to join with my colleagues in congratulating the Hon Bill English on
delivering his seventh Budget. I had the pleasure last night of delivering a presentation
to my local Rotar y club about Budget 2015. It showed many of the slides and graphs
about how we are tracking as a country compared with other countries, how we have
responsibly kept spending in check, and how we are getting our country back to a
position where it can start to pay down the debt incurred when we had to borrow during
the global financial crisis. The fact is that wages in this country are going up,
employment is coming down, and more New Zealanders are able to get into work, put
food on the table for their families, and, ultimately, live a better life.
It is good when one looks properly at the graphs around this Budget. There was an
executive summary with a whole lot of information in a visual format, which is quite
easy for taxpayers to look at. When you look at the spending that we have been tracking
and following for the last 7 years compared with the very large amounts of additional
expenditure that Labour was putting into its Budgets, you can see that this Government
has been extremely responsible during to ugh times. New Zealanders have tightened
their belts in a huge way as well, and we should be congratulating New Zealanders on
what they have done to try to help this country get back into a better fiscal position.
I have actually brought the graph along w ith me. When one looks at the 2008 year,
when Labour was spending $7 billion extra, that is in fact more in 1 year than what we
have spent in additional spending in all of our Budgets put together. That is responsible
spending, and it is only through that responsible spending that we see wages go up.
Wages are expected to go up by $7,000 on average for New Zealanders over the next 4
years. If we put that together with the fact that wages have gone up by $6,000 in the
past 4 years, we see that that is a $13, 000 average increase over that 8 -year period for
New Zealanders. That accounts for about a 25 percent increase in wages for New
Zealanders.
But the news gets better for New Zealanders, because over that same 8 -year period,
inflation will have tracked up by only about 14 percent. So New Zealanders are actually
getting wealthier. New Zealanders are seeing more money in their pockets. Inflation is
low in this country, and that is a good thing for New Zealanders. We are seeing wages
going up, and I say to thos e people who go out there and like to give the police a hard
time that when they are talking to the police about all the good work the police are
doing, they should go and talk to New Zealanders too about whether they are seeing
more money in their back pockets, because the answer absolutely is yes.
The fact that inflation in this country is pretty low at the moment has its positives and
it also has its negatives. One of the negatives, unfortunately, for the Government is that
it has not seen the amount of  revenue that it was expecting. Yes, we have not been able
to post a surplus this year as we were hoping to. We are expecting to post that next year.
When other members get up on their hind legs in this House and complain that we
have not posted a surplus  this year, that we are supposedly not doing enough for
families in hardship,  and that they want to spend more money in other areas of the
Budget—and at the same time say we should not have removed the KiwiSaver kick -
start—I say to those members that they simply cannot have everything. They simply
cannot have all those things on their wish list, go to the public, and credibly say that
they can put together a Budget properly. Look at the things on their wish list and the
fact that they complain that we do no t spend enough in certain areas and that we should
not be cutting back in other areas. To get a balanced Budget there are a whole lot of
things that have to come together, and Bill English has been able to do that.
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3979
I am also very proud that for the first time in 43 years we have a Government that is
willing to increase benefit rates. Whilst New Zealanders in work are seeing, on average,
their wages going up, the fact of the matter is that there is a range of New Zeal anders
who are in hardship and do need more assistance. Unashamedly, this Government is
prepared to step up to the plate and invest in the areas where New Zealanders need it.
The Hon Anne Tolley has been pushing hard for some time —alongside the Prime
Minister, I must add—to see those increases, to assist those who are most in need.
I have to say that it is not actually the parents who are getting the benefit that we are
really looking out for here. It is in fact the children in those families who will bene fit
from those increases through the welfare system. If the children who are most in need
and who are living in families in hardship do not get the assistance they require —for
example, children who may have seen their families intera ct with Child, Youth an d
Family or the corrections system, or their families may have been on a benefit for a long
period of time—then it is those children right at the bottom there who are at most risk in
our society, and they are the children who need the most investment by Government and
by New Zealanders as well.
There are 160,000 families in this country that will benefit from this $790 million
package. Some may think it is unusual for a National Government to be doing it, but I
have to say that if there is one thing that th ey have not worked out yet about John Key,
it is the fact that he is willing to step up  to put the money of the Government where his
mouth is, and he is prepared to invest in areas where New Zealanders need and require
investment. This Government is delivering for those people.
I also want to touch just briefly on the housing area in my last 2 minutes, because
housing is a significant issue for Auckland. Ultimately , we still stand by our view that
the housing supply needs to increase. We are seeing housing  increase at a very fast rate.
When we came into office , 200 houses per month were being built in Auckland. Now,
750 houses per month are being built in Auckland. The supply of housing is increasing
quite rapidly. The special housing areas are seeing more houses being built as well.
There are about 40,000 -odd sections that have been made available for the special
housing areas. New Zealanders have been giving us a clear message —and it is one that
we have been listening to —that we need to do more about those  who are buying and
selling properties and effectively speculating through the property system. The fact that
we are now stepping up and clarifying the tax situation for New Zealanders, and clearly
outlining that those who trade property within 2 years, re gardless of their intention, will
now be taxed, is, I think, a very positive thing, and one that shows that we are a
Government that does listen to New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: It took 7 years.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Although David Cunliffe, the man opposite who just spoke out,
wanted to go to New Zealanders with an unworkable full -scale capital gains tax, again,
we are doing things in a measured way, in a way in which New Zealanders understand
and appreciate, and in  a way that will make it easy for New Zealanders to understand
their tax obligations. Also, alongside the requirement for IRD numbers to be provided
for those offshore who are buying properties, this measure will see more impact on the
housing market, whic h will benefit Auckland and ultimately all New Zealanders. I
commend this Budget to the House. It is a very good one. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Imagine that t he member who
has just resumed his seat, Jami-Lee Ross, was a plumber or a builder, and that you had a
leaky roof and it took 7 long years for the plumber to come and fix it, and when he
turned up he put a few tiles on and left a few holes so that the wate r kept leaking
through. That is about as good as National’s attempt at solving the housing crisis. There
is a much bigger problem in this Budget. This Budget is a Budget of broken promises. It
3980 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
is a Budget that has a deficit of ideas as well as financing. I n my remarks today, I am
going to quickly run through the headline promises that have been broken. I am then
going to say why this Budget does nothing for the portfolios that it is my privilege to
represent: tertiary education, regional development, and innovation.
The No. 1 broken promise in this Budget is the return to surplus. It was a centrepiece
of National’s re -election campaign. It had been trumpeted for the last 5 years. It is the
reason the Government stopped funding superannuation, it is the reas on that it has
starved pay rises for hard-working New Zealanders, and it is the reason that it has short-
changed research and innovation. It is the reason that it has done a whole lot of things to
get back to surplus, but it did not get there. In the seven th innings —no home run.
Labour—nine out of nine. I wonder how long it is going to take New Zealanders to ask
the question: “If National is so good at managing the economy, why can’t it balance its
cheque book? What is wrong with the National Government tha t it can’t balance its
cheque book?”. If it took 7 years to get a plumber and they could not fix your roof, if it
took 7 years to get an accountant and he could not balance your cheque book, do you
know what you would do? You would get a different one. There may be a lesson in that.

items.speaker: The second broken promise
items.text: Mr Key said that over the next 2 years the Government
was going to create over 150,000 new jobs. Well, it has fallen 60,000 short —60,000
short. He said he would raise the average wage from $55,000 to $62,000. It is $3,000
short. It promised that it would retain the $1,000 kick -start contribution in KiwiSaver.
Hey presto! Next minute it is gone —it is gone. It said that it would not increase any
taxes or bring in any new taxes. This is like President Bus h: “Read my lips: no new
taxes”. Well, we got three in this year’s Budget alone. We got a broadband tax, we got a
visitor tax, and we got a kind of a half -pie capital gains tax with a leaky roof. That is
three new taxes. Just imagine if it could actually d o it properly, but it broke three
promises. It also said it would increase exports to 40 percent. Do you know what?
Exports are going backwards as a percentage of GDP.
This amounts to poor economic management —poor economic management. The
Government has surfed the upside of the recovery after the global financial crisis. That
is the time that you put some money away, you run a surplus, and you pay back the
deficit spending that we accept needed to be done when the economy was in a hole —
except the Governmen t did not, because it could not, because there was no surplus.
National staked its credibility on that and now it has none —now it has none. There is a
deficit of finance and a deficit of ideas.
Part of the reason that National cannot get back to surplus i s that our regions are
going backwards. Unemployment is stubbornly high in places like Northland, the East
Coast, the Manawatū, and the northern South Island. In a lot of our rural and provincial
regions unemployment is at 7 and 8 percent. People cannot ge t jobs and they cannot
move because they cannot sell their houses and move to a bigger centre, because their
house is worth not very much. It is called a poverty trap. The only way to address it is to
get jobs and growth in the regions —in every region—so that New Zealanders can work
their way to a better future. That is what Labour stands for. The clue is in the name:
work. We work to a better, fairer future for all New Zealanders. We stand for giving
hope and resources and a leg-up to every region.
Where is National’s systematic help for the East Coast —Te Tai Rāwhiti—and where
is it in Northland? Simon “Bridges” Bridges is here one day, gone tomorrow. People are
not so stupid. Where is the help in the Bay of Plenty? Where is that harbour project in
Ōpōtoki? Where is the railhead to Northport? Where are the breakthrough projects that
will drive the high -value manufacturing jobs in New Plymouth, where Jonathan Young
comes from, or up and down in Canterbury? Where is the high -tech manufacturing
boom? There is not one, because what has National put up in this Budget? A paltry $25
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3981
million for one to three so-called regional innovation centres. What happens in the other
20 regions? Irrigation New Zealand —Amy Adams’ friend —reckons it has already got
that sewn up. Well, nobody else need apply. I see in the Waikato Times that the Waikato
thinks it is getting one. Well, I do not think so. I think the irrigators have already
trickled away the money. There is nothing strategic for the regions. It is a bit of window
dressing.
What about tertiary education? What is needed is a tangible boost for a sector that
has been under a sinking lid for far too long. It is a sector that has been a driver and
should be a driver of smart ideas, smart graduates, and smart jobs that will help our
economy and our society flourish; a sector where the hard work and professionalism of
both academic and professional staff should be valued and rewarded; and one where all
three roles of higher education are recognised —research, teaching, and its role as a
critic and conscience of society. It should be one where students should be supported to
be the best that they can be, with fair allowances and fair, accessible, affordable loans
right throughout their education, not stopping halfway through a po st-graduate degree
like medicine, dentistry, or a PhD, so that only rich kids need apply.
That is not good enough. That is why Labour says that we will extend student
allowances and student loans for the full term of post -graduate education, including
medicine, dentistry, and doctorates. We are not going to leave our graduate students
high and dry halfway through.
What is the Government now doing for tertiary education? Well, it said it was
pumping in $113 million in the Budget. Really? It took away $17 m illion by limiting
fee rises to 3 percent. It took away $13 million, which is just unspent carry -overs from
last year, then takes away $50 million from the reduced number of tertiary students that
were forecast to come through from Vote Education and anoth er $20 million from the
Inland Revenue Department. And do you know what the result is? It is $113 million in,
$115 million out—there is no new money for tertiary education. There is no new money
for tertiary education at all. That is why Steven Joyce will continue to do what he has
been doing. He will simply say to the universities and the polytechs: “Just make do.
Pass on your costs to the poor old students, and if you really can’t make it, get a few
more students from China.”
That is how the Government i s robbing Peter to pay Paul. It may rearrange the
deckchairs. It gave agriculture —surprise, surprise; the farmers’ friend —20 percent
more and it cut funding for a whole lot of other courses. There was no real boost for the
really smart stuff: the informati on and communications technology that will power our
economy into the future. Like Oliver Twist, students were told to take the crumbs: “Be
grateful. Your fees are going up only 3 percent, not 4 percent. That’ll save you a whole
$60 a year.”

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: At a time when inflation is zero.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: At a time when inflation is zero. Well, Labour is
committed to a full review of student loans and allowances so that any Kiwi kid from
any part of New Zealand  and any family can get the training that they need to be the
best that they can be. It is good for them, it is good for their families, it is good for our
communities, and it is good for our country. That is how we become a small, smart
nation.
This brings me finally to innovation. Where is the boost for innovation? In last year’s
Budget there was $201,622,000. In this year’s Budget there is $201,622,000 —no new
money for innovation. There is no investment in the step change we need to be a smart
country. Broken promises, deficit of finance—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s time has
expired.
3982 Budget Debate 26 May 2015

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOU NG
items.text: Mr Cunliffe, the previous
speaker, asked a couple of questions: where are those high -tech manufacturing firms
and where is that investment that is going to power our economy into the future? I am
very happy to speak about a comp any from Taranaki, which right now is developing a
perpetual motion energy generator from wave energy, transferring it into electricity.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: There goes a first! The National Party believes in perpetual
motion—get the press release out!

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: Look, Labour members mock. They mock. They mock.
When they ask those questions and they are answered, they are not prepared to hear
about the innovation and the technical excellence that is being generated in t he regions.
This company, with the assistance of Callaghan Innovation, right now is testing its
invention off the waters of Hawaii, with great interest coming from international
investors all around the world. So I am quite surprised that Mr Cunliffe, who spouts off,
does not know any of this, because he seems to know everything else.
This is a very disappointing Budget for the Labour Party. It is a very exciting Budget
for thousands of New Zealanders. We saw from the Leader of the Opposition’s reply,
and even from the replies that have come into this House today, what a real lack of
substance there surely is in the attack on this Budget. You would think that the No. 1
attack against this Government, which we have seen for 6 long years, is that this Budget
is one that looks after the big end of town —as I have heard Mr Cunliffe talk about so
many times. But this Budget is exactly the opposite. Without wanting to be cliché -ish,
Mr Little and Mr Robertson were left gasping for air and grasping at straws when th ey
sought to attack this Budget. The strongest line of attack that has come has been that we
have introduced a new tax in the Border Processing (Arrivals and Departures) Levy
Bill.

items.speaker: Kelvin Davis
items.text: A broken promise.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: It is not. As we know, it is a user charge that principally
protects our primary industries from the incursions of biological threat from offshore
travellers. Is it not interesting that of those offshore travellers who come and go from
our country, half of them are not New Zealand citizens? So what we are doing is we are
transferring the cost of the threat they bring to those industries. Is that not smart
economics? And all the time we are protecting our primary industries, which are so
important. Those kiwifruit farmers up in the Bay of Plenty will applaud this legislation,
which will see increased resources for border protection. This is a responsible piece of
legislation that enhances our border security. It shifts the burden of costs away from the
non-travelling public—those who do not often go offshore and overseas —to those who
just by the mere fact of travel create the potential threat.
I come from regional New Zealand. I come from Taranaki, a region that is hard -
working, that is skilled, and that  is successful. We would say that in past years our
region has been very productive for this country. Right now, due to international
commodity prices, we are seeing a decrease in production and profitability coming out
of the Taranaki region, but I am ver y convinced that in due course and in time that will
bounce back, and once again we will see the Taranaki region producing ahead of every
other region in this nation.
When I look back on the past 6 years that I have been in this House, the Taranaki
region has received strong support from this Government. We have a new hospital, we
have a new police station, and we have roading projects that had been unattended and
unsupported now having investment put into them. When I think about the investment
into our transport system and into our roading system, which creates greater safety and
greater economic benefit for our region, I think: “Why haven’t we done this before?
Why in  those long 8 years of surplus did that party over there, which had the purse
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3983
strings of office, not invest? Why didn’t they spend? Why didn’t they spend that
money?”.
You know, the first time that the Waiwhakaiho Bridge and the Northgate route was
raised in a public forum was in 1968. All these years you were crowing about the
fantastic surplus, but you did very little with it. What we have done in the hardest of
times, what we have done in this Government during the time when Christchurch has
demanded su ch support, is we have continued to invest in the regions to enable the
regions to become more and more productive. That is because not only do we have
stronger financial management happening on this side of the House but we have a
commitment to our regions, as we have experienced in Taranaki.
What this Budget has done is commit $790 million over 4 years to the families in this
country who struggle the most. This is what took the Opposition parties by surprise.
You would say that is the response of a party  that cares for New Zealanders, and
Opposition members have never given us that credit. John Key, the Prime Minister of
this nation, continues to surprise people. He has reached back into his past as a young
boy who was raised just by his mum. As he descri bed this Budget, it is a compassionate
but conservative Budget. It is conservative in that we still believe that the way out of
poverty is work, and we will put incentives in place to lead people and incentivise them
to work, but at the same time we care. We want to help those people who, often for no
reason or fault of their own, find themselves in places of deprivation. Just this last
weekend, when I met with many of my colleagues, the Hon Anne Tolley spoke about
this at a conference. The resonance of agr eement in that conference was outstanding.
People felt that this Budget was going to make a real difference for New Zealanders.
This is the very heart of our spending in Budget 2015.
I often hear comments from civic leaders and sometimes from commerce lea ders
saying that in Taranaki we actually want more, and that out of all the royalties that this
region gives to this country, we want some more of that back. Funnily enough, this
became a little bit of an issue in the election campaign of 2014. I think that at a time like
this, when at the very best we have wafer thin margins between surplus and deficit, the
bit extra that some of the people in my region want is a significant bit that those
experiencing deprivation will not get. I found myself in September 2014, in election
2014, having to defend an egalitarian New Zealand against the call of the leader of the
Labour Party, who wanted Taranaki to get more and other regions to get less. I could
not understand it. I could not understand the flip-flop.
What people in New Zealand are starting to wake up to is that—Opposition members
across the way there have always said that the Government is looking after the big end
of town—this Government is looking after all New Zealanders. We understand that in
this country success is something that should be universal. We will go and make the
investment into people’s lives, to enable them to start on the ladder of education and
opportunity.
I have to ask —and I am going back to some figures from a couple of years ago —
when t his previous Government across the way had those 8 years of surplus, but it
claims nine, what did it do with the surplus for what I would say are the most deprived
communities in our country? I am talking about the families who have somebody in
prison. There are 24,000 kids who have a father or mother in prison. Today all prisons
have education screening, with individual learning plans designed for them. The number
of prisoners gaining qualifications has increased under this Government by 830 percent.
Almost 3,000 prisoners will start literacy, which is a 155 percent increase. There has
been an almost 1,500 percent increase in places on drug and alcohol treatment
programmes since 2008—
3984 Budget Debate 26 May 2015

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SP EAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s time has
expired.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: The speaker who has just resumed his seat,
Jonathan Young, asked what the Labour Government did with its n ine surpluses in a
row. We reduced Government debt—

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: There weren’t nine surpluses. There were eight.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: No, we ran nine surpluses in a row —nine. Every Budget
that we ran was a surplus, for 9 years in a row, in contrast —[Interruption] Obviously, it
is a matter of great sensitivity on the other side, because the score is currently 9  nil.
What did we do with those surpluses? We actually applied them to a range of things,
like improved education and health services, but we also used a large amount to reduce
Government debt. Gross Government debt was reduced from 40 percent of GDP to 18
percent of GDP, and net Government debt was reduced from roughly 18 percent of
GDP to zero, zilch, nothing, nada—none was left —so much so that when Bill English
inherited the books, one of the first things he said, when the global financial crisis hit
and he was asked about the state of the Government’s books, was that this was the rainy
day that the Government had been saving for. I think his exact words were: “This is the
rainy day that the Government has been saving for.”
It is true that the Budget bounced well for the Government on the first day. It is
normally the way in respect of Budgets, and it was also true of this Budget. Why was
that? In this case the Government had so depressed people’s expectations of the Budget
that they were expecting that its promise in respect of reaching surplus would be
broken, and they were not expecting any money in it whatsoever for the vulnerable. So
when the Government did announce $25 per week for beneficiary families, people were
surprised and gave the Government some credit for that. As Andrew Little has said on
our behalf, we give the Government some credit for  that. We make a couple of points:
the Government is now at the point where at long last it acknowledges that amongst
some of our families we have very serious levels of deprivation, and the Government’s
own surveys show that. In those measures of deprivat ion they include things like quite
often not having breakfast or quite often not having lunch, never being able to pay your
school fees, sometimes not having shoes or a raincoat —those sorts of things. The
Government now acknowledges that we have that sort of deprivation in New Zealand,
and yet the parents of those children have to look them in the eye and say that in this
wealthy country that is New Zealand, which has a rock star economy, you cannot get
breakfast until 1 April next year, because this $25 a week does not start until next year. I
contrast that with what the Labour Party plan was at the last election: for low -income
families it was $60 a week for every child for the first 3 years of their life.
I want to turn now to some of the other problems that are becoming clear, the longer
you look at the Budget. We, of course, now all know that the Government’s promise of
reaching surplus has not been met. We also know that its promise not to introduce new
taxes has not been met. We know that there is not hing meaningful to overcome the
problems that we have in housing, particularly in Auckland where we have the lowest
rate of homeownership since the 1950s. Indeed, one of the centrepieces of the
legislation passed following the Budget was stopping the Gover nment getting advice
from Housing New Zealand, despite the fact that we have a crisis in housing in
Auckland. We have also got some terribly substandard housing in other parts of the
country, including in the provinces.
I want to talk about the areas that  relate to my portfolio, which is export growth and
trade. Today’s figures of merchandise trade—they came out today, for April—show that
for April 2015, compared with April 2014, exports fell by 5.5 percent. It is a drop of 5.5
percent, year on year. This shows up in the Government’s forecasts, in the external
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3985
deficit that we have as a country. I know that I have taken many barbs over the years
from Bill English, saying that I rattle on too often about the external deficit. But the
truth is that an economy is a bit like a household budget. If your economy is leaking
money to the rest of the world, it is just like your own family budget leaking money to
somebody else. If you do not earn enough money to pay your bills, then at the end of
the year you either ha ve to sell something or take on debt. Our economy is exactly the
same. As an economy we do not sell enough in our exports to pay for our imports plus
our interest and the dividends that we pay overseas. The current account deficit this year
is projected to  go to $13.7 billion. It is a huge amount of money. It is an extra $13.7
billion that we owe to the rest of the world in a combination of debts to the rest of the
world and extra amounts that the rest of the world owns of us, because we sell more of
ourselves to them in order to meet that deficit.
It is against that background that you have to ask what it is that the Government has
done, since it came to power 7 years ago, to change the shape of the economy. How do
you judge it? Well, for a start you would  say that one of the ways you could reasonably
judge it is by assessing its progress against the very targets it set itself. The National
Government came to office saying that we consumed too much in New Zealand, we did
not save enough, and we needed to in crease exports and savings. What has happened?
Well, it is true that New Zealand in the last 7 years has saved a little bit more. The vast
majority of that is insurance receipts that have come in following the insurance claims
in Canterbury, following the Canterbury earthquakes, and also when New Zealanders
put their cheque books away because they felt vulnerable in the recession. But it is also
true that we are now verging on the point —if we have not already crossed over it —
where, as a nation, we are overa ll dissaving. We are overall dissaving at a household
level.
In addition to that, our exports, rather than going up from 30 percent of GDP to 40
percent of GDP, which was the Government’s target, have raced backwards. I say
“raced” because they started at  about 30 percent of GDP. The Government got them up
to close to 31 percent of GDP, and since then our exports as a percentage of the
economy have dropped back. A couple of years ago they went to under 30 percent of
GDP, and now in the year we are having they are forecast to be 26.4 percent of GDP. So
7 years after this Government came into power saying it was going to increase exports
from 30 to 40 percent of GDP, the figure has gone back to 26.4 percent of GDP. Indeed,
even to the end of the forecast period, which is 4 years out, it does not even get up to 28
percent of GDP. That is a massive fail. What is causing it? Well, as Gareth Morgan
says, in New Zealand we are a wealthy country but we misapply capital. We put our
capital in the wrong parts of the e conomy. We do not save enough because we do not
encourage enough savings, and then the capital that we do apply we apply to the wrong
parts of the economy rather than to the more productive parts of the economy. There is
no doubt that the biases we have that encourage that outcome remain.
That leads me to KiwiSaver. KiwiSaver has had the incentives for it cut. In the last
week, at great length, we went through the eight changes that have been made to
KiwiSaver by this National Government, seven of which ar e cuts. I could not
understand the Prime Minister at question time today when he said that this change will
not change savings behaviour. It is just a nonsense. I think that all of us know that the
days when economics was overrun with statistical formula a re over. Behavioural
economics is a very real part of economics, and we know that if you are a young person
starting out in your first part -time job, probably earning only $50 or $100 a week, and
you are saving only a few percent of that and your tax is de ducted from that, then the
amount of increments you are saving, of $2 or $3 a week, does not seem much. It would
almost seem like you are not going to give up much if you do not do it. So a lot of
3986 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
people will not. If you have already got $1,000 in your Kiw iSaver account from the
kick-start contribution and it is growing by $2 or $3 a week, when you are earning only
a small amount anyway, it seems like progress and it seems like you have already got a
significant nest egg.
Good Governments build countries; this Government does not. This Government
cannot build the export economy, it cannot even build enough houses for people to live
in, and it certainly has not built the diversity of economic output that we need in order
to employ people in well-paid jobs.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. I call Jo
Hayes—5 minutes.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: I am pleased and very proud to stand and speak on
this wonderful Budget. Last week we had a ripper of a week, ending at 10 o’clock on
Saturday night. The whole of New Zealand benefits from the wonderful Budget that this
Government has released to the public over the last few days.
I just want to talk a little bit about some of the Budget funds that are actually going
into the Christchurch rebuild. I want to talk a little bit about the anchor projects because
yesterday we were fortunate enough to be part an d parcel of the opening of the bus
interchange in Christchurch City. That was a $53 million project, and was one of our
major anchor projects in the city. That was just one of many anchor projects. The next
big project that we are looking at is the justice  precinct, where we will be bringing
1,700 employees back to the centre of Christchurch. It is co -locating them on a site at
the heart of Christchurch City. This is an amazing, amazing effort.
This Government has stood by Christchurch from September 2010, from the very
first earthquakes, and we will continue to stand by it until our projects have been
completed. I will quote a press release that came from Peter Townsend, who is the chief
executive officer of the Canterbury Employers’ Chamber of Commerce. Th is is what he
said: “It is once again a reinforcement” —that is what this Budget is —“of the
Government’s continuing involvement and its role in the rebuild of Christchurch and in
particular the central city.” That is an amazing statement from Peter Townsend , because
that is exactly what we are doing.
I want to focus a little bit on the east, because some of the projects that have been
happening and the investments that have been happening have been affecting the east —
and it has been a good effect, actually. On the education side of things, we are looking
at the development of the Aranui community education precinct. This is an amazing
project. It will start education right from preschool and will take students right through
to secondary school. This is amazin g because it grows the community from babies all
the way up to young adults, and it hooks up with the tertiary education organisations as
well—Canterbury University and Lincoln University.
I want to talk about the co -location of our secondary schools. We h ave got two
secondary schools—Avonside Girls High School and Shirley Boys High School —that
are being relocated to QEII Park Recreation and Sport Centre. That co-location has been
in the pipeline for a long time. There have been a lot of discussions about i t. The
Ministry of Education has been engaging with the community over a period of a good
18 months, and now the decision has been made that these two high schools will co -
locate to QEII Park Recreation and Sport Centre –the park where, during the
earthquakes, we lost the stadium and the swimming pool, and where quite a lot of the
sportsgrounds were devastated during that period of time. But now it is up and up for
the east. Here we have the co-location of these two high schools.
If that is not enough, take the funds that are going into health in Christchurch.
Burwood Hospital is going to be a beneficiary of the funding for the development of
Christchurch Hospital and Burwood Hospital. What we are going to see over the next 2
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3987
to 3 years is a blossoming of the  east and the Burwood -Queenspark area. We are going
to see that blossom as the schools take off and as the hospital is redeveloped, and the
people of the east are going to get facilities there that are second to none in this world.
Finally—I can see that t he clock is ticking away; 5 minutes is a very short time —I
want to talk a little bit about trades academy. The He Toki ki te Mahi apprenticeship
programme was launched at Rehua Marae just recently. That is a great initiative when it
comes to tertiary educa tion. I heard the Opposition speaker talk about there being no
investment in education. Here is a quote from the Lincoln University deputy vice
chancellor, international and business development, Jeremy Baker. He said: “A 20
percent increase in tertiary fu nding for aquaculture announced in today’s Budget is
being welcomed by the university.” If that is not proof of investment in tertiary
education, then I do not know what is. Christchurch is flourishing, it is growing, and we
are very, very proud to be part and parcel of that whole investment. Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Barbara Kuriger—5 minutes.

items.speaker: BARBARA KURIGER
items.text: It is a pleasure to
take a call this afternoon. I want to focus on how our Government is working for our
regions to reach their full potential. I find it really disappointing that we have heard t he
member David Cunliffe get up this afternoon and talk about the regions. He is a man
who actually has his roots in history in Te Kūiti. It is very disappointing to hear him say
to this House that regional people cannot afford to sell up their houses and buy in
Auckland. Let me tell you, Mr Cunliffe, it is very affordable for your people in
Auckland to actually sell up their houses and come and live in our regions. Let me tell
you something else: I do not know how long it is, Mr Cunliffe, since you have be en in
Te Kūiti, but come and have a look at the new developments and things that are going
on. As a regional electorate MP, I do not accept that people need to sell up their houses
and move back into Auckland. I am actually very focused on what is going on.
If you ever go back to Te Kūiti again, which I invite you to do, you will realise that it
runs off State Highway 3. I want to talk a bit about the roading  packages that are being
put in place. At the moment it takes me about half an hour longer to drive up my
electorate because of the roads that are being developed, particularly the roundabout at
Waitomo. Focusing forward, there is consultation going on about Mount Messenger and
Awakino, which is actually part of the Budget—

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: Is this in the Budget?

items.speaker: BARBARA KURIGER
items.text: Yes, it is. It is roading in the Budget package about
Taranaki, and just exactly —[Interruption] Yes, it is. And just exactly as Mr Young
alluded to before, around the Waiwhakaiho Bridge, State Highway 3—Awakino, Mount
Messenger—is a project that has been on the go for a very, very long time. I am really
proud to be standing here as the member for Taranaki  - King Country, saying that the
consultation is going on right now to get that road up and running because of this
Budget. The second thing is broadband. We have actually got a $100 million expansion
going into rural broadband. It is key to our regional electorates.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: BARBARA KURIGER
items.text: Earlier in the evening before dinner I alluded to the money
that was going towards the Accelerated Regional Roading Package, which is great for
the regions and partic ularly for State Highway 3 in my area in Awakino and Mount
Messenger. Then I got on to the topic of broadband, where there is a $100 -million
expansion of fast reliable broadband to our regions. That is just so critical. We are doing
really well with the schools. We want it spread across further so that the kids are able to
do their homework as well as they can do, so they can learn more, and so that we can
3988 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
have some more businesses that operate off the internet and high technology that is able
to operate out in the regions. As we said before, it is just such a wonderful place to live.
The other thing as part of the Budget package is $50 million to extend the mobile
coverage and black spots. As we all know we have got quite a number of black spots in
the regional roading network so it is good to see those fixed up, but it is also imperative
that we have the cellphone coverage to go with that. Unfortunately, when people do
have an accident they need the opportunity to ring for help as fast as they possibly can.
I would also like to commend the $25 million over 3 years that is going into regional
research institutes. That is really important because although there are some issues that
cover right across the region, each region has its unique features. It is really important to
do the research out in the regions, to talk to the local people about what is needed, and
apply it there. I have to say also that to get the border processing levy across the line the
other night was such a pleasure, because, actually, a bi g risk to our regions is having
some sort of disease or pest brought in. We all know that tourists are, unfortunately,
some of the big contributors to the dangers that are posed to our economy.
It is a real pleasure to take a call on this bill tonight. I a m really proud to be part of a
National Government that has presented a very, very good Budget 2015.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: This is a split call for the Green Party—5 minutes each.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: Talofa lava, Mr Deputy Speaker. Ngā mihi
nui ki a koutou i tēnei pō. Yep, the Budget. Yep, it happened. Yep, we survived. I was
looking for the plan. All I still hear is the “mine it to death” plan or “m ilk it dry” plan.
Amidst shaky international economic times we are going to mine it and milk it, which is
a continuation of the previous Budgets that I have heard, but it is a strategy that is not
really going to work, sorry. There is a group of people mis sing out. There is definitely a
group of people missing out, and they are the abandoned generation of people who do
not want to mine Aotearoa New Zealand and do not want it milked dry at the expense of
their rivers. They have nothing against milk; just not at the expense of their rivers.
It is important that we look at the Budget in the context of what is actually happening
for the generation of people who are going to have to pay for the decisions we make. If
we have 60 percent of our rivers unswimmable b ecause they are full of nitrates and
phosphorus, we are going to leave that cost with the next generation. If, as the Budget
did, we ignore climate change, we are going to leave that cost with another generation.
That generation has been out this week atte nding so -called consultation meetings on
climate change, etc., which were not reported on or considered seriously by the media
or by the Government, but they actually spoke for a generation of people who are not
going to keep quiet about what is going to h appen to them. We, as a party, are going to
stand up for those people because they actually need to have their issues addressed.
They should not be carrying the cost of our negligence. The Government is out of touch
with their economy, and those young people are our future economy.
Our present economy is swimming in debt. People cannot have their own home, their
wages are stagnating, and a quarter of our kids are still in poverty. This is not a Budget
that will deal with that. This is a Budget that has tou ched cleverly on a range of issues,
but it has lost touch with the every day, and it has chosen to build an economy that
works for only some of us. There is another way, and we do believe that we have got
some great ideas for doing it more positively.
Looking specifically at the money spend in some of my portfolios, in the area of
water, the Government has put more money in the Budget for more conversation about
water. But, meanwhile, the actual decisions are being made in the courts, some in a
precautionary manner and some in a business -as-usual manner. All we know and all we
can see, if you go out to the communities and look at water, is that the water is
deteriorating.
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3989
Meanwhile, the Government’s supposedly best -practice farm, Landcorp, is assisting
others to continue the conversions from forestry to dairying —despite the extremely
serious issues for dairy farmers around the price —and it wants to commodify our water
and use it for dairying and then dump the cost from the Upper Waikato conversions on
to the Lower Waikato farmers and communities. We are going to have approximately —
and this is, I am told, a conservative estimate —29,500 more cows in that catchment.
The nitrates will be leaching into the lakes and awa —the rivers—downstream, and this
Government is going to continue to fund a conversation about that. Actually, what it
could do is stop Landcorp from being an irresponsible farmer, but is it going to do that?
Pigs, let alone cows, will fly on that one.
The Government is also giving a subsidy to irri gators, with an additional $25 million
going to Irrigation New Zealand, the Government’s acceleration group, to promote
some unpopular and destructive dam projects that could add to these pollution statistics
and increase the pollution of our beautiful and  precious fresh water, which we, as a
Parliament, should be protecting. That $25 million is great news for the irrigators, but
not necessarily great news for the communities, so we wonder why the Government is
doing that. Why is it subsidising this industr y? Who chose irrigation? We are not
subsidising an awful lot —this is supposed to be the free market. What has happened?
How come these guys cannot manage on their own? How come they need a big handout
from the Government? Interesting —interesting who gets s ubsidised in this Budget.
Very interesting.
I would also like to touch briefly, in my short time, on the education appropriation.
That was not enough—a 1 percent increase in the operating grant for schools. Last year
it was a generous 2 percent, which was  not anywhere near enough, and now it is 1
percent. There are now two new charter schools being promoted without our having a
review of the existing models. Many of the existing first four charter schools, and then
the other nine, are not in the best shape , but they are a sop to Mr Seymour, so they have
got to go ahead. Lest we forget, this was supposedly about our priority learners, such as
Māori, Pasifika, and disabled students. Look closely at what is actually happening at the
charter schools and we can see that that is not what is happening. We are not making a
game-changer for those students.
So we are pretty disappointed with this Budget. We are concerned about the
abandoned generation, and we will keep talking about what else we can do better.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: A 5-minute call—Denise Roche.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: This is a Budget that has not addressed any of New
Zealand’s fundamental problems. It is a start, but it will not lift enough kids out of
poverty, it will not help address the gap between the haves and have -nots, and it
certainly does not address the fundamental issue of our time, which is climate change. It
is a political Budget that has made, or continue s to make, the thousands of cuts that
have happened under this Government. From the medical students who will not become
doctors because of the changes for fulltime -equivalent students to the single mum who
cannot upskill and move up due to the cutting of the retraining grant, this Government
has ignored people who are marginalised.
When and where the Government has paid attention, it has paid attention due to the
public outcry and attention from ordinary New Zealanders, and that includes things like
the zero-hour contracts and getting child poverty into the Budget at all this time. Credit
where credit is due, but I want a Government that cares about issues not because it is
popular and not because of the polls but because it genuinely cares about those who  are
marginalised.
One of those marginalised groups is refugees. This Budget will make life for
refugees even tougher than it is. The $1.5 million cut in funding for essential refugee
3990 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
protection services has the potential to send an already vulnerable gro up overseas. It
will strand them. Refugees live at risk of their lives in hot spots, and they stand to stay
stranded in those areas because of the bottleneck of the unheard cases.
We are going to spend $24.4 million over the next 2 years sending New Zealan ders
to support the Iraqi army. But for a fraction of that we could be taking concrete steps to
protect vulnerable refugees from human rights abuses in some of the places that they are
caught in. We think refugees need to be resettled as soon as possible s o that they can
integrate and get on with their lives. It will make a huge difference for the lives of so
many people.
What about migrant workers in New Zealand? They are another marginalised group.
How do they fare under this Budget? The Government annou nced a package of $33
million for immigration, but that money is going to be spent on border control, not
necessarily on seeing to the needs of migrant workers. Recent high -profile cases have
shown that there is a need for better education and information for employers about
minimum standards, but also for migrant workers so that they know their rights.
Essentially, we also need strong compliance to ensure migrant workers are not
exploited.
I recognise that the Government has announced a funding increase for six new labour
inspectors for Auckland. That is to be applauded. However, we lag behind international
standards in terms of the ratio of workers to compliance officers. In New Zealand it is
about one inspector for 14,162 workers. That is about double what happens in Australia.
With the deregulated labour market that we have —and workers’ rights have, basically,
been steadily eroded under this Government —it is essential that we have some kind of
compliance for workers and particularly for vulnerable worker s, like migrant workers.
Seasonal workers, for example, are also at risk of exploitation, and I note that we have
got only five labour inspectors who are specialists in this area for the recognised
seasonal workers’ scheme.
This Budget is a case of Peter being robbed to pay Paul. There is a reduced allocation
for WorkSafe New Zealand. There was a promised increase in health and safety
inspectors when WorkSafe New Zealand was set up in 2012 —$37 million over 4 years.
But this Budget says there will be a redu ction. And we still have not recovered the
number of health and safety inspectors we had before 2012. We need that compliance to
occur if we want people to come home safe and unharmed from their jobs. This Budget
leaves a lot of people behind. It makes it harder for families to get ahead, and we
certainly could be doing a lot better.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: It is with absolute
pleasure that I stand and actually get to put on record just how proud I am of this
National-led Government’s Budget for 2015. It has been my first Budget as an
Associate Minister of Finance, and so I have worked my way through it with  the
guidance of Bill English, actually looking at what needed to be done and where we
could address the needs of this country.
It is easy to forget, actually, that we have an average growth rate of 2.8 percent, and
that we are projecting 150,000 more jobs to come on board. I remember the calls when
we were saying that there would be 170,000 more jobs, and it would be fair to say t hat
we were derided by the left. They took every opportunity that they could to throw that
back at us. Well, here we are, saying: “No, no, we did not do 170,000. Actually, the
economy has produced 194,000 more jobs, which have been created since 2011.” And
that makes a fundamental difference for New Zealanders —that, and seeing the average
wage increase; that, and seeing, actually, people able to have more money in their
pockets and able to get the jobs that, quite frankly, they do deserve in this country; t hat,
and seeing us project that unemployment will continue to drop and employment will
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3991
continue to rise. You can see from the projections in this Budget that we are heading,
well and truly, to that 4.5 percent unemployment rate.
But what is different, wha t is fundamentally different, in how we look at that
unemployment rate is that we are actually not putting all of that sort of slightly
discretionary funding, where we assist people with CVs and skills and training, and help
them to get work -ready, on to j ust those who are on the unemployment benefit. What
you can see is that over the last 6½ years we have moved resources to those who
fundamentally need them the most. And, yes, we reset obligations, as we did a bit more
of in this Budget.
But I want to tak e people back to when we first came into Government in 2008. I
was the then Minister for Social Development and Employment, and I will never ever
forget sitting in a room in Paris with my colleagues, with welfare and employment
Ministers from around the wo rld, and they fundamentally could not believe —in fact I
had to repeat it about four times —that we had absolutely no work obligations for
someone who was on welfare, until their youngest turned 18, and who could then have
another baby and get another 18 yea rs of no work obligations. They fundamentally
could not believe that we did not have balance in what we expected of people.
As a consequence, it was actually worse than that. We did not put any resource or
extra into helping them get work-ready. So we did—we reset. We reset the balance. We
made sure that those people had hope and opportunities. We reset the balance that had
never been there in the welfare system, so that they could actually create a better life for
themselves and their children. As a conse quence of that and many changes, we now
have the lowest number of sole parents on welfare since the 1980s—1988 I think it is.
But what people forget is that we could not have actually made the changes to
welfare and given those families who still are ther e an extra $25 a week on average —
we could not do that if we had not reset the balance, if we had not actually got some
mutual obligations within the system in those previous years. It is not just the work of
the last 12 months that leads us to a place wher e we can produce a Budget that is giving
back to those who most certainly are having it tough and living hard lives on very
limited incomes, where we can put more in their pockets that goes to helping them and
their children. The way that we are able to do  that is over many years of resetting our
social policy to make sure that we are helping those who need it most, and making sure
that they actually recognise what changes need to be made.
I have heard many from the opposite side say that this does not mak e a difference.
Well, it makes a huge difference. Actually, $25 makes an absolutely huge difference.
Also, though, we really wanted to make sure, as we worked our way through this
package—and we have spent a lot of hours and a lot of time debating and look ing at it
from every angle—that we were also increasing Working for Families and making sure
that those who did go into jobs and were still on low wages were able to reap those
rewards as well. We are making sure that we have the obligations right, that pe ople are
able to get into work, that they get the extra assistance through agencies like the
Ministry of Social Development, through education and other skills and training —but
then, equally, for those who do go into jobs, making sure that they get assista nce on that
extra pay, so that we are keeping that balance right, that work really does pay. From
everything that you look at, it is work that makes the biggest and most fundamental
difference in people’s lives. When we could, we have. At the first chance that we have
had to increase benefits for the first time in nearly —what is it —43 years, we took that
opportunity to put money in the pockets of those who need it most.
If I am to be a little negative, which is not really my thing, I would have said that t he
Opposition was expecting us, if we were going to do anything, to do sort of nine or 10
bucks. Yeah? And we all then would have gone around thinking we had done a good
3992 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
