thing. We knew that we could, and it was absolutely important —as we worked our way
through what was actually quite a tough Budget process of trying to make sure that we
are actually looking after the needs of those who work for our agencies and are
expecting a wee pay rise, for those who have got cost pressures there —that we set real
money aside to go to real people who needed that help and assistance. That says, I think,
a lot for this Government, and a lot for the leadership, quite frankly, of our Prime
Minister. When he stood up  on election night, ladies and gentlemen, and said, having
accepted the win: “This National -led Government will govern for all people.”, here is
the evidence of it. It is in black and white. It is in this Budget that he stands by what he
said, and he stands there and says: “I will govern; we will govern. This Nation al-led
Government will be there for all people.” When he could give back, under his
leadership and under this hardship package, that is what he delivered to New
Zealanders.
I also want to just touch on another part of that hardship package that has not be en
touched on much, I do not think, from what I have heard so far, which is the increase in
the childcare subsidy. What perhaps some of us knew instinctively was that if you
removed barriers and believed in and backed these women and children, then they
would take every opportunity to make a difference in their lives and in the lives of their
children. They have proven that by the tens of thousands who have gone off welfare
when we have actually rebalanced.
What they also need, though, as I indicated, is t hose barriers removed. One of the
biggest barriers is the cost of childcare. So for those who are looking for extra
assistance, we have put the subsidy up from $4 to $5, which is a 20 percent increase in
what we will actually pay to help them while they ar e working, so that they can get that
extra assistance.
The other thing that I do not think people have realised so much —and it is not
necessarily in this Budget —is that about a year ago we also really relaxed the rules on
what we will pay for as far as ch ildcare is concerned. Too often it was just about the
creche down the road or the day care centre, although for many parents they are
working different hours and they want more flexibility with that. That is part of how we
are actually getting there and how we are rebalancing it.
You could hold this Budget up in the world —and I do not say that lightly —and
know that you are extremely proud of it and that New Zealand is more than punching
above its weight, as it does so well. As a country we actually have th e economy well
and truly on track and are delivering to all New Zealanders as we see the average wage
increase, as we see those on welfare being assisted with a bit more money, as we see
more jobs coming on board, the support for the regions, and also the support for our
businesses that is recognised daily through a Budget that is delivered like this.
I am incredibly proud to be a part of a team —and it is a pretty big team, and it is a
pretty great one —that cares a lot about this stuff and that has spent th e time on really
using the data analytics, using the information that we have, and making sure we pull
that together in the best interests of all New Zealanders. I am really proud to stand up
and support what, as I say, is a really strong team that is, act ually, backing a really
strong, growing economy. Thank you.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: Talofa lava. I will say something
for the Government members, and that is that they are goo d at the spin. They are good
at the political spin and they are good at telling you that everything is great when,
behind the scenes, it is another story. I listened to the previous speaker —the new
Associate Minister of Finance, Paula Bennett —talk about fu ndamentally moving
resources to where they are needed most. Well, how does that fit with what the
Government is doing to social housing —fundamentally dismantling the social housing
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3993
scheme and the role of the State in providing housing for the most vulnerab le in our
society? Not one more house is coming out of its grand new plan, which is not a new
plan.
I would also like to say something to a previous National speaker, new MP Barbara
Kuriger, who spoke about the importance of fast broadband in rural New Zea land,
which is so important. It is so important that there is the right investment and that the
investment goes where it is needed. I am sure she, as an MP in rural New Zealand and
Taranaki, would know—in fact, I know that she does know because I know that  she has
many people coming through her door complaining about their broadband —that,
unfortunately, the Government has already spent $300 million in rural New Zealand,
and it is still not working. That is a real problem, which is why Labour fought against
that piece of legislation pushed through under urgency on Friday night.
My colleague Grant Robertson described this as a politician’s Budget. It has also
been described as many things, but one of them is a Budget of broken promises around
the surplus, around wage and job targets, and, of course, around those three new taxes.
“No new taxes.” said the Prime Minister. “No new taxes.” said the campaign literature
before the election. But what have we got? We have got three new taxes. The economist
Rod Oram put it really well when he said in the Sunday Star-Times this weekend: “this
Budget, as the six before it, is a triumph of micro -management. The Government has
mastered the art of switching small sums [of money] around to give the illusion of
progress.” Well, how true that is. How true that is. This is the “sticking plaster Budget”
and the “piecemeal Budget”, with no vision, no plan, and no real hope.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: 25 bucks a week is not a small sum of money.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: Yes, I absolutely acknowledge that $25 a week is going to
make a small difference, but you tell me —excuse me, Mr Deputy Speaker, not you —
but can the Government tell me how that is going to address the fundamental causes of
child poverty. Well, it is just not. If you live in regional New Zealand you could be
forgiven for barely registering this Budget.
Once upon a time —as I am sure you would remember, Mr Deputy Speaker, and as
many of the people in the House would recall —the Budget was a must -listen-to yearly
event. There were big structural changes. There were wide -ranging visions. It was an
opportunity for Governments of the day to show their core thinking and direction. This
Budget has no structural shifts in it. There is no accounting for the ageing population.
There is no recognition of the rapid technological change and its impact on jobs. There
is no money for innovation. There is no money for regional development. There is no
money for the productive economy and for exports. There is no investment in those
things. Instead, we have had KiwiSaver’s kick -start snatched away —the savings of
future generations.
This is a Budget of broken promises. We have seen, firstly, the taxing of capital
gains—not a capital gains tax but the taxing of capital gains for propert y investors has
expanded—secondly, an airport tax charging people to enter or leave New Zealand; and,
thirdly, a broadband tax that increases the charge on the telecommunications industry,
which has already resulted in an increase of broadband prices. We h ave got a Minister
for Communications, Amy Adams, who does not talk to the industry, to the consumers,
or to consumer representatives. She does not listen. She insists that black is white. In
fact, she stood in this House on Friday night and insisted that a levy is not a tax.
I just want to show everybody Colin James’ piece in the Otago Daily Times  this
morning and the headline “We know a levy’s a tax, Mr English”. I think the
Government has lost on that one. It rammed through a special law under urgency to give
the Government power to levy or tax the telecommunications industry to implement
part two of a scheme for rural broadband, which was $150 million. So why did we fight
3994 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
it? We support better broadband, absolutely, for rural New Zealand. It was us who
provided the strong policy leading into the election for community -based rural
broadband to try to address the real issues that were happening in rural New Zealand,
but $300 million has already been spent in rural New Zealand, and that has not been a
great success. How do we know this? We know this because rural New Zealand keeps
telling us, whether there are petitions from communities, whether they have come to
select committees in Parliament, as three of them did last week, or whether it is
organisations like Rural Women, which come and talk to us about the state of rural
broadband. We know that Federated Farmers are worried. We even know that 68
percent of businesses and households are extremely frustrated in rural New Zealand,
because there was a piece o f market research by Colmar Brunton for Chorus done just
before the election. But there has been no analysis—no reports. The only figures that we
have show a few thousand connections, there have been towers upgraded and new ones
built, and the copper network has been improved, but this is infrastructure that is owned
by private companies, which are benefiting from it.
Is it benefiting rural New Zealand? Where is the analysis? Where are the reports? I
note that members have all got their heads down over the re because they know there are
not any. So what does the Minister say? Well, she says: “It’s my way or the highway.”,
she says to everybody. She says that it is a levy; it is not a tax. She said the
telecommunications companies would not pass it on. Well, within an hour of the debate
starting in Parliament last week, one of the telecommunications companies had already
announced it was passing it on because it was a tax. Whether that is a good thing or not
is to one side, but the fact is that that is what is  happening and it is a tax on consumers.
She, of course, said that that would not happen, and it did.
Is a levy a tax? No, it is a user charge, says the Minister. Is a tax on alcohol a user
charge? Is a tax on cigarettes a user charge? Is a tax on petrol a user charge? Well, the
Minister has certainly lost the argument on that one. The $150 million —there is no
guarantee it will work. There is no guarantee that that money will not be used to finish
off the first version of rural broadband. There is no guara ntee that smaller community
providers will get a look in. It needs an inquiry, it needs examination, it needs sunlight,
and it shows poor economic management, poor judgment, and a fundamental lack of
understanding and good project management.
Finishing up, Chorus came out today pleading with the Government to move fast on
Resource Management Act reforms in order to free up the roadblocks in the ultra -fast
broadband project.

items.speaker: Todd Barclay
items.text: Well, why don’t you support the RMA reform?

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: Well, we have always said we would consider sensible changes
to the Resource Management Act. We had some in our environment policy. We had a
policy on telecommunications companies that said we would fix these things as soon as
possible. It has been 8 months since the election. There has been no movement on this.

items.speaker: We say to the Minister for the Environment
items.text: “Put those changes on the table, Nick
Smith. Let us see them. Where are they?”. And good on Chorus for putting the pressure
on, on that issue.

items.speaker: DARROCH BALL
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise on behalf of New Zealand
First to make some comments on the Budget. I will be concentrating my comments on
the changes to the social services  area. The first thing I would like to do is to ask a
question. That question is about the Budget: has the Government addressed the very
worst levels of child poverty in New Zealand with its Budget announcement last
Thursday? The answer is, unsurprisingly,  a definitive no. After persistently ignoring 40
years of research on a topic, with expert advisory group recommendations largely
ignored, why all of a sudden a U -turn? The Government has been in power for 7 years,
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3995
and for 7 years it has denied it, denied the scale of the problem. We have the Prime
Minister, who usually shrugs most things off, including the problem of child poverty.
But worst of all is that in those 7 years the Government has failed to address it. So why
the U-turn? Probably because of the public pressure and post -election promises in the
face of widespread public protestation.
We are already witnessing the Government reverting to its ideological blind spot on
child poverty. On Thursday we had a Budget preaching about the focus on child poverty
and the needy, and just 2 days ago we had Mr English commenting about the anti -
poverty figures. The article in the New Zealand Herald has the title: “English hits back
at anti-poverty figures”. It goes on to say that “P rofessor Jonathan Boston refuted the
minister’s claims, saying Mr English ‘ doesn’t understand how poverty measures are
calculated’.” Mr English’s response to that, in an interview on Q+A, is that
“campaigners like Prof Boston and the Children’ s Commissioner used an unrealistic set
of measures to quantify poverty in New Zealand .” The funny thing is that during Mr
English’s Budget speech he said this: “Two -thirds of children in more severe material
hardship have a parent on a benefit, and nine out of 10 of those are sole parents”.
Where did he get that measure of severe hardship from? In order to get to this
conclusion, he would have to be using the very calculation of poverty used by Professor
Jonathan Boston, the same man he criticised on national TV for the way in which he
calculated it. So I challenge the Minister to prove where he got those figures from and
by which method. He cannot continue to contradict himself and say that Professor
Boston has an unrealistic set of measures, and yet use those exact same measures in his
speech. That is a blatant attempt to diminish expert opinion. The public can now quite
clearly see that the Minister of Finance has no idea about how poverty measures are
calculated. It is a poor start to the Government’s acknowledgment of the problem —far
less than a step in the right direction.
We know that the measures the Government announced on Thursday  will not lift
those children out of poverty. The Children’s Commissioner, someone else whom the
Government does not listen to, himself said that it will not bring families out of poverty,
and he is calling for a comprehensive plan. So all pre -Budget, all at the end of last year,
there was this promise from the Government, from the Minister for Social
Development, and from the Minister of Finance about a comprehensive plan to tackle
child poverty and vulnerable children. What we got was not even a skeleton of a plan.
They have not even done the map recce yet.
So where is the package? Where is the plan? The measures announced in the Budget
are piecemeal and they are disappointing. Put quite simply, this Government is
continuing to fund supported poverty. Bei ng a step in the right direction is not enough
to warrant a vote of confidence for, or indeed acceptance of, this Budget. One can never
win a game of cards if they are given only one single card to play with. How are these
people in poverty with vulnerable  children expected to get out of their way of poverty,
to work their way out of poverty, to fight their way out of poverty with just $25 a week?
The Government has given them that one card to play with. These moves are a token
effort to appease the general  concern of the New Zealand public at the plight of an
unacceptable number of our children. We want to hold on to the country we once
proudly advocated for, when we travelled around the globe proud of a land of equal
opportunity, but now we are reminded by  the National Government that times have
changed and that we need to focus on quite a long -term savings for the Crown—on cost
cutting, on more efficiency, and on better investment.
How did child poverty end up being about what these children will cost us in the
future? Why is it not about the New Zealand vision that every one of these children
should have an equal opportunity to contribute to our society? New Zealand First
3996 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
believes in the fundamentals of a social welfare system that provides a robust safet y net.
No one should fall below this most minimum of levels —no family and no child. It
should not be a reward; nor should it be a punishment. It should not be a matter of
approval for a Budget change; it should be an automatic expectation. Anything less
would mean we are all leaving our principles behind for the sake of financial
convenience and outright judgment.
The Government’s investment approach stretches it further. Now each person who
requires a social service has a dollar sign floating above their head. If their need does
not fit within the criteria of the Government’s targets, then the dollar is extinguished
and the individual is left to fend for themselves. If a social agency tries to look after all
of its clients’ needs, it will run adrift. If a service attempts to exist in the regions where
the client numbers are low, it will struggle, falter, and disappear. So if you are a young
person looking for support in a small provincial town, tough. Your need is not
financially sustainable. Where in this do we allow for a community to identify its own
needs and provide a response? Will a coupon system for social services mean less
supply and lower quality, just as it did with the voucher system for childcare that was
evaluated in Sweden and Australia?
We have seen social services retracting. Most recently, we have seen the struggles of
our biggest counselling agency, Relationships Aotearoa, and the release today of an
article “Government forces closure of Relationships Aotearoa”. It goes on to say:
“Unfortunately, our financial position worsened by Government’s needless delay means
we cannot afford to transition clients. We had hoped to transition clients  [more]. …
Government could have easily reached an agreement with us that was equitable for all
concerned. It is fair to say that we feel betrayed  … it is likely that our doors will be
closed to our 7000 current clients by the end of the week .” But this Government would
rather spend around $30 million on a flag referendum. Where is the priority shown by
this Government?
Two months ago we met with the Salvation Army youth education and employment
unit. It has just shut down branches in Kaikohe, Matamata, Wairoa, Waipukurau, and
Blenheim. The common theme in all of those is they are all regional. Why did they shut
down? They were not financially viable. One would have to ask where this will end.
Where is the plan by this Government to ensure that the essential safety net that is
faltering, in our provinces  especially, remains intact and maintains its integrity? This
Budget surely did not deliver confidence in that.
New Zealand First wants more than just a $2 a day down payment for the 250,000
children living in poverty. We want front -end investment focused on our youth. Simply
increasing the benefit is lazy. It lacks focus and it lacks realism of the understanding of
the real issue. Instead, it tries to plug a gap over the symptoms. The Government has
ignored our young people in this Budget. The Government m ay not care, but the vast
majority of New Zealand cares about the future generations. As Mark Powell, chief
executive officer of The Warehouse, said this weekend: “A flourishing society equals
flourishing business.”

items.speaker: May I lastly say this
items.text: if we are to mai ntain that minimum social floor that no one
should fall through, we need a heavy focus on our youth. Unemployed youth become
unemployed adults who remain on a benefit and bring children and families into
poverty. Acting too late with too little should never be acceptable.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: Talofa lava, Mr Assistant Speaker. It
was great to see you come into the House and greet us with a Samoan greeting. This
week we are celebrating Samoan Language Week. In New Zealand —the most diverse
country in the world —it is very important that we acknowledge the cultures that we
have adopted. The Samoan language is the third most spoken language in New Zealand,
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3997
and I appreciate those who are still continuing to speak their language and are
continuing with their culture. Today we also celebrate Africa Day in Parliament. It
shows another example of diversity in our country, and we are lucky to have people
from different ethnicities representing us in various areas.
It is my pleasure to participate in this debate on the Budget. As we know, the
appropriation bills are the basis on which Parliament authorises the executive to incur
expenses and capital expenditure. Each year, the Minis ter of Finance places in front of
this House the Budget, which provides appropriations for the coming year. I would like
to congratulate the Hon Bill English on presenting an excellent seventh Budget, and I
am proud to be part of this team. For the past 7 years, thanks to the strong leadership
provided by the Prime Minister and our finance Minister, this National -led Government
has provided prudent Budgets that have proven instrumental in the New Zealand
economy’s excellent growth.
I was talking to my frien ds based in Melbourne, and they were full of praise for our
Government for presenting an excellent Budget; so much so that one of my friends said
that he would like to move to New Zealand to live because it is a better place to live —
and that has been prove n in the last 7 years. There was a time when 50,000 Kiwis were
migrating to Australia each year, but the trends are changing. Now Australians are
moving to New Zealand.
A survey conducted by Statistics New Zealand and published today indicates that
New Zealanders are highly satisfied with their lives, with people rating their sense of
purpose highly. The New Zealand General Social Survey conducted by Statistics New
Zealand, which provided the above result, was based on a survey of 9,000 people. The
General Social Survey is the biggest social survey conducted by Statistics New Zealand
outside the 5 -yearly Census of Population and Dwellings. This independent survey by
the country’s most credible organisation proves what we in the National Party and the
Government have been sharing with this House and New Zealanders for some time. The
leadership of New Zealand has done an outstanding job in steering this country forward
in the difficult times. Here I would like to congratulate the Hon Paula Bennett, who did
a lot of work in social welfare, which has been appreciated worldwide and is now being
continued by the Hon Anne Tolley.
In this Budget, the honourable Minister of Finance has once again provided excellent
vision for New Zealanders. The Budget makes excellent allowances for issues that
matter to New Zealanders. The Minister of Finance has announced that this National-led
Government will deliver a $790 million package to support children who live in poor
families. This amount will be balanced between sole parent s and the provision of $25
per week more for families that may be on some form of income support. The
Government has also announced in the Budget that we will increase the Working for
Families payment. There is also an increased focus from our side of the House on
providing more childcare support for low-income families to help parents to be in work,
education, or training. Budget 2015 makes allowances for a further $60 million in extra
support for at-risk children. We know from experience that the best way to help families
and children out of hardship is through employment. Keeping this in mind, we are
allocating $32.5 million for services that help beneficiaries to move into the workforce.
I would like to reiterate that we are allocating $32.5 million to h elp beneficiaries to
move into the work force. These initiatives confirm that this National -led Government
focuses on building a stronger economy, and that delivering Better Public Services is
working for New Zealand families.
In addition to taking steps t o improve the economy, we have said from the very start
that this National -led Government has zero tolerance for corruption, and we remain
committed to maintaining New Zealand’s robust reputation. That is why this Budget has
3998 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
allocated $218 million to the j ustice sector. The Budget provides an extra $8.1 million
over the next 4 years for the operating fund of the Serious Fraud Office. This further
enables the Serious Fraud Office to fight bribery and corruption and to create a business
environment that is fr ee of serious financial crime. The Department of Corrections will
receive more than $6 million from the justice sector. Also, the new operating fund of
$164 million over the next 4 years for the New Zealand Police shows that the
Government is investing mor e and more in creating communities that are away from
crime-related activities. There has been a 22 percent drop in recorded crime over the
past 5 years, and we have been successful in disrupting organised crime. We have over
600 extra police officers on t he front line. They are helping to safeguard vulnerable
communities.
I take this opportunity to thank the New Zealand Police for making New Zealanders
feel secure, while at the same time developing constructive relationships with the people
who belong to different cultural backgrounds. The New Zealand Police has been able to
successfully identify issues of victimisation within ethnic communities and to develop
culturally appropriate strategies that are implemented in order to increase the
community’s safety. This funding will support the police in providing more effective
policing and will help in preventing crime, to a huge extent.
There are some positive points of our economy that I would like to share here. New
Zealand is on track for an average of 2.8 pe rcent growth a year over the next 4 years.
This strong growth is forecast to deliver another 150,000 new jobs over the next 4 years.
Government debt is expected to be less than 20 percent of GDP by 2020 -21, when we
can resume full contribution to the Super annuation Fund. This is a Budget that is
responsible and based on a plan. The Government can deliver when it is following a
plan that is working. It is because of the prudent plan in all areas that we have
announced a record investment of $15 billion in he alth. New Zealanders and their
families should have access to timely, quality health care no matter where they live. The
health budget will reach a record $15.9 billion this year —a clear sign of National’s
commitment to supporting the growing public health  service. We are investing $1.7
billion over the next 4 years in new initiatives and to meet cost pressures and population
growth. Budget 2015 also includes $12 billion to extend the Waitematā District Health
Board’s bowel cancer screening pilot, to start in December 2017.
Despite the economic challenges, National is focused on delivering high -quality
services for New Zealanders in areas that make a huge difference. Of course, we
understand that to continually pay for these and other services we need to ha ve a well-
trained and skilled workforce. We are spending $10.8 billion on education. These are
the plans we have for New Zealanders, and I commend this Budget to the House.

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: We heard a lot of statistics there but it
reminded me of a great quote, because that speaker uses statistics like a drunken man
uses a lamp post—for support not illumination.
There was a very interesting answer —[Interruption] Thanks for that, mate. T here
was a very interesting answer that John Key gave in question time today to a question
that was asked by, I think, Andrew Little. He talked about the number of overseas
investors buying houses in New Zealand. Mr Key said: “You don’t know that fact. No
one knows.” You know what? He is dead right, and that is the problem we have got. No
one knows how many foreigners are buying houses in New Zealand. Nobody knows the
impact that foreigners are having on the Auckland housing market. So when John Key
and Bill English come out and say that they are now going to require overseas investors
to have IRD numbers and bank accounts, what I would like to know is how they are
going to police that.
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3999
The reason I bring this up is that one of my shadow portfolios is land information.
Land Information New Zealand is responsible for overseeing the Overseas Investment
Act, and the Overseas Investment Act is about making sure that those who come in and
buy sensitive New Zealand assets or sensitive New Zealand land go through t he right
process. Looking through the Budget, I made an assumption —I could be wrong here —
that it would be the Overseas Investment Act that would be in charge of monitoring
foreigners buying houses in New Zealand.
The problem we have at the moment is that the Overseas Investment Office is way
behind in consents. Technically, it has to have a consent approved or a sale and
purchase agreement signed off within 65 days of signing if it requires Overseas
Investment Office consent. Technically, there are a whole  lot of sale and purchase
agreements now in place with foreign investors that are redundant, that have fallen by
the wayside, because the Overseas Investment Office has not got the staff to monitor
this consent process. If it is going to be asked to monito r this new process —and I, for
the life of me, could not figure out who else would do it—then I do not know where it is
going to get the resources for it, because there is not a cent extra in the Budget for this,
certainly not under Land Information or the Overseas Investment Office.
One thing I would like to talk about is that I am a provincial MP and I get a little bit
sick and tired of hearing people say that the provinces are failing because, as you know
yourself, Mr Deputy Speaker, the provinces are no t failing. In fact, there are some
fantastic stories of businesses that are doing incredibly well in the provinces, and
certainly there is a whole number of them in my electorate of Napier. But they could be
doing a lot better. My firm belief is that if we are to maximise economic development in
the regions, it has to be a partnership between local government, central government,
and key stakeholders. So what I was looking for in this Budget and what I would have
really liked to see is a commitment to regional economic development.
If I was writing this Budget, what I would put into it is a commitment to regional
economic development. What I would have done if I was the Minister of Finance is set
aside a decent chunk of money, let us say $500 million, and I  would have sent a very
clear message to the regional economic development agencies, and the regions as a
whole, to say “You come to us with plans around what you would like to see in the
regions, around where you see benefit being generated, around how the Government can
partner with the regions, and we will help you out.”
I am the first to admit that we cannot expect the Government to throw money in the
air at the regions, watch it settle, and hope it settles in the right place. That is not how
Governments spend money. But what we do need to see is a commitment to the regions.
By that I do not mean money thrown willy -nilly in an irresponsible way, but what I do
mean is a commitment to partner with those who make a difference in provincial New
Zealand. This is not what we have seen at the moment. I would suggest that one way to
deal with the booming Auckland housing market at the moment is to give businesses a
reason, an economic imperative, to move out of Auckland —not all businesses but
certain types of businesses—and into the regions.
Let me give you one example. We know how much money it costs to bring a 40 -foot
container or a 20 -foot container across the Port of Auckland, how much it costs to
transport that container from the port to a warehouse, and ho w it much it costs to
warehouse it and then distribute it around the country. It is about 40 percent more than
to do that sort of operation in Napier, where we have one of the most efficient ports in
the country. Even Mr Foss will agree with me on that poi nt. So there is a very, very
compelling business case for a number of these businesses to move out of Auckland and
to the regions. But what we do need is a real partnership between central government
and local government, and that will come only when centr al government sends the right
4000 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
signals to provincial New Zealand, and those signals were not sent in this Budget. It
would have been easy to do.
I wonder what the provincial MPs in the National caucus were saying to Bill English
when he was putting the Budget together. I suspect they were not saying much, because
they did not know what he was planning. [ Interruption] Exactly, they had no idea what
he was actually planning. But I would have thought, certainly as a provincial MP, as a
number of my colleagues here are, that the message we will send very clearly to our
party, and, as a result, the policy I think you will see us take into the next election, is
one of regional economic development and regional economic engagement.
While we are on that topic, one of my shadow portfolios is actually forestry. What
the Government did announce in this Budget is $5 million to spend over 3 years on
research into alternative species. I am not going to knock that, because it is quite an
important project, of that there is no doubt, but it does not deal with the fundamental
issue we are facing in the forestry sector at this point in time. In the last 10 years we
have gone from 6 million cubic metres, or 30 percent of the logs cut, to 17 milli on cubic
metres, or 56 percent of all logs cut, going across our wharves without a single cent of
value being added. Part of the problem we have got here is a lack of money going into
regional economic development, and especially into the wood processing sector.
In fact, one of the great policies Labour came out with and went into the 2014
election with was accelerated depreciation for those who want to invest in timber
processing facilities. It was a fantastic policy and the resonance it gained in the
processing sector was enormous. In fact, again, I would have thought that that would be
something that this Government signalled in the Budget because it was a great policy
that resonated right across the industry. We have got to do something about this. To b e
honest, we might not need sawmills in the future, and the reason I say that is that the
size of the planted estate has dropped by 76,000 hectares over the last 10 years. This is
an industry in decline yet this is the only industry that is going to get us  out of the
problems we face with our carbon emissions, in our global responsibilities as a clean,
green, “100% Pure New Zealand” branded country that allows us —that gives us —a
global competitive advantage.
The sawmilling and forestry sectors really are s uffering under this Government. As a
man from the provinces that have a number of plantation forests, I know that you,
yourself, Mr Deputy Speaker, must be bit a little frustrated with this.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Do not bring me into the debate.

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: I am sorry, Mr Deputy Speaker, but you know I get passionate
about the regions and I know you are as well, so I do apologise. There have been about
6,000 jobs lost in this whole industry.
I would like to conclude by sayin g three things. First and foremost, what this
Government—what a Government—really needs to do is to start engaging with regional
and provincial New Zealand, and go out to them with an action plan, even if it goes out
to provincial New Zealand and says “Thi s is what we would like to see from you.”
There needs to be a level of engagement. That is just not happening at the moment. The
second point I would like to make is that the forestry sector is a very important sector
for a whole raft of reasons. First of all it can transform commodity logs into specialty
products. Second, it employs a whole lot of people in the regions where there is high
unemployment, and, third, it will actually help us meet our Kyoto or Paris commitments
under the emissions trading scheme.
The third point I would like to make is that we really do need to get a handle on who
is buying our assets in this country; we really do. It is not a difficult thing to do. In fact,
it would be quite cheap to do. We would support it if it was done in a way that was
meaningful. I think, as parliamentarians, we need to work together to provide New
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4001
Zealanders with information around who is buying our houses, how much they are
paying, where they are buying, and what they are doing when they do buy. Thank y ou
very much.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: This is a 5 -minutes-each split call from the National
Party.

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: It is my absolute plea sure to take this
call on Budget 2015, firstly, because I am 50 percent of “Team South”, and apparently a
percentage, too, of the young wing of our caucus. So if 40 years of age is considered to
be youth, I will take that, along with taking it as read that  this is a triumphant Budget,
with thanks to the Hon Bill English and his team. Let us put the facts on the table, shall
we? This is a Government that has grown the economy and that has continued to put
measures in place to strengthen our position on the w orld stage. We have a clear
economic plan, with economic growth forecast to average 2.8 percent over the next 4
years. We have created 194,000 jobs since 2011 and have forecast 150,000 more over
the next 4 years. Average wages have increased by 15 percent —that is a rise of $7,000
by mid-2019—and unemployment is forecast to fall below 5 percent next year. For Mr
Nash, who waxed on about the regions, that is 3.3 percent unemployment in Southland
currently—

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: —3.3 percent, and our province is currently producing 15 percent
of total export receipts. So we are a province that is boxing above its weight, and we are
a province that is thriving and doing well under this National-led Government.
But it is work that I want to focus on. As we have heard from many social agencies,
including the Salvation Army and my very own Southland Beneficiaries and
Community Rights Centre, based in Invercargill, work is something tha t raises people
out of hardship  and g ives them dignity  and a better quality of life. A job provides
money and boost s standards of living. A job improves health and well -being, provides
social contact, and contributes to social cohesion. A job contributes to life satisfaction
and gives people a sense of identit y and belonging  and, of course, their efforts
contribute to society. That i s at the heart of our package —$790 million to help children
in hardship. As part of that package there are pragmatic things that we are doing to
support the vulner able, our families, and to support parents and mums back into work.
We have got a $25 a week after -tax rise in benefit rates for families with children —a
real increase in benefits, and the first Government to do so in 40 years.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: How long?

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: That is the first Government to do so in 40 years. It is supporting
the vulnerable and looking after people in hardship. We are giving $12.50 a week more
in Working for Families to lower -income families—$12.50 a week—and for very low -
income families, there is an increase of $24.50 per week. We are placing greater work
obligations on parents who are beneficiaries, including asking most sole parents to look
for work when the youngest child turns three. As part of that, to  remove the barriers, as
the Hon Paula Bennett covered earlier, we are increasing childcare assistance for low -
income families from $4 to $5 for up to 50 hours of childcare per week per child. The
parents get out to work and gain all the benefits of work. They earn money and move
themselves and their child out of hardship, and the child is engaged in early childhood
education, learns, and gets a good start in life.
I just want to focus on an example that I was given. Being a working mother, I was
lamenting this during the Budget —the guilt associated with working. When you are at
work you think you should be spending more time with the kids, and when you are with
the kids you think you should be meeting all those deadlines at work. A friend sent me
an editorial the other day from the Pew Research Center. It surveyed 50,000 adults in 25
4002 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
countries and the research showed that daughters whose mothers work are more likely
to stay in education longer, earn a higher qualification, be employed in a supervisory
role, and earn a higher income. So that is excellent all round for the movement of
women. But wait—there is more. Although the research found that mothers at work did
not affect males’ career choices, it did influence their sons in that. Sons of working
mothers did spend more time on childcare and housework. So I ask all those men out
there: can they iron a shirt? I commend this Budget to the House.

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: It is a privilege to carry on
with the second phase of “Team South”. I can quite proudly say that I have got an
ironed shirt, and it was fully thanks to my mother joining the workforce as soon as she
could, following my easy birth, I can imagine. It is a p leasure to speak on this Budget
for a number of reasons. Firstly, after a couple of the speeches that I have heard so far
tonight from the Opposition members, it is clear that they are not fit for Government.
They are not even fit for Opposition given that  they clearly have not read major aspects
of this Budget. They have talked about regional New Zealand not getting a look -in. We
can say —and we have heard from Sarah Dowie tonight —that Southland has
experienced 15 percent growth over the last year. It is on e of the largest growth-rates in
the country and we have got one of the lowest unemployment rates at 3.1 percent.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: How come I’ve got your constituents coming to my office?

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: The member over there for D unedin South, Clare Curran, as
well, speaking about information and communication technology and ultra -fast
broadband—these services are being rolled out continuously throughout New Zealand.
Regional New Zealand, whether it be through ultra -fast broadband or the Rural
Broadband Initiative, is getting great gains through the initiatives being driven by this
Government.
What I want to talk about tonight is the system of Government reforms, and that has
been touched on by Paula Bennett tonight, because she is  one of the main architects of
it, along with the Hon Bill English and Prime Minister John Key. This is,
fundamentally, one of the biggest things —and one that does not get enough attention, I
do not think —that this Government has done that is going to make  systemic changes
going forward. I hope that one day when, unfortunately, there is a future Labour
Government, some of these changes that we have put in place through the Better Public
Services framework will actually stay in place and help protect against  frivolous
spending and empty programmes that are simply not benefiting New Zealanders.
What we have done through these reforms is to say that for far too long they have
been focused on increasing spending in Government departments for the sake of
increasing spending in Government departments, whereas this Government is focused
on individuals and on people who need the investment the most. So what we have seen
through the work of Paula Bennett, Bill English, and now the Hon Anne Tolley in the
social welfare space is that they have identified some of the largest cost drivers in the
social welfare space and I want to touch on two of these groups.
First, I want to touch on teen sole parents. We know that since we have come into
Government we have reduced the number of these by almost 50 percent to a level of
about 2,600. We know that the average expected time that the teen sole parent will
spend on a benefit is 20 years, at a cost of around $250,000 each over their lifetime on a
benefit. But if they have a qua lification their time on a benefit automatically reduces
from 20 years to 7 years. So as part of Budget 2015 what was announced is that from 4
April 2016 the childcare assistance rate will increase from $4 to $5 an hour for low -
income families. This does not sound like a lot of money but for these families it is. It is
a significant amount of money over a long period of time. It helps lower -income parents
get access to affordable childcare, and supports them in employment, education, and
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4003
training. The benef it rates have increased in real value as well, for the first time in 43
years.
For the Labour Party members to say this is absolutely nothing and is not making an
impact is incredibly hilarious, actually, given they are meant to be the party that looks
out for the most vulnerable New Zealanders —or the self -proclaimed party that does
that. It is the National -led Government that has made some fundamental changes
affecting some of our most vulnerable New Zealanders. Just as a snapshot, going back
to teen sole parents, in my electorate alone we have got 185 teen sole parents in Gore,
168 in the Clutha district, and 98 in Queenstown. These are real people who will
experience real benefits from the change that this Government has put in place.
The next portion of high cost drivers, which relates directly to my electorate as well,
are children in care. We know that these members of society are hugely disproportionate
cost drivers. Within this group we know that there are a group of 2,000 kids whose
future prison co sts, based on 30 years’ worth of records, will be $750 million. Budget
2015 appropriates almost $60 million to help at -risk children through new operational
funding and capital grants to Child, Youth and Family for its Children’s Teams. In
Balclutha we have got 12 children who are in care, in Gore we have got 19, and we have
got a number of other kids across other parts of the electorate as well. We know that
included in one of these groups we have got one kid who is 12 years old and who has
had 95 foster f amilies. That is utterly outrageous and it is not something that this
Government wants to see continuing. That is why I wholeheartedly believe that these
changes will make an impact on real New Zealanders. Thank you.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: I rise to take a call in this, the Budget debate, and being the
third Southlander in a row feels particularly momentous.
I am sure that sole parents and children in care will be feeling quite proud and
understanding of their place in our society now, having been described as cost drivers in
the Government’s Budget. I would like to say that the Green Party’s perspective on our
society differs a little from seeing these people as cost drivers to the Government.
When an economy is no t working for everyone, it is not working, and we have had
many examples over the last few years and weeks that tell us clearly that our economy
is not working. But I do want to, firstly, acknowledge the Government, actually, for
raising base benefit rates for people with children.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Aw!

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: Yes, I think it is important to acknowledge this, because the Green
Party has been saying for well over a decade now that these incomes have needed to
increase. This was long, actually, before the National Government came to power,
because child poverty, which we have been talking about, was not created by this
National Government; it has existed for decades going right back to the fourth Labour
Government.
In question time toda y, the Minister of Foreign Affairs said that National had been
changing lots of policies at our request. We appreciate that but we cannot take all the
responsibility for the increase in base benefit rates, because it was not just us alone. It
was also the advocacy of Every Child Counts, Child Poverty Action Group, Plunket,
Unicef, Barnados, amongst many other community organisations, as well as, of course,
Bryan Bruce, Nigel Latta, and, most prominently probably, John Campbell. These
groups and people have been working tirelessly for years now to help everyone in New
Zealand to understand what child poverty looks and feels like, because there is a big
disconnect between our communities, and most people who are working hard on good
incomes do not necessarily get to see that real impact, and they did not before
understand the generational consequences of it. So I do really want to acknowledge
them and the people of New Zealand who made sure the Government knew that they
4004 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
were not happy with so many of our childr en suffering and dying because of
Government policies.
The Government members certainly seem very pleased that they have introduced this
policy, and they should, but I have got to say their pleasure does seem to verge on
crowing, and I am not really sure t hat that is the way to show that they genuinely care
about the well-being of our children. But the acknowledgement that poverty will not be
solved without addressing income is critical, and the Green Party is really relieved to
finally have that acknowledged.
But in some ways, all of this is about the politics, because although we know that
some people will get that $25 a week, many will not get that much. The degree of
poverty in this country with a quarter of a million children in poverty and 60,000 to
100,000 in severe deprivation without beds of their own, without decent meals every
day, without Christmas presents or birthday presents, without being able to afford to go
to the doctor, without transport, and being unable to go on school trips —we know that
that extra $25, even for those who get it, is not going to solve those problems. This is
one step; this is not a solution, and, sadly, it is still not a plan yet. We, desperately, on
behalf of those children need to keep advocating for that plan to be able to give them the
opportunity to live good lives.
I do want to specifically acknowledge too that that $25 increase does not compensate
for the cuts to the child disability allowance, which is an allowance that is not means -
tested. There have been very s ignificant cuts since 2009 and there are 11,000 fewer
children accessing that child disability allowance. That disability allowance is worth
$46.25 a week, so that has been a cut to 11,000 children of an amount that is
significantly more than what the Gove rnment is offering in this package, and they are
some of the children who are in the most need.
Those cuts have been made by the Government not telling people about the available
entitlements, and by tightening up the entitlements. There was a very moving article in
the New Zealand Herald at the end of last year talking about this, and some examples.
One of the Wellington beneficiary advocates, Graham Howell, was saying that one
family with an intellectually disabled child —a child with a learning disability —lost the
child disability allowance when the boy grew old enough to tie his own shoelaces, and a
boy with eczema lost the allowance when he became able to put on his own ointment.
That is the threshold where access to that disability support for beneficia ries and
working families has been put at such a level that I do not think any of us can
understand. There was an Onehunga mother, Emma -Rose Cottrell, who was quoted in
that article. Her husband works part -time and she is full -time caring. Her husband is
able to work only part -time, because otherwise they just would not cope as a family.
She said, referring to her husband: “He’s not allowed to do full -time, otherwise I’d die
of stress.” She said: “I have to do naps most days, because I am just so exhausted.”
This is the reality for some of our families. I really want to focus the House’s
attention on the fact that that was a two-parent family, and she is talking about that level
of exhaustion, when she is sharing the care of their child with a partner. Now, to put that
in focus around the increased work testing for sole parents that was also contained in
this Budget, when their child turns 3, regardless of whether their child has a disability or
special emotional needs, regardless of what trauma that family may have been through,
that parent is now going to be required to go and look for 20 hours’ work. Remember,
this is the story of a woman with a partner who is in work, who is saying she could not
cope without her partner being at home with her to care for her child. It would be just
too physically and emotionally demanding.
We need desperately to be supporting our families better and acknowledging the
different struggles that our families are coping with. One -size-fits-all policies like this
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4005
are likely to d o so much more harm. Sure, for some families, some parents, some
mothers, it is going to suit them to be able to go out to work and find a job, if they can
find one. But we also heard from Dr Nikki Turner, at the Child Poverty Action Group
breakfast, that she is seeing parents going out to work and the only jobs they are able to
get are evening or night jobs, and they are leaving their kids at home alone because of
that requirement and that pressure to be in work. Is that really what we want for our
children? Is that really in the best interests of our society, in the long term? I would say
very clearly that it is not. The Green Party advocates for child -centred policies, where
we consider the interests of the child first. They will be different for every si ngle child,
and we support families being able to do what is best for their children. That, sadly, is
not a blanket 20 hours of work a week, from the age of 3 —the work-test requirement
for parents—regardless of the needs of their children.
I know I do not have much time, but I do want to specifically also touch on—because
the Speaker told us this was the space to do it —the funding decision around
Relationships Aotearoa. That the largest counselling organisation in this country, with
7,000 clients, which ha s been in existence since 1949, will be closing its doors this
week without a publicly available transition plan for its clients is an outrage.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: It is a great pleasure to take a call on the
seventh Budget of this National -led Government that Bill English as our Minister of
Finance has led us through. I am very proud that this is a Budget that consolidates the
clear approach that we have brought to the Go vernment benches since 2008, and that is
recognising that actually you can have it both ways. You can get the Government’s
books back in order and deliver better services for our taxpayers and the New
Zealanders who need those services.
For many years we have seen Governments that just wanted to throw more money at
a problem. If it was not working and the spending was not effective, let us spend more
and that must cure all ills. Actually, we cannot afford to do that. We have said for a long
time that we ne ed to set the example of what we preach, which is to say that families
need to be saving and investing and thinking about the future. It would not be credible
for us to do that as a Government if we continued to live beyond our means, as had
become the pat tern particularly in the early years of the 2000s. Yep, this year we will
show a deficit of $684 million but the important thing is that year on year we have been
building a platform to get the Government’s books back into surplus. We will be one of
the first countries in the developed world post - global financial crisis to do that. That is
something we can be incredibly proud of, but we have not done it by cutting, slashing,
and burning.
Actually, in all of the core sectors we can point to real progress where the sector has
been encouraged, supported, and cajoled into delivering better services for New
Zealand. Whether you look at health, whether you look at education, whether you look
at law and order, the reality is that the numbers now show that New Ze alanders are
getting far better value for the money that we take from them. We have recognised that
for every dollar we take out of the pocket of a hard -working New Zealander, we owe
that taxpayer the respect of showing that we will spend that money as car efully as we
would our own.
That is what this Budget, to me, really talks about. It talks about the fact that we have
recognised there are areas of New Zealand and there are families in New Zealand who
are doing it pretty tough. We wanted to do more to su pport those 160,000 of the lowest-
income families, but we did not simply get the cheque book out and add some more
numbers on to the spend. We said that we need to do this responsibly, and that is about
targeting where we put money and where we do not. We did not do it, as I said, by
4006 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
adding to the deficit. We thought very carefully about what costs were fair, to fall
where, in our society.
I think the border processing levy that we passed under urgency on Thursday is a
fantastic example of that. Here you have a decision that asks “Should we be taxing all of
those lowest -paid families, to fund the international travel of foreigners and New
Zealanders who can afford international travel?”. My view, very simply, is no, we
should not. If we are travelling, the cost that we impose on an economy through doing
that should fall to us. Ditto, the foreigners who come through our airports should be
contributing to those costs.
I am not going to be taking money out of the pockets of some of those hard -working
families who are doing it tough and who certainly could not afford international travel,
to make them pay for it. It is my cost and I should pay it. Labour thinks that we should
tax the poorest families in New Zealand to pay for the travel of wealthy New Zealanders
and wealthy foreigners. I do not support that. Targeting that levy to those people who
incur the costs —[Interruption] They do not like it when you call them on their
hypocrisy, but actually that is the reality. They spark up when you highlight the facts.
They did not want us to have the costs of that expensive travel falling on those who
travel. They wanted it to fall on every taxpayer. I would far rather those costs fall where
they should, and the spare money can be reinvested in low -income families. That is the
difference between us. We ask “Where is our money best spent?”.
Let us see how that same approach applies in my own area of broadband. Again, we
had two options. We could have asked the companies that will profit from the
infrastructure to help fun d it on a communal basis, which is what we have done and
what every other party in Parliament supported except, of course, for Labour, or we
could have taxed people who actually do not get to make their living off that
infrastructure. In our view, you targ et it to those who will get the benefit from the
spend. You use the money that you create, the surplus spend that you create in the
Government finances, and put it where it will do the most good.
In this Budget that is about reaching out to those children  who are living in some of
our poorest families, supporting them, but also with that, sending the message that the
best path out of hardship and out of poverty is work. The best thing, bar none, that we
can do for those families who are really struggling i s to get them into a job. There are
many parts to that, of course. It means making sure they have the educational standards
they need, making sure national standards and our National Certificate of Educational
Achievement targets are supporting them to hav e that education, making sure our
tertiary system is set up to provide pathways and jobs and skill sets that will help them
into those jobs, making sure that their health is strong enough to support them working,
making sure there is drug and alcohol couns elling in our prisons, and making sure our
mental health services are strong.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Appropriate childcare, where it is needed.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: That is exactly right. If they need support with childcare,
putting those s ubsidies up —making them available. All of the parts of this Budget
facilitate that approach. The other side of that equation is making sure there are
opportunities for them —creating jobs in the regions, creating jobs in areas that need
them. This is a Gove rnment that has already seen the development of hundreds of
thousands of new jobs in our term in office. Budget 2015 shows that Treasury
modelling is that more new jobs will be created as a result of these settings.
We are ensuring people are supported to  get back to work, that they have the
opportunity to work, and that they have the skill set and the support in childcare to do
that job. That is the path out of hardship. There is no two ways about it. Although we
want to support those at the lowest ebb, i t cannot be into a pattern of dependency. We
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4007
are not helping anyone if the pattern is one of dependency and teaching them to rely on
the State. Self-reliance, self-responsibility, working for a living is the best thing that any
family can do for their fort unes and for their children. This is a Government that will
support them.
I just want to highlight a couple of the ways the Budget has helped areas like the one
that I represent because I think that often, when we look at the big packages and the
national approach, we lose some of the detail of the very real things that this Budget
will do in parts of rural and provincial New Zealand, like the electorate of Selwyn. I
have to comment on the $100 million set aside in this Budget to rebuild the science
facilities at Lincoln University, which, obviously, were significantly damaged during
the Canterbury earthquakes of 2010 and 2011.
This is the Budget and this is the Government that have set aside $100 million from
the proceeds of the mixed -ownership model to ma ke sure that Lincoln University gets
back on its feet, and I welcome it. As part of the $200 million - plus spending on new
school facilities, I am very proud that Rolleston in my electorate is already having its
third primary school built, an integrated C hristian school opened, another new primary
school in planning, and a high school on its way. This is the Government that is making
that funding happen.
I was also delighted to see the announcement in the Budget around the regional
research centre, recogn ising that some of the best innovation in this country is not
happening in the cities; it is happening in regional and rural New Zealand. Funding that
sort of regional research centre will do two things. One, it will create jobs and activity
in the regions. And, two, it will show that the Government recognises that some of the
most innovative parts of New Zealand are in the regions, and that we respect and want
to support that, and this is a Budget that certainly does that.
Finally, let me end my contribut ion talking about the funding in the Budget for the
extension of the Ultra -fast Broadband Initiative and the regional broadband initiative.
This is a Budget that puts $360 million more into our investment, making a total
Government investment of over $2 bi llion. This is the Government that will deliver
high-speed, high -quality broadband to as many New Zealanders as we possibly can,
because that is the foundation for all of the services that we need in the future —social,
cultural, economic, and Government se rvices. It is the digital highway that will really
enable our small towns and our communities to flourish.
The extension of the Ultra -fast Broadband Initiative will see another 200,000 New
Zealanders access absolutely world -leading connectivity infrastruc ture. I am incredibly
excited by that. We are going to see some of the smallest towns in New Zealand get
switched on and opened up in a way that we will not have seen since the railways were
first rolled out, since we took electricity into some of the comm unities. That is exciting.
I am excited by that. I am proud of it. There is a reason that New Zealand is held up
internationally, in terms of the success of our broadband programme. Around the world
you have got companies like Alcatel -Lucent saying New Zea land is a country that has
got this right, and that this is a model for the rest of the world and this is the
Government that enabled it. I am very proud to commend the Budget to the House.

items.speaker: JENNY SALESA
items.text: Malo soifua, talofa lava. The
National Government has repeatedly stated that it is improving the economy. The
Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister claim that Budget 2015 delivers to those
who are in hardshi p, but the people of Manukau East, along with many other ordinary,
hard-working Kiwis, are falling further behind. Their ability to live with dignity, to
support their families well, and to see their children flourish is being affected negatively
by this Government’s failure to deliver on its promises.
4008 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
The curtain has dramatically been drawn back and this Government’s Budget reveals
only that there is hardly anything there for ordinary, hard -working Kiwi families. For
hard-working families the cupboard is bare. The Budget surplus that was promised by
this Government is not there. The promise of a 150,000 increase in the number of jobs
and higher wages has not been reached. The promise of no new taxes has been broken—
we now have three sneaky new taxes. The p romise of more affordable houses has been
broken, and hard -working New Zealanders are losing their KiwiSaver kick -start
incentive to save for their future. This has been a Budget of broken promises, and there
is not even anything in this Budget for the high and ever-increasing rents for families.
Aotearoa New Zealand’s poor, vulnerable children do not choose the parents whom
they have. They do not choose their country or the neighbourhood they are born into,
and they do not choose their race or their relig ion. In fact, if they had been born into
another OECD country, they would probably be less likely to be born into poverty.
Having so many thousands of children —over 250,000 kids —grow up in poverty is
really expensive for all of us as taxpayers. Child pover ty is really expensive in the long
run for us all, and it is an issue we should address in a comprehensive and planned way.
The lost productivity, extra health costs, and law and order costs —to name but a few —
add up to millions and millions of dollars per year. For far too long, the Government has
allowed the level of child poverty to remain really high. The reason, or justification, if
any is given at all, is often that action to address child poverty is too expensive. But
inaction, as done by Budget 2015 —with a few tweaks here and there and a fiddle at the
margins—completely misses the other side of the equation, which is the fact that the
cost to all of us in society is much too expensive. Inaction and a lack of comprehensive
action to address child poverty has its costs.
Good things, better outcomes in life, are worth paying for. I believe that having food,
shelter—a house —and investment in early childhood education in order to get kids
ready for school and education in an equitable and fair way are thin gs that all children
should have. This is something that should be of a higher priority, instead of corporate
welfare and tax breaks. Why is it that National can afford tax breaks of over $3 billion
since it has been in Government thus far, and it is alrea dy promising tax cuts for 2017,
even though it cannot even balance the books right now? Why is it that the Government
is wasting $26 million on a flag referendum that most New Zealanders say is a waste of
money, and yet, in the same breath, it is saying th at we cannot afford to make sure that
every child is fed and every child is housed, or to invest in a comprehensive way in our
children, who are the future of our country?
A key driver of child poverty is the public policies that we have. We will know whe n
the Government is actually addressing child poverty, because, when it does, we will
actually see that it will apply principles of inclusivity and it will have principles of non -
discrimination, which will help protect our children from poverty as equally well as
they protect our elders from poverty. Child poverty matters to the Labour Party. Child
poverty matters to me, as a mother, and it matters to my electorate and to the rest of
New Zealand. Our children deserve to be treated fairly and they deserve to  be given
equal opportunities.
A responsible Government would be a Government that actually has a plan —a plan
to competently address the long -term challenges that New Zealand faces, a plan to lay
the foundations for a sustainable and healthy future, and a  plan that would grow
incomes and invest in a productive and diverse economy. This Budget has been long on
promises and short on solutions. It is a Budget that contains nothing significant for
diversifying the economy or for supporting our manufacturers an d our exporters, or for
developing the skills that our workers will need in the new economy. Growth has now
passed its peak and it is expected to halve by 2019, and not reaching surplus at the peak
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4009
of the economic cycle is a huge failure by this Government . It makes a mockery of
National members’ claim that they are good economic managers.
Our Prime Minister, John Key, in his open letter to New Zealanders after the
election, promised: “Over the next two years we expect to see about 150,000 jobs
created.” The National Government will fall short on this promise by 60,000 jobs, and it
has pushed the date of delivery back a few more years —yet another broken promise.
Also in John Key’s open letter to New Zealanders after the election, he promised: “Over
the next three years we expect the average wage to move from $55,000 to $62,000 …”.
The Budget shows that the Government will fall short by $3,000 on its wages promise.
In fact, we are unlikely to even get to the promised wage level until 2019 —in another 4
years.
Manukau East in South Auckland, which is the wonderful electorate that I represent,
is a young electorate. The median age in Manukau East is 29 years. The national median
age is 37 years, and one-third of the people living in Manukau East are under the ag e of
20. Many are on low and limited incomes. In order to get ahead and to contribute to the
future of New Zealand, they need properly funded education, correctly targeted skills
training, jobs to go to that pay decent wages, and the ability to save for the future.
New Zealand used to be the land that led the world, with the lowest unemployment
rates in the OECD. This was under Helen Clark and the last Labour -led Government.
Today we rank 13 th, and the general situation in my electorate is compounded by it
having one the highest unemployment rates in the country. This Budget will not fix that.
The Government is failing to act on jobs and wages for ordinary everyday New
Zealanders.
We have heard  the other side trumpeting the fact that for people on a benefit who
have children, receiving $25 extra a week will make a huge difference. Well, it will
make some difference, but I would not call it a huge difference. Although an increase in
benefit levels for those with children is good news, those who are working with children
and families and who have Working for Families will receive only $12 per week. This
makes working families relatively worse off than when this Budget was announced. For
families, t he Government will claw back this $25 through reduced accommodation
supplements. The Budget offers no firm pathway out of poverty, and the $25 a week
cannot—it cannot—fix 7 years of neglect and the mismanagement of our economy.
Cutting the $1,000 KiwiSave r kick-start initiative demonstrates the absolutely short -
term thinking that is typical of this National Government and this Budget. This cut will
detrimentally penalise our young people, who are going to be less able to get ahead and
to save for their fut ure. In 2011 the Prime Minister promised to retain the $1,000 kick -
start for new KiwiSaver members as it was at the time. The Government has now cut it
entirely—yet another broken promise. Now around 500,000 people, mainly young
people and children, will miss out as a result of this cut.
This Government is wandering aimlessly, with absolutely no long -term plans for our
economic future. It has failed to deliver a Budget surplus for 7 years now. We pay
millions per day in interest because the Government cann ot get the books into balance
or deliver a Budget surplus, and it is continuing to fail to meet the needs of New
Zealand families. The Government’s latest Budget might be clever in a political sense as
it has robbed Peter to pay Paul, but having a collecti on of short -term jabs and a few
high-profile targets does not a comprehensive strategy for the future make. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.role: Minister of Comm erce and Consumer Affairs
items.text: This
Budget shows what New Zealand can do after 7 years of a strong, stable Government
led by John Key, Bill English, and this National Government. We see great growth in
this economy—nearly 3 percent is projected for the next 4  years, which is one of the
fastest levels of growth in the OECD. We have seen a jobs boom in New Zealand, with
4010 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
194,000 jobs created in this economy since 2011. That impacts countless thousands of
lives of families across this nation who have had access to  work and the dignity of
work. We expect another 150,000 jobs to be created in this economy over the next 4
years. We see optimism, dynamism, and enthusiasm in this economy and in this
country.
This Budget has shown that we also have the ability to help t he most vulnerable
thanks to the prudent management of the economy, with a $790 million package for the
poorest families in New Zealand. It shows that this Government is managing this
country for everyone. It shows that we recognise that there are families  genuinely in
need in this economy and we can help them out. Some people —and we just heard it in
the latest speech, by Jenny Salesa—think that we did that because it is politically clever.
That is not the point at all. We have done it because it is the rig ht thing to do in this
country. We have done it because, thanks to the prudent management of this economy
over the past few years, we do have the resources to help those who are most in need.
We do it because it is the right thing to do.
At the same time we expect responsibility back from those we help. This Budget has
talked about solo parents being available for 20 hours of work once their youngest is 3,
and they need to reapply each year. Again, we do that not because we want to make life
difficult; we do it because we genuinely believe that the best thing you can do for
families is to encourage them back to work. We do it because, again, it is the right thing
to do. We have had decades of just giving people money, no questions asked, as long as
you like, and no understanding of the dependence that it has developed over decades.
This Government wants to do better and understands that it is important for the families
of this country that we do do better and that we encourage people to get back to work.
That is why I am so enthusiastic about this Budget.
We have seen an interesting survey come out from Statistics New Zealand that again
demonstrates the progress that has been made over these past 6 years. We have had this
review, the general social survey, s howing that families who say they have enough
money to live on has increased from just over 50 percent in 2008 to nearly 63 percent
last year. That is a significant improvement over a short period of time. We have seen
families who say that they do not hav e enough money to live on dropping from over 15
percent in 2008 down to 12 percent in 2014. We will see that the extra $25 a week that
will be delivered through this Budget will also help. That is showing the progress we
are making.
We constantly hear his tory lessons in this Budget debate from the other side. They
talk about 9 years of surpluses. They need to read and understand that there were 8
years of surpluses, yes, and good luck to them. At the start of the first term of the
Labour Government they were reasonably disciplined, but the final year is what counts.
They left a massive deficit for this economy. Conditions count. Yes, we inherited the
global financial crisis and we inherited the Christchurch earthquakes. Yes, we could
have slashed and burnt and got back to surplus faster, but we judged that the best thing
for the economy was to set a clear path back to surplus, to manage things carefully, and
to be disciplined with our spending.
When we talk about disciplined spending, we just have to look a t this graph here that
demonstrates in the last 5 years of the previous Labour Government, billions and
billions of dollars of extra spending was poured into each Budget. In the last Budget in
2008 there was $7 billion of new spending in 1 year, whereas th is Government has been
so much more disciplined, averaging well less than $1 billion a year of new spending —
$1 billion this year, but about $600 million or $700 million on average. It is that
extended period of a disciplined Government, seven Budgets in a row, that has led us to
this good, strong position that we are in today.
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4011
I also heard on the radio when I was driving around town a couple of days ago one
commentator saying that this Budget reflects a left -wing Government. What a load of
nonsense that wa s. What we have seen here is that strong, disciplined spending has
reduced core Government expenditure from nearly 34 percent in 2008 down to 30
percent, a very significant drop in the size of overall Government. We have actually got
control over the size of the Government. We are reducing it. We are focusing it on
actually doing the job well. The outcome is leaving a larger slice of the economy to the
private sector and job creators.
I also want to reflect on the biggest issue in my area where I come from , the Epsom
electorate, which has been the Auckland housing market and the rapid growth in prices
that we have seen there recently. I hear every day lots of speculation and lots of rumours
about what is going on. There is some concern and some Opposition s caremongering,
talking about every other country coming in. The Opposition seems to be very anti -
