migrants in some areas, which is interesting again. Going back to that survey that I just
referred to before, about three -quarters of New Zealanders are very c omfortable with
people of different ethnicities and migrants coming in and living next to them. Most
New Zealanders are very tolerant and welcoming of new people. We are naturally
concerned about what is influencing the Auckland housing market. It is a serious matter.
That is why this Government has put a huge amount of focus on that in the last few
years, working with Auckland Council to try to free up more land for the building of
houses is the best thing we can do. We are trying to reform the Resource Ma nagement
Act. I only wish some of the Opposition parties would get in there and support us, New
Zealand First included.
This Budget has brought in new measures, such as requiring IRD numbers or the
equivalent from overseas buyers and new buyers when purcha sing extra property, and
that, for the first time, will give us a good, clear understanding of what exactly is going
on in the Auckland market. It will help the Inland Revenue Department to enforce the
current tax law, which shows that if you are buying an d selling property with the
intention of trading, then you do pay tax in this country. We are extending that, making
it clear, putting a brightline test in place, and giving the Inland Revenue Department the
resources to police that. That is an important s tep to deal with the demand for an
important issue. We have considered these things carefully and we are making good
progress. The Budget also refers to extending Crown land available for building new
houses in Auckland.
This Budget is also about building  a more competitive and international economy.
One of the areas that I am responsible for is the New Zealand Business Number. We are
investing $12 million there to provide a unique identifier for businesses, so that Kiwi
businesses do not have to go out an d constantly update information with a plethora of
different Government departments. It is just one small way in which we are helping
New Zealand businesses get ahead.
The other thing that I want to refer to is that it is important that we have strong
financial markets to give the capital resources for businesses to grow, and that is why
we continue to invest strongly in the Financial Markets Authority and why we are
reviewing the Financial Advisers Act, which I announced today and outlined the details
of.
We are also focused on improving the living standards of all New Zealanders, and
that is the focus of the Business Growth Agenda. It is the focus of the Better Public
Services, so that people get quality resources in health and education, and safer
communities through a good and effective police force and justice system. It is also
about trying to keep control of the costs of everything, and that is why good, strong
competition laws are so important to the economy. That is why this year we will be
4012 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
reviewing section 36 of our competition law, which relates to the misuse of market
power. This is an important element of making sure that the New Zealand economy is
competitive, so that New Zealand living standards can be maintained. And so this is a
great Budget. It confirms 7 years of good, solid, stable, sensible Government in New
Zealand, and we are starting to see the fruits of that. I commend it to the House. Thank
you.

items.speaker: PITA PARAONE
items.text: Tēnā ko e, Mr Assistant Speaker. Talofa lava. I
preface my presentation tonight by acknowledging our Pacific Island relatives. Given
the contribution that they have made to the industrial development of our country, I
think that they would be very disappointed in the Budget, particularly as it affects them
and the amount that has been allocated for them. Just over $8.8 million has been
allocated to the Ministry of Pacific Island Affairs and, of course, one of the things that
was mentioned in the Budget was that the re will be a name change to the department. I
just wonder how much that will cost, and whether or not the funding involved in that
change of name could have been better utilised in terms of the development of that
community.
I also want to make the point that there was a programme running in Auckland where
they previously had $1.1 million allocated. This Budget provides only $50,000, because
it is seen as the end of the programme. But I believe that there is need for such a
programme and it should be maint ained, but that has not been recognised in this year’s
Budget. I suppose we should not be surprised because, given the debate so far —
particularly from that side of the House—no mention has ever been made of that part of
our community. They talk about diver sity and the need to get on with the rest of our
fellow man, but in terms of this Budget reflecting the needs of that community it is very
limited.
I now want to move on to the main part of my contribution to this debate tonight, and
that is in the area of Māori affairs. On Budget day we heard from the Minister for Māori
Development and the Leader of the Māori Party, Te Ururoa Flavell, just how much the
Māori Party had contributed to this year’s Budget, and the fact it was were responsible
for a lot of the  funds that have been allocated in the direction of Māori affairs. But a
closer analysis of the figures will show that there is not really any new money. What the
Government has done is it has just moved the different allocations  around, and the
Māori Party told us it was responsible for an increased level of funding for the Māori
affairs portfolio.
One of the elements of the contribution to that part of the Budget was the reference
to Whānau Ora. Any discussion on this part of the Budget without a mention of Whānau
Ora would be very remiss. So I want to remind this House that of the $137 million
already allocated to this programme, $40 million has been allocated towards
administration. I want to say that when the officials came before the Māori Affairs
Committee and were questioned about this programme, we asked what the major issue
facing Whānau Ora was. The response was: to inform people as to what it was. After 5
years in existence, that was the only response that they could come up with. And in
spite of a damning report from the Office of the Auditor -General, what does the Budget
provide? Another $50 million. Another $50 million for a programme that, although it
does have its merits —I will be the first to say that —I think the way that it has been
administered and managed certainly does bring the programme into disrepute. What it
does is pass the responsibility of Government to service providers out in the
community, and therein lies the difficulty. I wonder about the value of this Budget
giving further funding to a programme that clearly is in disarray. I am not being critical
of those service providers out there who are clearly making the best effort to deliver
something that the Government is responsible for.
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4013
I just want to remind the Minister for Māori Development and the Māori Party, that,
although they might jump up and down with glee about being able to sit at the table, at
the end of the day it depends on where you are sitting at that table —whether it is
underneath or at the head of the table. I would suggest that the Māori Party is certainly
not sitting at the head of the table, notwithstanding the joy that it might have in terms of
the level of funding that it has been able to get out of this Budget. Almo st $220
million—it sounds a lot, but when we have a look at the way that the Government has
split it up, one needs to question some of the decisions that have been made in this area.
I want to comment about the allocation made to specific Māori Potential
programmes, including the Māori Registration Service, Māori Wardens Project, the
New Zealand Māori Council, and the Māori Women’s Development Fund. I want to say
that when New Zealand First was part of the Treasury benches, it was able to get $7
million al one just for the Māori wardens. All of a sudden, we see in this year’s
Budget—and, of course, it has headed a plan that is working —that that level of funding
has been reduced. I just wonder why that is the case, given that the Māori wardens are
one of the few groups within the Māori community that have been very successful in
caring for their community—with nothing.
I also want to point out that if what the leader of the Māori Party said —that it had
done so much for the Māori community —is true, then why is it that after the 8 years
that it has been associated with the Government in power Māori make up the worst
figures in all of the social indices: unemployment, poor housing, and low incomes? To
me that suggests that the Māori Party is not as cracked up as it would like us to believe.
The other thing is the question that it has had to provide funding for rangatahi Māori
suicide—just over $2 million. If we have to provide funding for that sort of issue, then
that begs the question: what has the Māori Party be en doing for the Māori community?
Why is that suicide rates amongst young Māori are the highest in this country? I have
got to ask that question of the Māori Party, because if it says that it is that good, then
why is it that we are having such a poor—[Interruption]
The other thing is that the Māori Party talks about having gained $35.3 million in
investment for Māori housing. I can recall in the old Department of Māori Affairs days
that each region was able to build 60 new homes every year. This $35 millio n that the
party talks about for housing is going to be over a number of years. So what has
happened? Is it because the predominant party in the Government has overtaken the
Māori Party and it is not as effective as it would like us to believe? Although th e
Government may talk about how good this Budget it is, at the end of the day it ends up
the wrong colour: red, red, red. Kia ora.

items.speaker: PEENI HENARE
items.text: Tēnā koe. Fa‘atalofa i le Paia
Ma Le Mamalu o Le aofia, faafetai I lau susuga I Le pule fono mo lenei avanoa.
Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker, and thank you for this opportunity. Can I take this
opportunity to highlight a significant day for Ngāti Whātua ki Ōrākei , the peo ple of
Tāmaki Makaurau and, indeed, Māori in its entirety.
Yesterday, 25 May, marked 37 years since my whānau were evicted from Bastion
Point after 507 days of protest occupation. The National Government, under the
Muldoon administration at the time, was shameless—I say shameless—in its attempt at
a land-grab of prime real estate. I am proud to say that under a Labour -led Government,
the Lange administration agreed with the Waitangi Tribunal recommendations and
Ngāti Whātua ki Ōrākei are still there today.
Why do I bring up this marker in our history? I bring this up because it is an
important moment and because 37 years on, under a National Government, many of the
people of Tāmaki Makaurau find themselves still in a desperate position. There are also
parallels that can be drawn between the Muldoon administration and this administration.
4014 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
As a result of poor fiscal management by this Government, we see nothing in this
Budget to really help the hard-working people of Tāmaki Makaurau.
In my maiden speech in t his House I spoke about how the backyards of family
houses in Tāmaki Makaurau  will be the playground of property developers and land
speculators. Let me add to that list foreign investors. Nowhere in this Budget do the
people of Tāmaki Makaurau get a sense of relief. Nowhere in this Budget are young or
first-time homebuyers given any hope of entering the housing market that they long to
enter into.
I dare not claim any Nostradamus abilities here, because what the people of Tāmaki
Makaurau have known for th e past 7 years is that there is a crisis, something that this
Government has ignored for far too long. I believe it has come to a head and it is time
for some real opportunities, some real plans, and some real vision to go into Tāmaki
Makaurau to ease the housing crisis.
Can I turn the attention of this House to the paltry sum of $500,000 allocated to
addressing Treaty and contemporary claims matters. This means very little to the many
claimants who currently have longstanding claims with the Waitangi Trib unal, an
organisation that is already currently under-resourced in dealing with true reconciliation
for the people of this country —reconciliation that the Māori people, in particular,
deserve—to build a stronger bicultural New Zealand leading into the future.

items.speaker: Some might ask
items.text: well, what is the Labour Party doing about this? What are our plans
in the future? Can I first congratulate my staff, who work extremely hard in Tāmaki
Makaurau to pick up the pieces of those families and those whānau who are left behi nd
in this Budget —those whānau who, despite the paltry sum of $25 being offered to
beneficiaries in the latest Budget, are still being left behind in Tāmaki Makaurau, which
is far too expensive for them to live in. It is a place that they have called home for
many, many years. All of a sudden they find themselves being pushed out into the
regions. I wonder whether this is the true regional development plan that this
Government has—to force all of those families out of Auckland, to leave Auckland to
foreign investors, and to price the people of Aotearoa New Zealand out of the housing
market and force them into the regions.
Can I also speak on behalf of Tāmaki Makaurau  and say to this Government that
shifting Māori Television to Rotorua is not a sound regional growth development plan. I
stand by the people of Tāmaki Makaurau  and insist that Māori Television stays in
Tāmaki Makaurau. It has been looked after for the past 10 years, and I hope that this
tradition of looking after Māori Television continues long i nto the future within the
boundaries of Tāmaki Makaurau.
A responsible Government that holds the Treasury benches would not deliver a
deficit to this country time and time again. I have already spoken about the blowout in
the debt that matches, in fact ex ceeds, that of the Muldoon administration. At this point
in time I cannot see a plan and given that this Government is very good at talking to
itself, I daresay that the rest of New Zealand cannot see a long -term plan for this
country.
I am concerned as a young parent to know that our families will be forced, I believe,
back into the workforce too early. We know what the research says. It says that the first
5 years of a child’s life are the most important. Sure, more money into the household
will help tho se families. I agree with that. So let us give proper growth to wages that
will benefit our people. Do not force them back into the workforce far too early, where
families, as already pointed out by my esteemed colleagues, who are stuck in a cycle of
poverty at the moment just cannot seem to get their heads above water.
These are, of course, huge concerns to the Labour Party and we are committed to
making sure that we keep this Government accountable —accountable to the Budget it
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4015
has delivered. Some might argue it is a “Claytons Budget”, and I am not referring to my
esteemed colleague in the New Zealand First Party. What I am saying is that this is fake
and it is false. We have heard many other words to describe this Budget and I believe
them to be true. I b elieve that the people of Tāmaki -Makaurau will not be better off
under this Budget, they cannot see a brighter future for themselves or their whānau, and
these are, of course, concerns right across the country.
When I say “right across the country”, it is  well known in this House that I am also
from the rural heartland of Northland. I am from the rural heartland of Northland and I
can tell you that after years of that seat being held by a National member, still nothing
has been done up there. There is stil l no clear plan for the people of Northland to grow.
Some people might argue a Ngāpuhi settlement might do that. But I doubt that. I doubt
that because in this Government’s rush to settle many of the claims —and you will hear
Government members boasting and  beating their chests about how many claims the
Government has settled—what it does not realise is that it leaves a wake of destruction
behind it, and one that does not recognise whānau, one that does not recognise hapū.
The Government thinks that if you p our enough money into the situation it will fix
itself. That is not the case.
I also have a little chuckle regularly when I consider the recent by -election in
Northland and the pledge to make two -lane bridges and the Government is going to fix
up 10 singl e-lane bridges. Yet if it is serious about tourism, the one bridge it did not
promise to fix was the one -lane bridge in Waitangi, the biggest port for tourism in
Northland. There was no promise to develop that bridge to allow more numbers to
access our beautiful Bay of Islands. If the Government was serious about that, it would
fix that bridge. But what that tells me is that Government members are actually scared.
What they are scared of is that on every Waitangi Day they will see an increase in foot
traffic protesting at what this Government is doing —whether they be Māori, whether
they be Pākehā, or whether they be from the Pacific Islands or from any other place in
the world. We are going to beat that bridge, protesting against what this Government is
doing to this country, leading us into nowhere, into the abyss. Fa‘afetai.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. Andrew
Bayly—5 minutes.

items.speaker: ANDREW BAYLY
items.text: Compassionate conservativism —this is
what this Budget is all about. It is about the chance of creating a better New Zealand
where every New Zealander can get a job and can live in a warm house, i n the comfort
of a secure community, with the knowledge that their children are going to get a great
education. Unless we continue upskilling New Zealanders and creating higher -paying,
meaningful jobs, the chances of improving New Zealand as a country are limited.
We can take no pride in the fact that there is a group that feels disconnected. This
Budget is a continuum, where this Government has constantly put the individual and
family at the heart of the issue. This Budget addresses some of the perceived inequities.
I am proud of the initiatives that this Government is making to strengthen families and
children. The $790 million child hardship package to assist beneficiaries and working
families is well-timed. Obviously, the rate increases of up to $25 per  week after tax will
not address all the financial pressures some of our families face. It is, however, an
important step. It should not be understated that it represents the first real increase in 43
years.
When that is considered in the context of the o ther recent announcements this
Government has made, it represents yet another step in a range of well -considered
initiatives. Specifically, I am talking about increasing paid parental leave to 16 weeks,
which is going to increase to 18 weeks next year; ext ending payments to primary
caregivers, recognising that there are over 12,000 Kiwi kids being looked after by
4016 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
members of a wider family group; and increasing the parental tax credit from $150 to
$220 per week. In the area of health, the free visits to gene ral practitioners and free
prescriptions for under-13-year-olds, effective this year, together with the target to have
95 percent of our toddlers and youngsters immunised, all mean that our children will be
healthy. Healthy children learn better. Healthy c hildren get ahead faster in their schools
and in their education.
We have also invested more in education. Of particular note is the investment that we
have made into special -needs children and their education. We are currently spending
over $500 million per year, and this Budget commits an additional $63 million to this
important area. We have also put another $75 million into early childhood education.
We are committed to achieving that ambitious target of getting the participation rate up
from 96 percent, where it is at the moment, to 98 percent. This is important to create a
dynamic learning environment and a safe haven for our youngsters.
This Government’s support for families goes further. Every New Zealander knows
that the family home is the foundat ion of a secure childhood. Our $280 million
HomeStart package is an important ingredient in assisting Kiwi families to buy their
own homes. We do want Kiwis to have their own homes, to manage their own homes,
and to actually control their own destinies. Ev en though we have insulated in excess of
300,000 homes, this Budget goes further in committing a further $35 million over the
next 4 years to improving housing outcomes for Māori.
Every one of us, as either a parent, uncle or aunt, or grandparent, wants t he best for
our children. We are prepared to make sacrifices, and sometimes even difficult choices,
but we want to make sure that our children are healthy, happy, and well educated, and
that their future holds opportunity for optimism. The changes in this Budget give our
children the possibility of a better start. This Government has understood the
importance of this. This is a caring, compassionate Government.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Stuart Smith—5 minutes.

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: It is a great pleasure to put a
contribution towards this Budget debate, and might I say before I start that last week
was a lot of fu n. It was my first Budget and my first time in extended urgency, and to
have all the people lined up on our benches on Saturday night —it was really great to be
a part of that and it was a great moment. I look forward to many more.
I want to focus tonight on ultra-fast broadband and the roll -out of the Rural
Broadband Initiative. To my colleague the Hon Amy Adams, I say that this is a fantastic
initiative. I think that the importance of it to rural New Zealand and to New Zealand as a
whole has gone past many people, and I would like to just make sure that we dwell on
it.

items.speaker: Hon Amy Adams
items.text: Especially those in New Lynn who say we shouldn’t care about
the regions.

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: That is right. This is $360 mil lion of funding targeted to deal
with ultra-fast broadband, rural broadband, and mobile black spots. If we take those one
at a time—where I live in Blenheim, I have just recently seen a piece that was prepared
in the New Zealand Herald  and in the local Marlborough Express  about a deputy
principal at Marlborough Boys’ College who has shifted down from Auckland. He
realised that reaching his Kiwi dream of having a good house in a good place to live in
Auckland was going to be very difficult for him. He looked  around the country and
decided to settle in Blenheim. So he and his wife moved down there. They had no
connections to Blenheim. They have now ended up owning a much higher-quality house
than they would have been able to buy in Auckland at a much lower price with a smaller
mortgage. They have a very short drive to work—

items.speaker: Andrew Bayly
items.text: And a great place.
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4017

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: —and a great place to live. But, of course, one of the things that
those people will be looking for is to enjoy t he connectivity that they can enjoy in a
major metropolitan area. Fortunately, Blenheim is one of those towns that is now fully
fibred, and so they are able to enjoy that. That is one of the things that people look to
when they make a decision about where they are going to live. This is a major
opportunity for rural New Zealand, provincial New Zealand. People are struggling in
Auckland trying to buy houses, and we are trying to deal with that, but in the meantime
there is a wonderful opportunity for regiona l New Zealand. All you have to do is put
your hand up and tell a good story.
Moving on to rural broadband, farms and rural businesses today are modern
businesses that absolutely rely on good connectivity. It is not just internet banking,
although that is a very important part of it. Farmers have had to deal with satellite
internet connections, in the most part, in quite isolated areas. Unfortunately, with the
security systems that banking requires on the internet and the way that satellites work,
with bursts of information going up and down, in most cases it simply will not work on
a banking system. So that does not work for them. That is not the answer. They are
working on those satellite systems, but they are very expensive. The Rural Broadband
Initiative offers a really good way for solutions to be found locally, and I had the
pleasure on Monday night of attending two meetings in my electorate, Kaikōura, around
putting a bid together for a Marlborough solution alongside the contestable fund for the
Rural Broadband Initiative. This is really a great example of a community getting
together and working together for a local initiative to solve a local problem.
And we can do it in a very cost -effective way. I can give you an example. In the
southern part of th e electorate, the Āmuri Basin had the same problem, and a local guy
got sick of trying to deal with it through the normal channels, so he got off his backside
and started Amuri.net. This provides high-speed broadband via wireless right around the
Āmuri Basin, and it has extended it out to much greater areas than that. That is a local
solution for a local problem, but a very modern solution, with high -speed internet. That
technology is moving on as we speak. I heard yesterday from a local person in
Marlborough. They are putting together a package for a 14 -home subdivision where
they can provide 1.2 gigabit via wireless. I hope in the near future to hold an event here,
in the Beehive, to demonstrate that technology, which is a major step forward.
So fibre is the ultimate, but it is not suitable everywhere —but there are other
solutions. So it is with great pleasure that I commend what is a very commendable
Budget to the House.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Well, Nati onal has called Budget 2015 a plan that is
working. It might be working for some New Zealanders like Fonterra and the big dairy
farmers who stand to benefit from $100 million in subsidies for irrigation and more
water pollution. It might be benefiting and be a plan that is working for all the offshore
speculators who are free to buy up residential properties in Auckland. It might be
working for the big corporates that have bought off shares in our energy companies. But
Budget 2015 and National’s economic policies are not working for our climate and they
are not working for our environment. National is building an economy that works only
for New Zealanders who already have a lot.
National has failed to reach a surplus this year, but even worse is the environ mental
deficit that it is creating for present and future generations. The environment did not get
very much attention at all in the Minister of Finance’s Budget speech, and nor did the
greatest challenge of our time: climate change. Our national icon, the  kiwi, was briefly
mentioned, but even that had a strong element of public relations spin and Budget day
smoke and mirrors. The much-vaunted $11.2 million that the Minister is directing to the
grandly titled “Save our Iconic Kiwi” initiative is being funde d from the Department of
4018 Budget Debate 26 May 2015
Conservation’s natural heritage programme. It is not new money, and that programme
has actually been cut by $7 million, from $166 million budgeted this year to $159
million in 2015 -16. More funds should certainly be dedicated to sa ving the kiwi, but
that should not be at the expense of the 2,800 other species that are threatened with
extinction. But that is what National is doing, because it is cutting conservation funding,
not significantly increasing it.
The Department of Conserv ation desperately needs more operational funding and it
has not got it. In the post -election briefing to the Minister, the department said:
“effective pest control is the single biggest determinant of ecosystem health and
biodiversity loss or gain. Less th an 25 percent of conservation land receives
interventions on key threats, with around 8 percent receiving possum, rat and stoat
control.”—other than in the Battle for our Birds year. So we have the kiwi population
declining. We need a significant investmen t in conservation and in more pest control,
but that is not what the Government has provided. That is, of course, in total contrast to
its spendthrift approach and its $46 million in subsidies to the oil industry! And what
are we seeing with the Department  of Conservation? It is actually having to reduce the
area under sustained possum control from a million hectares in the current year to
785,000 hectares in the coming financial year. That is right —reduce the area subject to
sustained possum control. That is despite the fact that the department’s own advice to
the Minister said that that is the key issue that needs more funding. And most of this
kiwi money only comes in 2017 and 2018, so it is not an immediate programme.
What have we heard today? We have h eard that the population of Māui’s dolphins is
declining. It has fallen from 55 adults to an estimated 43 to 47 adult individuals. Māui’s
dolphins could be extinct by 2029. The marine mammal sanctuary needs to be extended.
There needs to be proper protecti on from fishing -related mortalities there, but we are
not seeing measures in the Budget to assist species like Māui’s dolphin.
Then we go on to the climate, which was barely mentioned in the Budget. I have
been to two of the Government’s consultation meet ings on New Zealand’s target for
emission reduction. Everyone who spoke at those meetings did so with aroha, with
passion, and with information. They were talking about our future for themselves and
those who come after us. They want real action and real t argets. There was a strong
sense of disappointment that the Government has not fostered a strong national
conversation about climate change and about what individuals, whānau, and families
can actually do to reduce our emissions. It is not just at the cons ultation meetings where
people have been calling for action. The Motu Economic and Public Policy Research
Trust produced a report this month that showed that 87 percent of New Zealanders are
concerned about climate change and want action. So the Budget is very disappointing in
its failure to engage on the climate.
The Government has certainly taken a small step towards a capital gains tax to try to
discourage property speculation, but it has done absolutely nothing to put a real price on
carbon. It has gut ted the emissions trading scheme and the Budget has nothing in it to
stop Fonterra continuing to put in place new coal -fired boilers in its new plants, like at
Darfield, and in its expanded plants, like at Studholme. All we are getting in the
consultation document is the Government making excuses on what the cost of real
action will be and making excuses as to why our emissions, at 17 tonnes, are more than
double the global average. It is really disappointing that we have not seen in this Budget
measures to help us make the transition to a low -carbon economy. Instead, we get the
Government talking about the cost. As someone at the Christchurch meeting said: “The
Government talks about cost, but what cost do you put on the collapse of civilisation,
with a 4 d egree rise in global temperatures? Please, Mr Groser, don’t talk to me about
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4019
cost; talk to me about my children.” This Government is not investing in future
generations. It is not investing in protecting our planet and our climate.
There has been a comple te failure of imagination in the Budget and in the
Government’s whole approach to climate change. Instead of moving out of industries
like dairy, it is focusing on encouraging and promoting industries like dairy and oil,
which just increase our emissions r ather than reduce them. The Government is missing
the chance to create new jobs in industries that can help us make that transition. It is
missing the chance to invest in renewables, it has not got a plan for positioning us so
that we are in a good positio n for the fast uptake of new technology like electric
vehicles, and there is no real plan of transition. By spending up on motorways and by
weakening the Resource Management Act to encourage urban sprawl, it is missing the
chance to have compact, livable c ities where it is easy to take a bike, to take a bus, to
get on the train, and to have new residential developments clustered around public
transport routes. It is missing the opportunity to improve the health of the New Zealand
population and to reduce ob esity by encouraging more active transport. Yes, we have
$35 million in this Budget being spent on urban cycleways, but that is a pittance
compared with the hundreds of millions being spent on new motorways.
We can rework our economy for a better, cleaner  future that is innovative and that
provides opportunities for everyone, but that is not what National’s plan is about. The
Green Party wants prosperity for everyone. We want to make that transition to a zero -
carbon economy, and we have got a plan to do th at. If it had been a Green Budget, we
would have seen a research and development tax credit.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.

26 May 2015 Oral Questions  3933 
 
TUESDAY, 26 MAY 2015 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
ORAL QUESTIONS  
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
KiwiSaver—Government Contributions 
1. METIRIA TUREI (Co -Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister: Does he stand 
by all his statements? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
Metiria Turei : Does he stand by his reported statement that no one had been 
disadvantaged by the move to scrap the $1,000 KiwiSaver kick-start payment? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: The member might want to table the source for that because I 
cannot recall it. 
Metiria Turei: Has the Prime Minister seen that New Zealand ranks 22 nd out of 24 
countries in the OECD for savings, and will his removal of the $1,000 KiwiSaver kick -
start contribution make this poor savings record better or worse? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Firstly, savings records have improved under this 
Government. Secondly, there are multiple ways of measuring those things. And, thirdly, 
the removal of the $1,000 kick -start contribution will not make a blind bit of difference 
to the number of people who join KiwiSaver. 
Metiria Turei: What evidence does the Prime Minister have that the sign -up rates 
for KiwiSaver will not be affected? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : That is t he formal advice from the Inland Revenue 
Department, and it is supported by the view that the people who are joining KiwiSaver 
are essentially doing so because it is now well organised within the workplace. Some of 
the big scheme providers are extremely we ll organised. We have got about 15,000 to 
20,000 people joining in a month. I would be very, very surprised if it changes at all as a 
result of this. 
Metiria Turei: Does the Prime Minister agree with the Service and Food Workers 
Union, which said that low -paid workers said that they would be the hardest hit by his 
decision to axe the kick-start? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Definitely not. The lowest -paid workers will be supported by 
the fact that the Government increased the Working for Families contribution by $12.50 
a week. They will also be supported if they were ever on a benefit by the increase of 
$25. But, overall, I  do not think the removal of $1,000 that people would get in 40 
years’ time will be that material.  
Metiria Turei : Has the Prime Minister seen that savings in New Zealand are 
currently concentrated in the top one-fifth of all income earners, and will his removal of 
the $1,000 KiwiSaver kick -start make saving for those in the bottom four -fifths of 
income earners easier or harder? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Well, it is logical, actually —and, I suspect, consistent around 
pretty much eve ry OECD country —that those who earn the most technically save the 
most, because savings, of course, is for gone consumption. It is one of the very reasons 
why this political party will never be means testing New Zealand superannuation, as 
Labour is now promoting.  
Metiria Turei: Does the Prime Minister understand that wealth inequality in New 
Zealand is twice as large as income inequality, and will his removal of the $1,000 
3934 Oral Questions  26 May 2015 
 
KiwiSaver kick -start strengthen or weaken the incentives for all New Zealanders to 
build wealth through savings? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I think it is important to remember that KiwiSaver is a scheme 
where after you put in your 3 percent contribution, employers put in 3 percent and the 
Government puts in the memb er’s tax credit. If you look at all of those numbers over 
the normal sort of 45-year working period for most people, $1,000 is immaterial.  
Budget 2015—Support for Vulnerable New Zealanders 
2. TIM MACINDOE (National —Hamilton West)  to the Minister of Finance : 
How does Budget 2015 continue the Government’s plan to manage the public finances 
while supporting the most vulnerable? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : The Government has continued its 
plan to be careful with spending and to choose carefully where it allocates new 
spending. As a result of that, despite fiscal constraints, we have continued an ongoing 
programme of supporting New Zealand families to get ahead. This has resulted in a 
number of changes. From 1 April this year paid parental leave increased by 2 weeks to 
16 weeks. It will increase by another 2 weeks next April. On 1 April the adult minimum 
wage increased to $14.75. New Zealand superannuation increased by another 2 percent. 
From 1 July this year children under 13 will have access to free GP visits and free 
prescriptions. From 1 April next year the benefit rates for beneficiary families with 
children will go up by $25 a week.  
Tim Macindoe: How will Budget 2015 support more jobs and higher wages for New 
Zealand families? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : One of the most important things we can do for vulnerable 
families is to assist the parents into work. When they are in work, of course, it is 
important for them to see the prospect of steadily rising incomes. This is occurring. The 
Budget forecast shows 194,000 extra jobs since late 2010, and another 150,000 jobs are 
expected by 2019. Average annual wages have increased by $5,700 in the last 4 years 
and are forecast to rise by a further $7,000 to where the annual average wage will be 
$63,000 a year in 4 years’ time. We can assist more people into work because there are 
more jobs, and when they are in jobs both the minimum wage and the average wage will 
continue to rise.  
Tim Macindoe : How will the Government’s $790 million child hardship pa ckage 
deliver more support for the families who need it most? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The evidence shows that those families who are most in 
need are those who are persistently on low incomes, for a long time on benefit, where 
there are children. Therefore, the Government’s package is targeted at lifting the benefit 
rates for families with children. This is the first time that core benefit rates have been 
increased, apart from inflation adjustments, since 1972. We also recognise that low -
income working families are under pressure, and so there are increases in the minimum 
family tax credit and in the base rate of the in -work tax credit. And, in addition to that, 
childcare assistance will be increased. The package targets around 160,000 families, 
with 300,000 children, on incomes of less than $36,350 per year. 
Tim Macindoe : What other measures were progressed as part of Budget 2015 to 
support vulnerable New Zealanders? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The Government is continuing to advance its social 
investment approach, which is aimed at resolving some of the most complex social and 
family problems that there are in our community. Outside of the child hardship package, 
the Budget also provides over $100 million for these further initiatives, and they are 
initiatives aimed at breaking the cycles that lock fam ilies into long-term dependency—
that is, the cycles of drug and alcohol addiction, criminal offending, persistently low 
26 May 2015 Oral Questions  3935 
 
incomes, low educational achievement, and domestic viole nce. This Government is not 
afraid to try to address those issues directly, because, in a sense, it does not matter how 
much income those families have, they have got more serious long -term problems that 
need sustained support in order to resolve them. 
Prime Minister—Statements 
3. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister: Why 
has he reneged on his commitment made in 2011 that “the $1,000 kick -start for new 
KiwiSaver members will remain as it is now” by removing the kick -start in this year’s 
Budget, and did he renege on any other commitments in the Budget? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : Those comments were made with re gard to 
KiwiSaver changes in Budget 2011—when Labour’s policy was from about four leaders 
ago—raising the retirement age at the time. As I said, the Government intends to reduce 
the amount of money it has to borrow from overseas to put into KiwiSaver, and increase 
the amount of genuine savings from the private sector. That is precisely what we have 
done. The only reneging I have seen since the Budget has actually been from the Labour 
leader, who spent Friday talking about means testing, then sort of reneged, then went— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! 
Andrew Little : Why has he broken his promise made last year to invest $212 
million in regional highways, with Budget 2015 allocating less than half that amount 
over 3 years? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Sorry, could you just repeat the question? I could not hear one 
word— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I will ask Andrew Little to repeat the question. 
Andrew Little : Why has he broken his promise made last year to invest $212 
million in regional highways, with Budget 2015 allocating less than half that amount 
over 3 years? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : You really need to direct that question to the Minister of 
Transport, because there will be a log ical explanation. We are totally committed to 
those roads, but they will be accounted for in a certain way. 
Andrew Little : Why has he broken his promise made in September last year to 
create 150,000 jobs in 2 years, given that the Budget sh ows him missing that target by 
50,000 jobs? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: The member is wrong, again. 
Andrew Little : Why has he broken his promise made in September last year to 
increase the average wage by $7,000 in 3 years, given tha t the Budget shows the 
average wage will rise only half that much? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I think the Budget showed that wage growth over the next 3 
will be about $7,000. Prior to that it was $5,600. But what is true is that average wages 
are g rowing faster than inflation under this Government, something that the previous 
Government could not achieve. 
Tim Macindoe: What reports has the Prime Minister received on other approaches 
to managing retirement savings policy? 
Mr SPEAKER: Provided it is within the prime ministerial responsibility, I call the 
Rt Hon Prime Minister. 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I have seen a number of conflicting reports on other 
approaches to retirement savings policy. One included a questio n about means testing 
New Zealander superannuation. The answer was: “Yep, I don’t think we can avoid 
looking at that.” and “You’ve got people over 65 able to keep on working, earning a 
good income, working alongside people who are doing the same or similar  work not 
3936 Oral Questions  26 May 2015 
 
getting it. Is it right that the person over 65 on a full -time income should also get this 
income supplement?”. 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! [ Interruption] Order! Would the Prime Minister resume his 
seat. This answer is only going to lead to disorder. 
Andrew Little: Why has he broken his promise made last year not to impose new 
taxes, by putting a new levy on people entering and leaving the country and hiking the 
levy on broadband users, bearing in mind the Oxford Dictionary says a levy is “a tax 
raised by levying”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : We have not broken our promise. What we have done is 
ensure that there will be more money for biosecurity. Mr Little can spend all his time in 
question time asking these questions if he wants, but the real question is: will he get 
back on side with his caucus , who now hate him because he is polling 25 percent 
because he wants to means test New Zealand superannuation? It ain’t going well, 
Andrew. 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! Before I call the honourable member Tim Macindoe 
[Interruption] Order! Before I call him I will need him to be aware of Speaker’s ruling 
154/2A: “It is not reasonable to use questions from the governing party or its support 
parties to attack other members of the House.”  
Tim Macindoe: What measures has the Government taken to ensure its retirement 
savings policies are sustainable over the long term? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : What an excellent question. We have set out a responsible 
path for overall Government spending so that current settings for New Zealand 
superannuation are both affordable and fully factored into our long -term forecast. As 
Treasury notes, New Zealand’s current superannuation costs are quite low by world 
standards, at less than 5 percent of GDP, compared with over 9 percent, on average, 
across the OECD. By 2060 —that is 45 years from now —New Zealand’s annual 
superannuation costs are forecast to be 8 percent of GDP. That is lower than the current 
OECD average. If one was reall y worried about this issue, as one political party in 
Parliament says it is, there are only three ways of resolving this issue: raise the age of 
superannuation, means test, or make it less generous to everybody. Mr Little has ruled 
out two; it must be No. 3. No wonder your caucus— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! 
Andrew Little: Why has he broken his promise to stop Kiwis becoming tenants in 
their own country, by failing in this Budget to stop foreign buyers who are purchasing 
one in every 10 h ouses sold in Auckland, and instead announcing a range of measures, 
none of which will make a difference to the Auckland house price crisis? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : The member would be a lot more credible if he did not make 
up numbers. It is not  one in 10. He has no evidence to support that. Actually, nobody 
knows. In fact, if he stopped making up policy on the hoof, like the means testing of 
superannuation, he would do a bit better as well. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Speaking about the primary question, which was “renege 
on any other commitments”— 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! Can I just have the supplementary question without the 
preamble, please. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: You are getting it right now. I a m relating it to the primary 
question. 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The member will resume his seat. There is simply no need to 
relate it to the primary question. The Standing Orders require that the supplementary 
question is related to the primary quest ion. I call on the member to simply ask his 
supplementary question. 
26 May 2015 Oral Questions  3937 
 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am asking a 
supplementary question. I have used five words, and you have stopped me. 
Mr SPEAKER: I am very tempted to not allow the member to ask a supplementary 
question. When he wants to ask a supplementary question, I give the member the call. 
He rises and asks the question. There is no need for an introduction about relating it to 
the primary question. I do not want to have to repeat this for the member. We will be 
moving to somebody else if I need to. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. With the greatest of 
respect, and I have been here longer than you—[Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER: Order! It is a point of order. I intend to listen in silence. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : If I intend there to be some relativity to the primary 
question in what I am about to ask, that is  up to my discretion. With the greatest of 
respect, this is the first time I have had someone make the ruling you have just made 
from that Chair. 
Mr SPEAKER : Well, then, I suggest the member needs to listen more often in 
question time. You are required to—[Interruption] Order! The member will stand and 
withdraw that remark immediately. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: I withdraw. 
Mr SPEAKER: Supplementary question, Andrew Little.  
Rt Hon Winston Peters: Supplementary question, Mr Speaker. 
Mr SPEAKER: No, supplementary question, Andrew Little. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.  
Mr SPEAKER : Order! The member will also be very familiar with the Standing 
Orders. I have the right to decide where I will take a supplementary question. I warned 
the member that he would not get a sec ond chance. I am going to hear a supplementary 
question from Andrew Little. I may change my mind and then let the member ask a 
supplementary question. I may do so. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. You did not tell me 
that I would not get a supplementary question. You have— 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! [ Interruption] The member will immediately —
[Interruption] The member will now leave the Chamber. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters withdrew from the Chamber.  
Andrew Little: Why does he not just keep his promises rather than inventing new 
excuses for breaking them? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : This Government keeps its promises, and that is why it keeps 
getting re -elected. I f the member wants to recreate history he is welcome to it, but, 
actually, he knows, like I know, that the most popular thing on Thursday and Friday 
was our Budget, and the least popular thing was his decision to means test New Zealand 
superannuation. 
Budget 2015—Water Management 
4. BARBARA KURIGER (National—Taranaki - King Country) to the Minister 
for Primary Industries : How will Budget 2015 help develop more water storage and 
irrigation projects? 
Hon NATHAN GUY (Minister for Primary Industries) : As part of Budget 2015, 
irrigation projects will now receive through the Irrigation Acceleration Fund a kick-start 
of $25 million in operating funding for 5 years from 2016 -17. The Irrigation 
Acceleration Fund helps support the development of irrigation infrastructure proposals 
to the stage where they are investment -ready, which means that they  must be 
commercially robust and demonstrate a high level of user and community support. 
3938 Oral Questions  26 May 2015 
 
Around 100,000 hectares of new irrigated areas are expected from the Irrigation 
Acceleration Fund - funded projects to date, with around 36,000 hectares of that 
commissioned or currently being constructed.  
Barbara Kuriger: Why is this funding boost so important for our regions? 
Hon NATHAN GUY : That is a good question. The need for water storage projects 
is obvious, given that nearly e very part of the country has suffered through droughts at 
some stage over the last 3 or so years. We do not have a water shortage issue in New 
Zealand; we have a water storage issue. It just does not rain in the right place at the right 
time. Providing a consistent, reliable water supply for farmers and growers has massive 
potential to boost growth, create jobs, and grow our exports from provincial regions. 
Barbara Kuriger: What other ways does the Government help support water storage 
in irrigation projects? 
Hon NATHAN GUY: The Government also supports water storage projects through 
Crown Irrigation Investments Ltd., which acts as a bridging investor for regional water 
infrastructure development. Over the last 2 years, $12 0 million has been allocated to 
Crown Irrigation Investments Ltd, with the potential to provide a further 125,000 
hectares of new irrigation. Work is under way to enable greater collaboration between 
Crown Irrigation Investments Ltd and the Irrigation Acceleration Fund. This will help to 
ensure that more of these critical regional water storage projects get to the construction 
stage. This is hugely exciting for rural New Zealand. 
Richard Prosser: Will the Government’s funding initiatives in the Budget assist in 
the promotion of the Ruataniwha Dam scheme? 
Hon NATHAN GUY: I could not hear him. [Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER: Order! It was difficult to hear. I did hear the question but I suspect 
some members did not. The mike might not have been on. I will ask Richard Prosser to 
repeat the question. 
Richard Prosser: Will the Government’s irrigation initiatives in the Budget assist in 
the promotion of the Ruataniwha Dam project? 
Hon NA THAN GUY : Currently  the Irrigation Acceleration Fund has invested 
almost $6 million in Ruataniwha, and that is now working through a process of getting a 
consent. Then it will need to prove to Crown Irrigation Investments Ltd that it is indeed 
investment-ready for them to have a look at it. 
Iraq, Military Deployment—Iraqi Army 
5. RON MARK (NZ First)  to the Prime Minister : Does he stand by all his 
statements? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
Ron Mark : When he said in the House “Get some guts”, was he talking to the 
Opposition parties or to the Iraqi Army, which has been in retreat for the last 2 months 
and was routed at Ramadi by a force that it outnumbered ten to one? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Well, really specifically, I was speaking to the Leader of the 
Opposition, who I think, in his heart of hearts, knows that the right thing for this country 
to do on a bipartisan bas is is to actually stand up to the people who undertake these 
atrocities, and I hope that he will eventually see it our way, because we are right on this 
side of the House.  
Ron Mark: Does he stand by his statement “If Iraq is to gain control of i ts cities, it 
will need strong and well-trained forces.”; if so, does he not realise that you cannot train 
cowards to fight? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : In terms of the first part of the question, yes, you do need 
strong forces; in terms of the latt er part of the question, I think that the member should 
26 May 2015 Oral Questions  3939 
 
really probably reflect on that. To put that generalisation across a whole country’s 
population is either foolhardy or harsh. He can choose which one he prefers.  
Ron Mark: When he received his most recent briefing from the Defence Force on 
Iraq, did that briefing state that there was a possibility that our troops would be 
surrounded at Camp Taji? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I am not going to go into the individual briefings I get, 
because I think that it would not be in the national interest to do so, but what I am quite 
prepared to say is that the safety and security of our men and women who are in Taji 
airbase is our No. 1 priority. There is obviously work done to make sure we contin ually 
assess that situation. There is a variety of trigger points that we would look at if we 
thought that it was appropriate to bring our people home, and we have always said that 
we would do that. But I am quite comfortable in the advice I have at the mo ment that, 
notwithstanding it is obviously a dangerous environment in Iraq, our people are in the 
safest position they can be in, actually—in Taji airbase. 
Ron Mark: Does the Prime Minister agree with the US Chairman of the Joint Chiefs 
of Staff, General Martin Dempsey, who said that the Iraqi security force “was not driven 
out of Ramadi. They drove out of Ramadi.”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I am not going to be a Monday morning quarterback on what 
happened in Ramadi, but I have seen the comments from Prime Minister al -Abadi, who 
said that they are keen to retake that ground. Certainly, the advice that we have had is 
that some ground was lost and some ground was gained. But if you take a step back on 
the overall thing, if the member’s logic is followed to the obvious conclusion, what he is 
basically saying is that Iraq should surrender itself to the Islamic State of Iraq and the 
Levant (ISIL). I simply say to the member that if he thinks that is not going to increase 
the risks to New Zealan ders, then it is really unbelievable. If the member wants to go 
out there and tell New Zealanders that he is quite prepared, through his own inactions, 
to put them at greater risk, then he is welcome to go and campaign on doing that. But he 
will run a million miles from that when I start pointing it out publicly, and that is what I 
intend to do. 
Ron Mark: Does he think that troops who flee and leave tanks and artillery worth 
millions of dollars behind and troops who flee when they outnumber the en emy ten to 
one are able and capable of being trained to fight? 
Mr SPEAKER : In so far as there is prime ministerial responsibility, the right 
honourable Prime Minister. 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : All I can say is that if you listen to the Chief of Defence 
Force, he is very confident of the training capability that our people have. He has seen 
that demonstrated in places like Afghanistan, where we have made a difference, and I 
am confident, actually, that in time we will make a difference in improving the skills of 
the Iraqis. 
Ron Mark : What is the Prime Minister’s view of Ash Carter, the United States 
Secretary of Defense, who said “What apparently happened was that the Iraqi forces just 
showed no will to fight. They were not outnumbered. In fact, they vastly outnumbered 
the opposing force … that says to me, and I think to most of us, that we have an issue 
with the will of Iraqis to fight ISIL and defend themselves.”? What is the Prime 
Minister’s view of that statement? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I am the Prime Minister of New Zealand, not a commentator 
on what other politicians around the world say. 
Ron Mark: Does he not realise that he sent our brave New Zealand soldiers t o Iraq 
on a fool’s errand and the training the Iraqi Army to stand and fight is literally Mission: 
Impossible? 
3940 Oral Questions  26 May 2015 
 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : No. What I do think is that ISIL presents a threat not only in 
the region but also presents a regional threat to countries that New Zealanders travel to, 
and I think it presents a domestic threat. The member can sit there all he likes and say 
that we should abdicate our responsibilities and do nothing, but I simply say to the 
member that that would put them at gre ater risk. I think that if you look at the public 
polling that has been undertaken on this matter, the most recent poll that we saw in the 
New Zealand Herald indicated that on a ratio of 3:1 New Zealanders actually do think 
we should do something to protec t ourselves from people who are abhorrent. If the 
member does not believe in doing that, I am quite surprised, because he is a former 
military man and I would have thought he would understand that. 
Hon Phil Goff: When the Prime Minister said  the trigger for changing his stance on 
deployment to Iraq was if the New Zealand Defence Force thought there was “an 
absolute threat” to New Zealand troops, how does he define “absolute threat”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : That is the very point —I do not. They decide that. T hey are 
the ones who tell us, through their advice. On the back of our advice, we will decide 
whether they come or no, but they define the risks. 
Finance, Minister—Tax Revenue 
6. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of 
Finance: Does he agree with National Party finance spokesperson Bill English: “We 
don’t believe in new and more taxes. We think we can manage with the tax revenue we 
have”? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : Yes, I do agree with my party’s 
finance spokesman, which is more than I can say for Andrew Little, who does not agree 
with his party’s finance spokesman. [Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I am having trouble hearing because of the yelling from my 
left here. [Interruption] Well, no, it was this one who was distracting me. 
Grant Robertson: In lig ht of that answer, why, then, did he and John Key promise 
New Zealanders in the 2014 election campaign that there would be no new taxes when 
he has introduced a property tax, an arrivals and departures tax, and extended the 
broadband tax? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The extension of broadband was certainly discussed prior to 
the election. As we have discussed, the tax measures are an extension of existing taxes, 
which the member may not have known about in his case. The levy at the airports is a 
user charge, and we would expect to be able to continue to expand the use of user 
charges. 
Grant Robertson: What is the difference between a levy and a tax? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The levy is a user charge, and that is different  from an 
income test on national superannuation. 
Grant Robertson: Will every dollar collected under the regime brought into place 
by the Border Processing (Arrivals and Departures) Levy Bill go towards the cost of 
border processing? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: Yes, and I would imagine that every dollar of expenditure on 
those services is going to be heavily scrutinised by passengers, airlines, airports, and 
anyone else who is interested in getting those levies down, as we are. 
Grant Robertson: Does he stand by his statement: “Further extension of the current 
tax on capital gains is likely to have high compliance costs, and that is a conclusion that 
three tax inquiries and several Governments have come to over the last 20 years. If it 
excludes the family home,”—like it does—“it will not [make] much difference, … ”; if 
so, why has he now introduced a tax that he says that he does not know the impact of, 
does not know how much revenue it will raise, and that has such high compliance costs? 
26 May 2015 Oral Questions  3941 
 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : I do stand by the statement, and part of the point of 
introducing a brightline test is to avoid excessive compliance costs. We have yet to see 
how much impact the introduction of that test will have on the housing market. 
Grant Robertson : Can he confirm his statement in the weekend that he does not 
know whether this tax that he has introduced on property speculators will work? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The question has be en about what impact we expect it will 
have on the Auckland housing market. The member will be familiar with the discussion. 
If the Auckland house prices are driven significantly by speculators turning over 
properties within 2 years, then the tax may have an impact. If the prices are not driven 
primarily by that but are driven by other factors such as restricted supply of land or 
costs of construction, then it will not make much difference.  
Budget 2015—Benefit-dependent Households 
7. TODD MULLER (Nation al—Bay of Plenty)  to the Minister for Social 
Development: How does Budget 2015 help parents who receive a benefit? 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY (Minister for Social Development) : Last week we 
announced a $790 million child hardship package as part of Budget 2015. The package

something is better than nothing. The party that used to sa y it was ambitious for New 
Zealand has now resigned itself to the level of the micro-managing and the tinkering.

say: “There’s the chance for me to be a success. There’s the c hance for me to grow up 
in a regional town in New Zealand, get a job, raise my family there, and buy a house.”? 
Where is that in this Budget? All we saw was a Budget with its eye firmly on one thing:

the 2017 election and promising tax cuts. Mark my words,  that is what this Budget is 
about. Throw out $25 a week that, by all means, will be welcome in those households, 
but that is the build -up to 2017. It is the build -up to once again —just as this National 
Government did in 2010 —putting forward a package of t ax cuts designed to bribe and 
win National an election, rather than dealing with the social and economic problems that 
are in front of New Zealand today. It is irresponsible. It is a politician’s Budget; it is not 
a Budget for the people of New Zealand.  
But if we take a look at the deficit of money in this Budget, let us be clear. Yes, 
National promised surpluses to New Zealand for 2014 -15. It promised that at two 
elections. It promised that right throughout the last 4 or 5 years and it has completely 
failed to deliver on that promise. But it is much worse than that, because what this 
Budget does is kick the fiscal can down the road. Even in the optimistic scenario that 
Treasury put up for New Zealand, we will see growth halved on an annual basis from 
now through until 2019. That growth today is built on the shaky foundations of milk, of 
selling houses in Auckland, and of recovering from disaster, but even that, in the 
optimistic scenario, halves over the next period.  
Debt as a percentage of GDP peaks in 20 16, but get this clear. Not a single cent of 
the current $88 billion worth of debt will be paid off until 2019. That is the real casualty 
of failing to post a surplus. It is the fact that future generations of New Zealanders are 
again being saddled by a Na tional Government with huge levels of debt, and that is in 
the optimistic scenario that Treasury is putting forward. We see exports remaining 
stagnant at about 27 percent of GDP in the most optimistic scenario, and then today we 
hear that dairy exports are  now down 27 percent compared with where they were last 
April. We have got the largest current account deficit in 6 years.  
These are the scenarios in which National would say good times are ahead for New 
Zealand. But if we look into the detail of the Budg et, look at what is called the 
downside scenario, included in the downside scenario is falling commodity prices. Let 
us be realistic here. Everyone in the world is telling the National Government that dairy 
prices will continue to fall. Last year Goldman S achs put out a report that said there is a 
5-year glut in milk products being supplied into the global market, and commodity 
prices will keep falling. It also says that there will be higher inflation. We have seen no 
evidence of that. The Reserve Bank Governor cannot guarantee that.  
In that scenario there will be no surplus next year. There will not be a surplus until 
2018 in that scenario. There will not be any debt paid back before 2019 in that scenario. 
In fact, the percentage of debt as a percentage of  GDP will be 26 percent —miles away 
from where those members are now. The current account deficit hits 7.7 percent of GDP 
in 2016-17 under that scenario.  
The numbers in this Budget are clear: the economy is standing still in the best 
scenario and going backwards in the worst scenario. That is the economic legacy of Bill 
English and John Key kicking the fiscal can down the road. They made promises to 
New Zealand that wages would go up by $7,000 and that there would be 140,000 more 
jobs. They made that promis e last year. It was to happen in 2017. What they do in this 
Budget, in the most optimistic of scenarios, is kick the can down the road to 2019. It is 
always jam tomorrow, with Bill English. We are always on the cusp of something 
special. The only something special in the National Government is Nick Smith and he is 
very special indeed. We are always on the cusp of something special with Bill English, 
and it never comes.  
Government members like to crow about being the great economic managers. Well, 
the reality is seven Budgets, seven deficits, no debt being paid back, and exports flat -
lining. There is no real growth, sustainable growth, in this economy going forward for 
New Zealand under the settings of this Government and it is all done in a sacrifice at the 
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3951 
 
altar of tax cuts in 2017. That is irresponsible Government. That is irresponsible 
management of the New Zealand economy.  
So what should the Government have been doing in this Budget? Well, it should 
have been investing in the regions of New Zealand. No doubt someone on the 
Government side will get up and tell us: “No, there’s a great initiative in there. There 
are the regional research institutes.” Well, to start with, there are only three of them and 
it may have escaped members on the other side, but th ere are more than three regions. 
The other thing is that the amount of money for them is pitiful. What it typifies is an 
approach to economic development driven by Steven Joyce. We do not want to see 
more money going to Steven Joyce’s mates, whom he talks to in the Koru Club. What 
we want to see is real investment in the regions, making sure that we get alongside all of 
regional New Zealand, and build on the strengths.  
I was in Gisborne last week. There are people there doing amazing, innovative things 
in engineering, in adding value to wood products. They need to be backed by a 
Government, and that is what the Labour Government will do after 2017 —not pick 
winners out of Steven Joyce’s rolodex, and not put Steven Joyce, who thinks a big night 
out is at Skyc ity on the pokies, in charge of economic development. We need real 
economic development in our regions. That was shockingly absent from this Budget.  
Also shockingly absent from this Budget was a proper plan to diversify the New 
Zealand economy. How long w ill this Government go on believing that it can simply 
supply one product to one big customer and think that that is a proper strategy for the 
New Zealand economy? We must have real initiatives to add value, but they were 
absent from this Budget.  
Then there is the housing crisis, where Bill English’s solution is to come up with a 
tax that will not work —which he has acknowledged himself —and a housing 
programme that Nick Smith has admitted today will not build even a fraction of the 
houses that have been pro mised in Auckland. The failure of this Government to deal 
with the housing crisis in New Zealand was emphasised by the fact that the Budget 
documents did not even contain most of the housing initiatives because it was such a 
panicked, last-minute reaction to being told off by the Reserve Bank Governor. 
The biggest deficit in this Budget is not actually the deficit in the finances; it is the 
deficit of ideas, the deficit of hope, and the deficit of opportunity for New Zealanders. A 
young New Zealander today, with the world at their feet, will be looking at this Budget 
and asking themselves: “What is here in New Zealand for me? What future is here?”. 
New Zealanders deserve far, far better than a Budget that focuses so much on micro -
issues, that is so much abou t political management, and that breaks every promise that 
has been made. New Zealanders deserve far better than this Budget, and they will get it 
after 2017 with a Labour Government.

Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co -Leader—Green): I rise to speak on the Budget. 
Before I begin, I would just like to say to National Party members and Labour Party 
members that the jokes about gender reassignment surgery are pretty disgusting. They 
are ugly, and I think they should stop.  
I would like to start by acknowledging the positive dimensions of the Budget. I 
would like to identify four particular parts of it. The first is the benefit increases above

taken back by the changes forcing parents to go to work when their children are only

poverty in our country  is, I think, a good thing. I acknowledge the work of Child

gains tax and the foreign buyers tax identity changes. The introduction of a capital gains

Parker, who  provided, along with the Green Party, the momentum to actually get a 
capital gains tax introduced, and over time it will be regularised and made more 
sensible, as it should be. I think that those two initiatives —the increase in benefits and 
the capital gains tax —are ones that the Green Party has also campaigned on for many 
years, and we are very pleased to see them, as limited as they are. 
Thirdly, I would like to identify the user -pays airport charges. I think that they are 
important. Biosecurity is an important issue for New Zealand, and this is a good way to 
fund it. 
Fourthly, I would like to congratu late National on abandoning the fetish around the 
surplus that characterised its election campaign. It was always ridiculous the way that 
National characterised the surplus as the defining feature of prudent economic 
management, and I think Bill English ha s now acknowledged that. I wish that he had 
done so during the election campaign. 
Aside from the good elements of the Budget —and there are some —there are, 
unfortunately, many other elements of the Budget that are quite bad. Let me start with 
climate change. We now have about 421 billion tonnes of ice being lost each year from 
the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets as a result of climate change. We are losing 
about 421 billion tonnes as the planet warms. The south Antarctic Peninsula ice sheet is 
starting to  break up. This is the greatest challenge on the face of the planet facing 
humanity right now, and, unfortunately, this Government is accelerating New Zealand’s 
emissions rather than cutting them. When we look at an economy like New Zealand’s, 
which is dep endent on a stable climate, and when we look at the floods in Wellington 
and the drought in Canterbury—the 2013 drought, which had such a big impact on New 
Zealand—we can see that New Zealand should be at the forefront of taking action to 
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3955 
 
reduce emissions and taking action on climate change. An economy like ours is 
particularly susceptible to extreme weather events like floods and droughts and the 
changes that are coming our way as a result of our increased greenhouse gas emissions 
globally. 
When we look at what New Zealand is doing, it is actually shameful. New Zealand’s 
gross emissions increased 20 percent from 1990 to 2013. New Zealand’s net greenhouse 
gas emissions increased by 42 percent from 1990 to 2013. I think it is worth dwelling on 
how amazingly i rresponsible we have been as a country. Increasing our net emissions 
by 42 percent from 1990 to 2013 is an incredibly irresponsible thing to do, and there is 
no getting away from that. The Ministry for the Environment has produced forward 
projections that say that New Zealand plans to increase its net emissions by a further 50 
percent in the next 10 years. So not only have we increased our net emissions by 42 
percent over this period but, looking forward, the Ministry for the Environment’s 
projections say t hat New Zealand’s net greenhouse gas emissions will increase by a 
further 50 percent in just one decade. That is an incredibly, grossly irresponsible thing 
to do, and future generations will curse us for it, as they rightly should. 
The reason why these emi ssions are increasing is that we have policy settings 
designed to increase emissions. Since this Government got into office, it has gutted the 
emissions trading scheme, which was meant to put a price on greenhouse emissions in 
order to be an effective econ omic instrument to drive down greenhouse emissions. 
Every economic report you read tells you very clearly that the most effective way to do 
this is to put a price on emissions. That has an effect right across an economy and 
reduces emissions. Unfortunately , when this Government got in, it gutted the key 
elements of the emissions trading scheme. We now have the emissions trading scheme 
as a major liability for the New Zealand Government. It is projected in the 
Government’s papers that the cost of the emissio ns trading scheme to the Government, 
because the subsidies to pollution are now so large, is $684 million of taxpayer 
spending over 2 years. So we plan to subsidise greenhouse pollution via the emissions 
trading scheme —the system that is supposed to cut po llution—to the tune of $684 
million in just 2 years. That is the subsidy that taxpayers are giving to climate polluters 
in New Zealand. The subsidy since the scheme started now totals $859 million of 
taxpayers’ money that has been given to polluters via th e emissions trading scheme. 
That is not a scheme designed to cut emissions; that is a scheme designed to increase 
emissions. 
Treasury has tried to estimate what the cost of the failure to cut greenhouse gas 
emissions will be to the New Zealand public. Its estimate is that our failure to cut 
greenhouse gas emissions means that we are going to have to buy carbon credits 
offshore. Depending on the cost of those carbon credits, Treasury says that it could cost 
us up to $52 billion to buy offshore  carbon credits  to cover the big increases in 
emissions coming out of the New Zealand economy, because all the policy settings are 
set up to increase emissions. We are going to have to buy carbon credits offshore. 
Treasury says that it could cost up to $52 billion of tax payers’ money to buy those 
offshore carbon credits because we have increased our emissions so radically over this 
period. Do we really want to spend $52 billion buying offshore carbon credits that may 
be worthless—but, you know, they make the grade for acc ounting purposes—or would 
we rather spend that money in New Zealand to reduce our own emissions? The 
Government’s answer to that is very clear. It would prefer to buy offshore carbon 
credits because its plan is to increase emissions. I think that is incred ibly irresponsible 
and stupid. It is hard, really, to characterise how stupid it is for a Government to have a 
whole bunch of policy settings to increase emissions and then to spend $50 billion 
buying worthless hot air offshore. That is an amazingly short-sighted and stupid policy.

The thing is, it is not just the emissions trading scheme. Of course, there are 
subsidies in many sectors in New Zealand to increase emissions. Just think of the dairy 
sector. If you are in the dairy sector, you do not pay for yo ur methane emissions  or 
nitrous oxide emissions. The taxpayer covers the cost of those for you. They are free to 
the dairy sector. Plus, you get free fresh water. You do not have to pay any charge for 
the water. You get free water pollution. There is no ch arge when you pollute a stream.
