sector—the irrigation subsidies, which is $400 mill ion of subsidies going directly into 
the dairy sector in order to expand it so that its emissions will increase and water quality 
will decline. It is an amazingly short -sighted policy to spend that much money to 
increase pollution. 
Then, of course, beyond that, we have the poor old forestry sector —the forestry 
sector sequesters our carbon and actually reduces our net emissions. Because the price 
of carbon emissions is so low in New Zealand now, the forestry sector is cutting down a 
larger area of trees than  it is replanting. As a result of the Government’s policies, the 
forestry sector is now a net emitter in New Zealand. 
Then we have the subsidies for road freight and road transport. Literally tens of 
billions of dollars are given to motorways and road freight companies for free so that we 
can increase emissions coming out of the roading sector. 
Then we have the subsidies  for fossil fuel exploration. The Government is very keen 
on, and very proud of, the high level of subsidies that  it provides to oil explor ation 
companies in order to look for fossil fuels. So we are subsidising that as well. Is it any 
wonder that Fonterra is literally building coal-fired boilers right now, in the 21st century, 
when we should be cutting emissions? Fonterra, which does not see m to care in the 
slightest about its global brand, is building coal -fired boilers in New Zealand. Is it any 
wonder that the rail network is talking about removing electrification from the main 
trunk line? Could anything signify more how backward and mid - 20th century we have 
become at the beginning of the 21 st century than the rail industry talking not about 
electrifying the rail network but about de -electrifying the rail network in New Zealand? 
We are so out of the loop about what is going on in the world , in terms of the smart 
green economic revolution that is taking the whole of the rest of the world by storm. In 
New Zealand we are determined to drive back to the mid - 20th century. We are going to 
have coal. We are going to have motorways. We are going to subsidise oil exploration. 
We are going to get rid of electrification on rail because “Oh, who wants that 
electrification stuff?”. 
That is the reality of where climate policy has got to in our country, and it is a total, 
total disaster. New Zealand can embrace the smart Green economic revolution, we can 
be part of this global change, we can do the right thing by our kids, but we need the 
Government to change direction.

JULIE ANNE GENTER (Green) : Like many Aucklanders, I am an immigrant to 
Aotearoa New Ze aland. I chose to make my home here because I love this country. I 
love the mountains, I love the beaches, I love the old -growth forest, and I love the 
people of New Zealand, whom I have found very warm, welcoming, practical, and, 
above all, fair-minded.  
I had a successful career as a transportation analyst, and I did that because I wanted 
to have a job that allowed me to find creative solutions to some of the biggest, most 
pressing challenges of the 21 st century. So I did a lot of work in the areas of 
transportation planning and economics because I wanted to be part of the solution. I 
ended up joining the Green Party, firstly, because it is the party that shares my values —
looking after the environment; ensuring that we have a fair society and democracy, th at 
decisions are made at the lowest level at which they affect people—but, most important, 
because the Green Party in Aotearoa was the only political party that was really 
championing the proven, practical policies that should be mainstream but are not bei ng 
implemented here in New Zealand. 
We know they have been proven overseas in very successful northern European 
countries that are managing to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions and reduce 
pollution, and that do not have the levels of increasing inequal ity that we see here in 
New Zealand. I think that we could follow that path —we do not have to reinvent the 
wheel. Unfortunately, neither of the two larger parties has grasped the opportunities that 
are provided by understanding all the interconnections bet ween our environment, our 
economy, and our society. It is common sense to respond to climate change as soon as 
possible, because we have to respond sooner or later. The sooner we take action, the less 
it will cost us. It is common sense to reduce the growi ng gap between the rich and the 
poor, because it is better for everyone in society. It ensures that we are all better off. It 
ensures that we build a much more successful society and economy in the future if we 
invest in our poorest kids. 
The National Government members—and in particular I heard the previous speaker, 
the Hon Nikki Kaye—claim some of these values. They want to say that they care about 
the economy, they care about fairness, they care about the environment, and they are 
doing all these things.  But when you get down to it and you look at the numbers and 
you look at the policies they are implementing, they are simply not taking us in a 
smarter, greener, and fairer direction. They are taking us in a direction of greater 
inequality and more polluti on. I would say the Green Party is the only party that is 
really prepared to stand up for younger New Zealanders, who are being let down by this 
National Government. 
I think the National Government is deeply out of touch if it says the economy is 
working for everyone. We have got a younger generation that is drowning in student 
debt, and is unable to afford a home in Auckland and unlikely to afford one any time 
soon, even if those people get a job and work hard. Wages are actually stagnating for at 
least half of the people in this country, and a quarter of all children are still living in 
poverty. So I would say National has really lost touch with everyday New Zealanders. It 
is choosing to build an economy that relies on increasing pollution in the extractio n of 
natural resources. It only really works for the New Zealanders who already have a lot. It 
works very well for them. They have got tax cuts and were able to buy shares in our 
State-owned energy companies. They are doing quite well. They are not paying any tax 
on the capital gains they have seen in Auckland over the last few years. 
3972 Budget Debate 26 May 2015 
 
There is an alternative to this. There is an alternative to just tinkering around the 
edges, which is what this Government has done. The Green Party has a costed plan to 
retool the economy to get a better, cleaner future that provides opportunity and 
prosperity for everyone. 
I want to speak specifically about two issues —firstly, environmental protection and 
the Resource Management Act, and, secondly, transport —because those are  two areas 
in particular where this Government is missing huge opportunities.  John Key admitted 
last week after the Budget that National cannot get support for its most radical proposed 
changes to the Resource Management Act. These are the changes to secti on 6 and 
section 7, which would fundamentally gut our world -leading environmental protection 
law. The reason it cannot get support for these changes is that they are very radical and 
cut to the heart of our national identity. I know New Zealanders love the ir natural 
environment. They are proud of it. They know there is huge value in protecting it —
immeasurable value. We set environmental bottom lines to protect the things that we 
value. If you really believe in the ingenuity of people, as I believe the Green  Party does, 
we know that people can adapt. Any economic activity must respect those bottom lines. 
As we know, the economy is a wholly -owned subsidiary of the natural environment, 
and once something is gone it is gone for good. When a developer in Auckland  
proposed to cut down a 500 -year-old kauri tree to build a house, 93 percent of New 
Zealanders agreed that the tree should be protected. That is where the rubber hits the 
road, because National’s changes to the Resource Management Act have already made 
it more difficult for communities to protect trees, to protect the places they love, and to 
have a say on the development that is happening. Changing the purpose and principles 
of the Act would fundamentally change the balance in a way that means no 
environmental bottom lines —communities cannot protect trees, they cannot protect the 
things they really care about. 
Giving up environmental protection does not make us richer. You only need to look 
at China to see where this trade -off has occurred. It has managed t o achieve huge GDP 
growth, but it has been at the cost of clean air, clean water, and healthy communities. I 
know that is not what New Zealanders want here. We do not need growth of an 
economy that is reliant on increasing pollution and the extraction of n on-renewable 
resources. That is just going to end up costing us in the long run. 
National has used the housing crisis in Auckland as a Trojan Horse for these reforms 
to the Resource Management Act. It is claiming that we cannot have affordable housing 
and protect our environment. I know that is not true. There is no evidence to support 
Nick Smith’s claims that planning rules are entirely responsible for the housing crisis. 
In fact, if you look at the research, you can see that pretty clearly. We have got re search 
here in New Zealand from 2014 -15 from the New Zealand Institute of Economic 
Research, Arthur Grimes, and Ian Mitchell. In this graph, we have got estimates of what 
the impact of planning rules has been on development in Auckland. If you believe the 
Government, which likes to listen to a pro - urban sprawl thinktank called 
Demographia, you would guess that the whole difference in the increase in house price 
costs is due to planning regulations, when the actual research in New Zealand shows 
that they h ave a much smaller impact. Maybe 20 to 30 percent of the price can be 
explained by planning regulations, but most of the cost is actually on apartments or 
medium-rise density—you know, the development not just of apartments but of town 
houses, character flats. 
These are all things that the Green Party has been saying for a long time we should 
be developing, because it is better for the environment and it means people can live 
where they want to live in compact, walkable neighbourhoods where they can access 
goods, services, and jobs through public transport or by walking and cycling.  That is 
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3973 
 
what people really want. Land values are highest on the isthmus, not out on the fringe, 
because people want to be on the isthmus. They want to be close to where things ar e. 
The reason they cannot afford it is that the planning rules do not allow that high-quality 
mid-rise intensification, which is what we have been arguing for and are quite happy to 
work on with the Government. 
Of course, that is just the supply side. I wo uld say that on the supply side the Greens 
have got it right. We have got a smart solution that not only reduces housing costs but 
reduces transport costs, reduces pollution, and enables people to live where they want to 
live. On the demand side it is clea r that the tax treatment of income has fuelled 
speculation in residential property. The Green Party has long called for smart measures 
like a capital gains tax, limiting the amount of capital coming in from overseas —
limiting the purchase of land and proper ty to citizens and residents here in New 
Zealand—and also having minimum standards for rental accommodation. All of that 
would help take the heat out of the housing market. And on the supply side we would 
welcome central government leadership, with a natio nal policy statement and 
environmental standards on good-quality mid -rise development  in the central city, 
because that is where the evidence says people want to be. 
The other side of the coin is, of course, transport. There is no point in building cheap 
houses on the fringe, where people just have to spend more on cars and transport to 
access education and jobs. A smart, green approach enables people to live closer to jobs 
and closer to public transport, but we need that investment in public transport 
infrastructure first. This is where National is really failing Auckland and future New 
Zealanders, because there is no money in this Budget for new public transport 
infrastructure in Auckland. In fact, since National came to power there has been no new 
money announced for rail projects in Auckland. All of it was committed under Labour, 
thanks to the pressure of the Green Party, 8 years ago.  If you look at the next 10 years, 
this chart shows what the National Party is planning to spend the transport budget on —
mostly on a bunch of motorways that have no business case when growth in rail in 
Auckland is at 20 percent a year and there has been no growth in vehicle kilometres 
travelled. So this is where the investment should go, because it is smart, it reduces 
pollution, it increases people’s quality of life, it reduces costs for Government, and it 
reduces costs for households. 
We can have this smart, green revolution here in New Zealand. We can have a fair 
society and we can respond to climate change, but we need a Government that is willing 
to actually take on the evidence and take us in a better direction. The Green Party would 
do that. Thank you.

Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Labour —New Lynn) : Imagine that t he member who 
has just resumed his seat, Jami-Lee Ross, was a plumber or a builder, and that you had a 
leaky roof and it took 7 long years for the plumber to come and fix it, and when he 
turned up he put a few tiles on and left a few holes so that the wate r kept leaking 
through. That is about as good as National’s attempt at solving the housing crisis. There 
is a much bigger problem in this Budget. This Budget is a Budget of broken promises. It 
3980 Budget Debate 26 May 2015 
 
is a Budget that has a deficit of ideas as well as financing. I n my remarks today, I am 
going to quickly run through the headline promises that have been broken. I am then 
going to say why this Budget does nothing for the portfolios that it is my privilege to 
represent: tertiary education, regional development, and innovation.  
The No. 1 broken promise in this Budget is the return to surplus. It was a centrepiece

starved pay rises for hard-working New Zealanders, and it is the reason that it has short-
changed research and innovation. It is the reason that it has done a whole lot of things to 
get back to surplus, but it did not get there. In the seven th innings —no home run. 
Labour—nine out of nine. I wonder how long it is going to take New Zealanders to ask 
the question: “If National is so good at managing the economy, why can’t it balance its 
cheque book? What is wrong with the National Government tha t it can’t balance its 
cheque book?”. If it took 7 years to get a plumber and they could not fix your roof, if it 
took 7 years to get an accountant and he could not balance your cheque book, do you 
know what you would do? You would get a different one. There may be a lesson in that.  
The second broken promise: Mr Key said that over the next 2 years the Government

short. He said he would raise the average wage from $55,000 to $62,000. It is $3,000

promises. It also said it would increase exports to 40 percent. Do you know what?

Government has surfed the upside of the recovery after the global financial crisis. That 
is the time that you put some money away, you run a surplus, and you pay back the 
deficit spending that we accept needed to be done when the economy was in a hole —
except the Governmen t did not, because it could not, because there was no surplus. 
National staked its credibility on that and now it has none —now it has none. There is a 
deficit of finance and a deficit of ideas.

going backwards. Unemployment is stubbornly high in places like Northland, the East 
Coast, the Manawatū, and the northern South Island. In a lot of our rural and provincial

house is worth not very much. It is called a poverty trap. The only way to address it is to 
get jobs and growth in the regions —in every region—so that New Zealanders can work 
their way to a better future. That is what Labour stands for. The clue is in the name: 
work. We work to a better, fairer future for all New Zealanders. We stand for giving 
hope and resources and a leg-up to every region.

percent, year on year. This shows up in the Government’s forecasts, in the external 
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3985 
 
deficit that we have as a country. I know that I have taken many barbs over the years 
from Bill English, saying that I rattle on too often about the external deficit. But the 
truth is that an economy is a bit like a household budget. If your economy is leaking 
money to the rest of the world, it is just like your own family budget leaking money to 
somebody else. If you do not earn enough money to pay your bills, then at the end of 
the year you either ha ve to sell something or take on debt. Our economy is exactly the 
same. As an economy we do not sell enough in our exports to pay for our imports plus 
our interest and the dividends that we pay overseas. The current account deficit this year 
is projected to  go to $13.7 billion. It is a huge amount of money. It is an extra $13.7

world and extra amounts that the rest of the world owns of us, because we sell more of 
ourselves to them in order to meet that deficit.  
It is against that background that you have to ask what it is that the Government has 
done, since it came to power 7 years ago, to change the shape of the economy. How do 
you judge it? Well, for a start you would  say that one of the ways you could reasonably 
judge it is by assessing its progress against the very targets it set itself. The National 
Government came to office saying that we consumed too much in New Zealand, we did 
not save enough, and we needed to in crease exports and savings. What has happened? 
Well, it is true that New Zealand in the last 7 years has saved a little bit more. The vast 
majority of that is insurance receipts that have come in following the insurance claims 
in Canterbury, following the Canterbury earthquakes, and also when New Zealanders 
put their cheque books away because they felt vulnerable in the recession. But it is also 
true that we are now verging on the point —if we have not already crossed over it —
where, as a nation, we are overa ll dissaving. We are overall dissaving at a household 
level.  
In addition to that, our exports, rather than going up from 30 percent of GDP to 40 
percent of GDP, which was the Government’s target, have raced backwards. I say

percent of GDP. That is a massive fail. What is causing it? Well, as Gareth Morgan 
says, in New Zealand we are a wealthy country but we misapply capital. We put our 
capital in the wrong parts of the e conomy. We do not save enough because we do not 
encourage enough savings, and then the capital that we do apply we apply to the wrong 
parts of the economy rather than to the more productive parts of the economy. There is 
no doubt that the biases we have that encourage that outcome remain.  
That leads me to KiwiSaver. KiwiSaver has had the incentives for it cut. In the last 
week, at great length, we went through the eight changes that have been made to 
KiwiSaver by this National Government, seven of which ar e cuts. I could not

almost seem like you are not going to give up much if you do not do it. So a lot of

Good Governments build countries; this Government does not. This Government

integrate and get on with their lives. It will make a huge difference for the lives of so 
many people.  
What about migrant workers in New Zealand? They are another marginalised group. 
How do they fare under this Budget? The Government annou nced a package of $33 
million for immigration, but that money is going to be spent on border control, not 
necessarily on seeing to the needs of migrant workers. Recent high -profile cases have 
shown that there is a need for better education and information for employers about 
minimum standards, but also for migrant workers so that they know their rights. 
Essentially, we also need strong compliance to ensure migrant workers are not 
exploited.  
I recognise that the Government has announced a funding increase for six new labour 
inspectors for Auckland. That is to be applauded. However, we lag behind international 
standards in terms of the ratio of workers to compliance officers. In New Zealand it is 
about one inspector for 14,162 workers. That is about double what happens in Australia. 
With the deregulated labour market that we have —and workers’ rights have, basically, 
been steadily eroded under this Government —it is essential that we have some kind of 
compliance for workers and particularly for vulnerable worker s, like migrant workers. 
Seasonal workers, for example, are also at risk of exploitation, and I note that we have 
got only five labour inspectors who are specialists in this area for the recognised 
seasonal workers’ scheme.  
This Budget is a case of Peter being robbed to pay Paul. There is a reduced allocation 
for WorkSafe New Zealand. There was a promised increase in health and safety 
inspectors when WorkSafe New Zealand was set up in 2012 —$37 million over 4 years. 
But this Budget says there will be a redu ction. And we still have not recovered the 
number of health and safety inspectors we had before 2012. We need that compliance to 
occur if we want people to come home safe and unharmed from their jobs. This Budget 
leaves a lot of people behind. It makes it harder for families to get ahead, and we 
certainly could be doing a lot better. 
Hon PAULA BENNETT (Associate Minister of Finance) : It is with absolute 
pleasure that I stand and actually get to put on record just how proud I am of this 
National-led Government’s Budget for 2015. It has been my first Budget as an 
Associate Minister of Finance, and so I have worked my way through it with  the 
guidance of Bill English, actually looking at what needed to be done and where we 
could address the needs of this country.  
It is easy to forget, actually, that we have an average growth rate of 2.8 percent, and 
that we are projecting 150,000 more jobs to come on board. I remember the calls when 
we were saying that there would be 170,000 more jobs, and it would be fair to say t hat 
we were derided by the left. They took every opportunity that they could to throw that 
back at us. Well, here we are, saying: “No, no, we did not do 170,000. Actually, the 
economy has produced 194,000 more jobs, which have been created since 2011.” And  
that makes a fundamental difference for New Zealanders —that, and seeing the average 
wage increase; that, and seeing, actually, people able to have more money in their 
pockets and able to get the jobs that, quite frankly, they do deserve in this country; t hat, 
and seeing us project that unemployment will continue to drop and employment will 
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3991 
 
continue to rise. You can see from the projections in this Budget that we are heading, 
well and truly, to that 4.5 percent unemployment rate.  
But what is different, wha t is fundamentally different, in how we look at that 
unemployment rate is that we are actually not putting all of that sort of slightly 
discretionary funding, where we assist people with CVs and skills and training, and help 
them to get work -ready, on to j ust those who are on the unemployment benefit. What 
you can see is that over the last 6½ years we have moved resources to those who 
fundamentally need them the most. And, yes, we reset obligations, as we did a bit more 
of in this Budget.  
But I want to tak e people back to when we first came into Government in 2008. I 
was the then Minister for Social Development and Employment, and I will never ever 
forget sitting in a room in Paris with my colleagues, with welfare and employment 
Ministers from around the wo rld, and they fundamentally could not believe —in fact I 
had to repeat it about four times —that we had absolutely no work obligations for 
someone who was on welfare, until their youngest turned 18, and who could then have 
another baby and get another 18 yea rs of no work obligations. They fundamentally 
could not believe that we did not have balance in what we expected of people.  
As a consequence, it was actually worse than that. We did not put any resource or 
extra into helping them get work-ready. So we did—we reset. We reset the balance. We 
made sure that those people had hope and opportunities. We reset the balance that had 
never been there in the welfare system, so that they could actually create a better life for 
themselves and their children. As a conse quence of that and many changes, we now 
have the lowest number of sole parents on welfare since the 1980s—1988 I think it is.  
But what people forget is that we could not have actually made the changes to 
welfare and given those families who still are ther e an extra $25 a week on average —
we could not do that if we had not reset the balance, if we had not actually got some 
mutual obligations within the system in those previous years. It is not just the work of 
the last 12 months that leads us to a place wher e we can produce a Budget that is giving 
back to those who most certainly are having it tough and living hard lives on very 
limited incomes, where we can put more in their pockets that goes to helping them and 
their children. The way that we are able to do  that is over many years of resetting our 
social policy to make sure that we are helping those who need it most, and making sure 
that they actually recognise what changes need to be made.  
I have heard many from the opposite side say that this does not mak e a difference. 
Well, it makes a huge difference. Actually, $25 makes an absolutely huge difference. 
Also, though, we really wanted to make sure, as we worked our way through this 
package—and we have spent a lot of hours and a lot of time debating and look ing at it 
from every angle—that we were also increasing Working for Families and making sure 
that those who did go into jobs and were still on low wages were able to reap those 
rewards as well. We are making sure that we have the obligations right, that pe ople are 
able to get into work, that they get the extra assistance through agencies like the 
Ministry of Social Development, through education and other skills and training —but 
then, equally, for those who do go into jobs, making sure that they get assista nce on that 
extra pay, so that we are keeping that balance right, that work really does pay. From 
everything that you look at, it is work that makes the biggest and most fundamental 
difference in people’s lives. When we could, we have. At the first chance that we have 
had to increase benefits for the first time in nearly —what is it —43 years, we took that 
opportunity to put money in the pockets of those who need it most.  
If I am to be a little negative, which is not really my thing, I would have said that t he 
Opposition was expecting us, if we were going to do anything, to do sort of nine or 10 
bucks. Yeah? And we all then would have gone around thinking we had done a good 
3992 Budget Debate 26 May 2015 
 
thing. We knew that we could, and it was absolutely important —as we worked our way 
through what was actually quite a tough Budget process of trying to make sure that we 
are actually looking after the needs of those who work for our agencies and are 
expecting a wee pay rise, for those who have got cost pressures there —that we set real 
money aside to go to real people who needed that help and assistance. That says, I think, 
a lot for this Government, and a lot for the leadership, quite frankly, of our Prime 
Minister. When he stood up  on election night, ladies and gentlemen, and said, having 
accepted the win: “This National -led Government will govern for all people.”, here is 
the evidence of it. It is in black and white. It is in this Budget that he stands by what he 
said, and he stands there and says: “I will govern; we will govern. This Nation al-led 
Government will be there for all people.” When he could give back, under his 
leadership and under this hardship package, that is what he delivered to New 
Zealanders.  
I also want to just touch on another part of that hardship package that has not be en 
touched on much, I do not think, from what I have heard so far, which is the increase in 
the childcare subsidy. What perhaps some of us knew instinctively was that if you 
removed barriers and believed in and backed these women and children, then they 
would take every opportunity to make a difference in their lives and in the lives of their 
children. They have proven that by the tens of thousands who have gone off welfare 
when we have actually rebalanced.  
What they also need, though, as I indicated, is t hose barriers removed. One of the 
biggest barriers is the cost of childcare. So for those who are looking for extra 
assistance, we have put the subsidy up from $4 to $5, which is a 20 percent increase in 
what we will actually pay to help them while they ar e working, so that they can get that 
extra assistance.  
The other thing that I do not think people have realised so much —and it is not 
necessarily in this Budget —is that about a year ago we also really relaxed the rules on 
what we will pay for as far as ch ildcare is concerned. Too often it was just about the 
creche down the road or the day care centre, although for many parents they are 
working different hours and they want more flexibility with that. That is part of how we 
are actually getting there and how we are rebalancing it.  
You could hold this Budget up in the world —and I do not say that lightly —and 
know that you are extremely proud of it and that New Zealand is more than punching 
above its weight, as it does so well. As a country we actually have th e economy well 
and truly on track and are delivering to all New Zealanders as we see the average wage 
increase, as we see those on welfare being assisted with a bit more money, as we see 
more jobs coming on board, the support for the regions, and also the support for our 
businesses that is recognised daily through a Budget that is delivered like this. 
I am incredibly proud to be a part of a team —and it is a pretty big team, and it is a 
pretty great one —that cares a lot about this stuff and that has spent th e time on really 
using the data analytics, using the information that we have, and making sure we pull 
that together in the best interests of all New Zealanders. I am really proud to stand up 
and support what, as I say, is a really strong team that is, act ually, backing a really 
strong, growing economy. Thank you. 
CLARE CURRAN (Labour —Dunedin South): Talofa lava. I will say something 
for the Government members, and that is that they are goo d at the spin. They are good 
at the political spin and they are good at telling you that everything is great when, 
behind the scenes, it is another story. I listened to the previous speaker —the new 
Associate Minister of Finance, Paula Bennett —talk about fu ndamentally moving 
resources to where they are needed most. Well, how does that fit with what the 
Government is doing to social housing —fundamentally dismantling the social housing 
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3993 
 
scheme and the role of the State in providing housing for the most vulnerab le in our 
society? Not one more house is coming out of its grand new plan, which is not a new 
plan. 
I would also like to say something to a previous National speaker, new MP Barbara 
Kuriger, who spoke about the importance of fast broadband in rural New Zea land, 
which is so important. It is so important that there is the right investment and that the 
investment goes where it is needed. I am sure she, as an MP in rural New Zealand and 
Taranaki, would know—in fact, I know that she does know because I know that  she has 
many people coming through her door complaining about their broadband —that, 
unfortunately, the Government has already spent $300 million in rural New Zealand, 
and it is still not working. That is a real problem, which is why Labour fought against 
that piece of legislation pushed through under urgency on Friday night.  
My colleague Grant Robertson described this as a politician’s Budget. It has also 
been described as many things, but one of them is a Budget of broken promises around 
the surplus, around wage and job targets, and, of course, around those three new taxes. 
“No new taxes.” said the Prime Minister. “No new taxes.” said the campaign literature 
before the election. But what have we got? We have got three new taxes. The economist 
Rod Oram put it really well when he said in the Sunday Star-Times this weekend: “this 
Budget, as the six before it, is a triumph of micro -management. The Government has 
mastered the art of switching small sums [of money] around to give the illusion of 
progress.” Well, how true that is. How true that is. This is the “sticking plaster Budget” 
and the “piecemeal Budget”, with no vision, no plan, and no real hope. 
Chris Bishop: 25 bucks a week is not a small sum of money. 
CLARE CURRAN : Yes, I absolutely acknowledge that $25 a week is going to 
make a small difference, but you tell me —excuse me, Mr Deputy Speaker, not you —
but can the Government tell me how that is going to address the fundamental causes of 
child poverty. Well, it is just not. If you live in regional New Zealand you could be 
forgiven for barely registering this Budget.  
Once upon a time —as I am sure you would remember, Mr Deputy Speaker, and as 
many of the people in the House would recall —the Budget was a must -listen-to yearly 
event. There were big structural changes. There were wide -ranging visions. It was an 
opportunity for Governments of the day to show their core thinking and direction. This 
Budget has no structural shifts in it. There is no accounting for the ageing population.  
There is no recognition of the rapid technological change and its impact on jobs. There 
is no money for innovation. There is no money for regional development. There is no 
money for the productive economy and for exports. There is no investment in those 
things. Instead, we have had KiwiSaver’s kick -start snatched away —the savings of 
future generations.  
This is a Budget of broken promises. We have seen, firstly, the taxing of capital 
gains—not a capital gains tax but the taxing of capital gains for propert y investors has 
expanded—secondly, an airport tax charging people to enter or leave New Zealand; and, 
thirdly, a broadband tax that increases the charge on the telecommunications industry, 
which has already resulted in an increase of broadband prices. We h ave got a Minister 
for Communications, Amy Adams, who does not talk to the industry, to the consumers, 
or to consumer representatives. She does not listen. She insists that black is white. In 
fact, she stood in this House on Friday night and insisted that a levy is not a tax.  
I just want to show everybody Colin James’ piece in the Otago Daily Times  this 
morning and the headline “We know a levy’s a tax, Mr English”. I think the 
Government has lost on that one. It rammed through a special law under urgency to give 
the Government power to levy or tax the telecommunications industry to implement 
part two of a scheme for rural broadband, which was $150 million. So why did we fight 
3994 Budget Debate 26 May 2015 
 
it? We support better broadband, absolutely, for rural New Zealand. It was us who 
provided the strong policy leading into the election for community -based rural 
broadband to try to address the real issues that were happening in rural New Zealand, 
but $300 million has already been spent in rural New Zealand, and that has not been a 
great success. How do we know this? We know this because rural New Zealand keeps 
telling us, whether there are petitions from communities, whether they have come to 
select committees in Parliament, as three of them did last week, or whether it is 
organisations like Rural Women, which come and talk to us about the state of rural 
broadband. We know that Federated Farmers are worried. We even know that 68 
percent of businesses and households are extremely frustrated in rural New Zealand, 
because there was a piece o f market research by Colmar Brunton for Chorus done just 
before the election. But there has been no analysis—no reports. The only figures that we 
have show a few thousand connections, there have been towers upgraded and new ones 
built, and the copper network has been improved, but this is infrastructure that is owned 
by private companies, which are benefiting from it.  
Is it benefiting rural New Zealand? Where is the analysis? Where are the reports? I 
note that members have all got their heads down over the re because they know there are 
not any. So what does the Minister say? Well, she says: “It’s my way or the highway.”, 
she says to everybody. She says that it is a levy; it is not a tax. She said the 
telecommunications companies would not pass it on. Well, within an hour of the debate 
starting in Parliament last week, one of the telecommunications companies had already 
announced it was passing it on because it was a tax. Whether that is a good thing or not 
is to one side, but the fact is that that is what is  happening and it is a tax on consumers. 
She, of course, said that that would not happen, and it did.  
Is a levy a tax? No, it is a user charge, says the Minister. Is a tax on alcohol a user 
charge? Is a tax on cigarettes a user charge? Is a tax on petrol a user charge? Well, the 
Minister has certainly lost the argument on that one. The $150 million —there is no 
guarantee it will work. There is no guarantee that that money will not be used to finish 
off the first version of rural broadband. There is no guara ntee that smaller community 
providers will get a look in. It needs an inquiry, it needs examination, it needs sunlight, 
and it shows poor economic management, poor judgment, and a fundamental lack of 
understanding and good project management.  
Finishing up, Chorus came out today pleading with the Government to move fast on 
Resource Management Act reforms in order to free up the roadblocks in the ultra -fast 
broadband project.  
Todd Barclay: Well, why don’t you support the RMA reform? 
CLARE CURRAN: Well, we have always said we would consider sensible changes 
to the Resource Management Act. We had some in our environment policy. We had a 
policy on telecommunications companies that said we would fix these things as soon as 
possible. It has been 8 months since the election. There has been no movement on this. 
We say to the Minister for the Environment: “Put those changes on the table, Nick 
Smith. Let us see them. Where are they?”. And good on Chorus for putting the pressure 
on, on that issue. 
DARROCH BALL (NZ First) : It is a pleasure to rise on behalf of New Zealand 
First to make some comments on the Budget. I will be concentrating my comments on 
the changes to the social services  area. The first thing I would like to do is to ask a 
question. That question is about the Budget: has the Government addressed the very 
worst levels of child poverty in New Zealand with its Budget announcement last 
Thursday? The answer is, unsurprisingly,  a definitive no. After persistently ignoring 40 
years of research on a topic, with expert advisory group recommendations largely 
ignored, why all of a sudden a U -turn? The Government has been in power for 7 years, 
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3995 
 
and for 7 years it has denied it, denied the scale of the problem. We have the Prime 
Minister, who usually shrugs most things off, including the problem of child poverty. 
But worst of all is that in those 7 years the Government has failed to address it. So why 
the U-turn? Probably because of the public pressure and post -election promises in the 
face of widespread public protestation.  
We are already witnessing the Government reverting to its ideological blind spot on 
child poverty. On Thursday we had a Budget preaching about the focus on child poverty 
and the needy, and just 2 days ago we had Mr English commenting about the anti -
poverty figures. The article in the New Zealand Herald has the title: “English hits back 
at anti-poverty figures”. It goes on to say that “P rofessor Jonathan Boston refuted the 
minister’s claims, saying Mr English ‘ doesn’t understand how poverty measures are 
calculated’.” Mr English’s response to that, in an interview on Q+A, is that 
“campaigners like Prof Boston and the Children’ s Commissioner used an unrealistic set 
of measures to quantify poverty in New Zealand .” The funny thing is that during Mr 
English’s Budget speech he said this: “Two -thirds of children in more severe material 
hardship have a parent on a benefit, and nine out of 10 of those are sole parents”.  
Where did he get that measure of severe hardship from? In order to get to this 
conclusion, he would have to be using the very calculation of poverty used by Professor 
Jonathan Boston, the same man he criticised on national TV for the way in which he 
calculated it. So I challenge the Minister to prove where he got those figures from and 
by which method. He cannot continue to contradict himself and say that Professor 
Boston has an unrealistic set of measures, and yet use those exact same measures in his 
speech. That is a blatant attempt to diminish expert opinion. The public can now quite 
clearly see that the Minister of Finance has no idea about how poverty measures are 
calculated. It is a poor start to the Government’s acknowledgment of the problem —far 
less than a step in the right direction.  
We know that the measures the Government announced on Thursday  will not lift 
those children out of poverty. The Children’s Commissioner, someone else whom the 
Government does not listen to, himself said that it will not bring families out of poverty, 
and he is calling for a comprehensive plan. So all pre -Budget, all at the end of last year, 
there was this promise from the Government, from the Minister for Social 
Development, and from the Minister of Finance about a comprehensive plan to tackle 
child poverty and vulnerable children. What we got was not even a skeleton of a plan. 
They have not even done the map recce yet.  
So where is the package? Where is the plan? The measures announced in the Budget 
are piecemeal and they are disappointing. Put quite simply, this Government is 
continuing to fund supported poverty. Bei ng a step in the right direction is not enough 
to warrant a vote of confidence for, or indeed acceptance of, this Budget. One can never 
win a game of cards if they are given only one single card to play with. How are these 
people in poverty with vulnerable  children expected to get out of their way of poverty, 
to work their way out of poverty, to fight their way out of poverty with just $25 a week? 
The Government has given them that one card to play with. These moves are a token 
effort to appease the general  concern of the New Zealand public at the plight of an 
unacceptable number of our children. We want to hold on to the country we once 
proudly advocated for, when we travelled around the globe proud of a land of equal 
opportunity, but now we are reminded by  the National Government that times have 
changed and that we need to focus on quite a long -term savings for the Crown—on cost 
cutting, on more efficiency, and on better investment.  
How did child poverty end up being about what these children will cost us in the 
future? Why is it not about the New Zealand vision that every one of these children 
should have an equal opportunity to contribute to our society? New Zealand First 
3996 Budget Debate 26 May 2015 
 
believes in the fundamentals of a social welfare system that provides a robust safet y net. 
No one should fall below this most minimum of levels —no family and no child. It 
should not be a reward; nor should it be a punishment. It should not be a matter of 
approval for a Budget change; it should be an automatic expectation. Anything less 
would mean we are all leaving our principles behind for the sake of financial 
convenience and outright judgment.  
The Government’s investment approach stretches it further. Now each person who 
requires a social service has a dollar sign floating above their head. If their need does 
not fit within the criteria of the Government’s targets, then the dollar is extinguished 
and the individual is left to fend for themselves. If a social agency tries to look after all 
of its clients’ needs, it will run adrift. If a service attempts to exist in the regions where 
the client numbers are low, it will struggle, falter, and disappear. So if you are a young 
person looking for support in a small provincial town, tough. Your need is not 
financially sustainable. Where in this do we allow for a community to identify its own 
needs and provide a response? Will a coupon system for social services mean less 
supply and lower quality, just as it did with the voucher system for childcare that was 
evaluated in Sweden and Australia?  
We have seen social services retracting. Most recently, we have seen the struggles of 
our biggest counselling agency, Relationships Aotearoa, and the release today of an 
article “Government forces closure of Relationships Aotearoa”. It goes on to say: 
“Unfortunately, our financial position worsened by Government’s needless delay means 
we cannot afford to transition clients. We had hoped to transition clients  [more]. …  
Government could have easily reached an agreement with us that was equitable for all 
concerned. It is fair to say that we feel betrayed  … it is likely that our doors will be 
closed to our 7000 current clients by the end of the week .” But this Government would 
rather spend around $30 million on a flag referendum. Where is the priority shown by 
this Government?  
Two months ago we met with the Salvation Army youth education and employment 
unit. It has just shut down branches in Kaikohe, Matamata, Wairoa, Waipukurau, and 
Blenheim. The common theme in all of those is they are all regional. Why did they shut 
down? They were not financially viable. One would have to ask where this will end. 
Where is the plan by this Government to ensure that the essential safety net that is 
faltering, in our provinces  especially, remains intact and maintains its integrity? This 
Budget surely did not deliver confidence in that.  
New Zealand First wants more than just a $2 a day down payment for the 250,000 
children living in poverty. We want front -end investment focused on our youth. Simply 
increasing the benefit is lazy. It lacks focus and it lacks realism of the understanding of 
the real issue. Instead, it tries to plug a gap over the symptoms. The Government has 
ignored our young people in this Budget. The Government m ay not care, but the vast 
majority of New Zealand cares about the future generations. As Mark Powell, chief 
executive officer of The Warehouse, said this weekend: “A flourishing society equals 
flourishing business.”  
May I lastly say this: if we are to mai ntain that minimum social floor that no one 
should fall through, we need a heavy focus on our youth. Unemployed youth become 
unemployed adults who remain on a benefit and bring children and families into 
poverty. Acting too late with too little should never be acceptable.  
KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI (National) : Talofa lava, Mr Assistant Speaker. It 
was great to see you come into the House and greet us with a Samoan greeting. This 
week we are celebrating Samoan Language Week. In New Zealand —the most diverse 
country in the world —it is very important that we acknowledge the cultures that we 
have adopted. The Samoan language is the third most spoken language in New Zealand, 
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 3997 
 
and I appreciate those who are still continuing to speak their language and are 
continuing with their culture. Today we also celebrate Africa Day in Parliament. It 
shows another example of diversity in our country, and we are lucky to have people 
from different ethnicities representing us in various areas. 
It is my pleasure to participate in this debate on the Budget. As we know, the 
appropriation bills are the basis on which Parliament authorises the executive to incur 
expenses and capital expenditure. Each year, the Minis ter of Finance places in front of 
this House the Budget, which provides appropriations for the coming year. I would like 
to congratulate the Hon Bill English on presenting an excellent seventh Budget, and I 
am proud to be part of this team. For the past 7 years, thanks to the strong leadership 
provided by the Prime Minister and our finance Minister, this National -led Government 
has provided prudent Budgets that have proven instrumental in the New Zealand 
economy’s excellent growth. 
I was talking to my frien ds based in Melbourne, and they were full of praise for our 
Government for presenting an excellent Budget; so much so that one of my friends said 
that he would like to move to New Zealand to live because it is a better place to live —
and that has been prove n in the last 7 years. There was a time when 50,000 Kiwis were 
migrating to Australia each year, but the trends are changing. Now Australians are 
moving to New Zealand. 
A survey conducted by Statistics New Zealand and published today indicates that 
New Zealanders are highly satisfied with their lives, with people rating their sense of 
purpose highly. The New Zealand General Social Survey conducted by Statistics New 
Zealand, which provided the above result, was based on a survey of 9,000 people. The 
General Social Survey is the biggest social survey conducted by Statistics New Zealand 
outside the 5 -yearly Census of Population and Dwellings. This independent survey by 
the country’s most credible organisation proves what we in the National Party and the 
Government have been sharing with this House and New Zealanders for some time. The 
leadership of New Zealand has done an outstanding job in steering this country forward 
in the difficult times. Here I would like to congratulate the Hon Paula Bennett, who did 
a lot of work in social welfare, which has been appreciated worldwide and is now being 
continued by the Hon Anne Tolley. 
In this Budget, the honourable Minister of Finance has once again provided excellent 
vision for New Zealanders. The Budget makes excellent allowances for issues that 
matter to New Zealanders. The Minister of Finance has announced that this National-led 
Government will deliver a $790 million package to support children who live in poor 
families. This amount will be balanced between sole parent s and the provision of $25 
per week more for families that may be on some form of income support. The 
Government has also announced in the Budget that we will increase the Working for 
Families payment. There is also an increased focus from our side of the House on 
providing more childcare support for low-income families to help parents to be in work, 
education, or training. Budget 2015 makes allowances for a further $60 million in extra 
support for at-risk children. We know from experience that the best way to help families 
and children out of hardship is through employment. Keeping this in mind, we are 
allocating $32.5 million for services that help beneficiaries to move into the workforce. 
I would like to reiterate that we are allocating $32.5 million to h elp beneficiaries to 
move into the work force. These initiatives confirm that this National -led Government 
focuses on building a stronger economy, and that delivering Better Public Services is 
working for New Zealand families. 
In addition to taking steps t o improve the economy, we have said from the very start 
that this National -led Government has zero tolerance for corruption, and we remain 
committed to maintaining New Zealand’s robust reputation. That is why this Budget has 
3998 Budget Debate 26 May 2015 
 
allocated $218 million to the j ustice sector. The Budget provides an extra $8.1 million 
over the next 4 years for the operating fund of the Serious Fraud Office. This further 
enables the Serious Fraud Office to fight bribery and corruption and to create a business 
environment that is fr ee of serious financial crime. The Department of Corrections will 
receive more than $6 million from the justice sector. Also, the new operating fund of 
$164 million over the next 4 years for the New Zealand Police shows that the 
Government is investing mor e and more in creating communities that are away from 
crime-related activities. There has been a 22 percent drop in recorded crime over the 
past 5 years, and we have been successful in disrupting organised crime. We have over 
600 extra police officers on t he front line. They are helping to safeguard vulnerable 
communities. 
I take this opportunity to thank the New Zealand Police for making New Zealanders 
feel secure, while at the same time developing constructive relationships with the people 
who belong to different cultural backgrounds. The New Zealand Police has been able to 
successfully identify issues of victimisation within ethnic communities and to develop 
culturally appropriate strategies that are implemented in order to increase the 
community’s safety. This funding will support the police in providing more effective 
policing and will help in preventing crime, to a huge extent. 
There are some positive points of our economy that I would like to share here. New

STUART NASH (Labour —Napier): We heard a lot of statistics there but it

seventh Budget of this National -led Government that Bill English as our Minister of 
Finance has led us through. I am very proud that this is a Budget that consolidates the 
clear approach that we have brought to the Go vernment benches since 2008, and that is

Zealanders who need those services.

targeting where we put money and where we do not. We did not do it, as I said, by
