infrastructure. In our view, you targ et it to those who will get the benefit from the 
spend. You use the money that you create, the surplus spend that you create in the 
Government finances, and put it where it will do the most good.  
In this Budget that is about reaching out to those children  who are living in some of 
our poorest families, supporting them, but also with that, sending the message that the 
best path out of hardship and out of poverty is work. The best thing, bar none, that we 
can do for those families who are really struggling i s to get them into a job. There are 
many parts to that, of course. It means making sure they have the educational standards 
they need, making sure national standards and our National Certificate of Educational 
Achievement targets are supporting them to hav e that education, making sure our 
tertiary system is set up to provide pathways and jobs and skill sets that will help them 
into those jobs, making sure that their health is strong enough to support them working, 
making sure there is drug and alcohol couns elling in our prisons, and making sure our 
mental health services are strong. 
Tim Macindoe: Appropriate childcare, where it is needed. 
Hon AMY ADAMS : That is exactly right. If they need support with childcare, 
putting those s ubsidies up —making them available. All of the parts of this Budget 
facilitate that approach. The other side of that equation is making sure there are 
opportunities for them —creating jobs in the regions, creating jobs in areas that need 
them. This is a Gove rnment that has already seen the development of hundreds of 
thousands of new jobs in our term in office. Budget 2015 shows that Treasury 
modelling is that more new jobs will be created as a result of these settings.  
We are ensuring people are supported to  get back to work, that they have the 
opportunity to work, and that they have the skill set and the support in childcare to do 
that job. That is the path out of hardship. There is no two ways about it. Although we 
want to support those at the lowest ebb, i t cannot be into a pattern of dependency. We 
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4007 
 
are not helping anyone if the pattern is one of dependency and teaching them to rely on 
the State. Self-reliance, self-responsibility, working for a living is the best thing that any 
family can do for their fort unes and for their children. This is a Government that will 
support them. 
I just want to highlight a couple of the ways the Budget has helped areas like the one 
that I represent because I think that often, when we look at the big packages and the 
national approach, we lose some of the detail of the very real things that this Budget 
will do in parts of rural and provincial New Zealand, like the electorate of Selwyn. I 
have to comment on the $100 million set aside in this Budget to rebuild the science 
facilities at Lincoln University, which, obviously, were significantly damaged during 
the Canterbury earthquakes of 2010 and 2011.  
This is the Budget and this is the Government that have set aside $100 million from 
the proceeds of the mixed -ownership model to ma ke sure that Lincoln University gets 
back on its feet, and I welcome it. As part of the $200 million - plus spending on new 
school facilities, I am very proud that Rolleston in my electorate is already having its 
third primary school built, an integrated C hristian school opened, another new primary 
school in planning, and a high school on its way. This is the Government that is making 
that funding happen.  
I was also delighted to see the announcement in the Budget around the regional 
research centre, recogn ising that some of the best innovation in this country is not 
happening in the cities; it is happening in regional and rural New Zealand. Funding that 
sort of regional research centre will do two things. One, it will create jobs and activity 
in the regions. And, two, it will show that the Government recognises that some of the 
most innovative parts of New Zealand are in the regions, and that we respect and want 
to support that, and this is a Budget that certainly does that.  
Finally, let me end my contribut ion talking about the funding in the Budget for the 
extension of the Ultra -fast Broadband Initiative and the regional broadband initiative. 
This is a Budget that puts $360 million more into our investment, making a total 
Government investment of over $2 bi llion. This is the Government that will deliver 
high-speed, high -quality broadband to as many New Zealanders as we possibly can, 
because that is the foundation for all of the services that we need in the future —social, 
cultural, economic, and Government se rvices. It is the digital highway that will really 
enable our small towns and our communities to flourish.  
The extension of the Ultra -fast Broadband Initiative will see another 200,000 New 
Zealanders access absolutely world -leading connectivity infrastruc ture. I am incredibly 
excited by that. We are going to see some of the smallest towns in New Zealand get 
switched on and opened up in a way that we will not have seen since the railways were 
first rolled out, since we took electricity into some of the comm unities. That is exciting. 
I am excited by that. I am proud of it. There is a reason that New Zealand is held up 
internationally, in terms of the success of our broadband programme. Around the world 
you have got companies like Alcatel -Lucent saying New Zea land is a country that has 
got this right, and that this is a model for the rest of the world and this is the 
Government that enabled it. I am very proud to commend the Budget to the House. 
JENNY SALESA (Labour —Manukau East) : Malo soifua, talofa lava. The 
National Government has repeatedly stated that it is improving the economy. The 
Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister claim that Budget 2015 delivers to those 
who are in hardshi p, but the people of Manukau East, along with many other ordinary, 
hard-working Kiwis, are falling further behind. Their ability to live with dignity, to 
support their families well, and to see their children flourish is being affected negatively 
by this Government’s failure to deliver on its promises.  
4008 Budget Debate 26 May 2015 
 
The curtain has dramatically been drawn back and this Government’s Budget reveals 
only that there is hardly anything there for ordinary, hard -working Kiwi families. For 
hard-working families the cupboard is bare. The Budget surplus that was promised by 
this Government is not there. The promise of a 150,000 increase in the number of jobs 
and higher wages has not been reached. The promise of no new taxes has been broken—
we now have three sneaky new taxes. The p romise of more affordable houses has been 
broken, and hard -working New Zealanders are losing their KiwiSaver kick -start 
incentive to save for their future. This has been a Budget of broken promises, and there 
is not even anything in this Budget for the high and ever-increasing rents for families.  
Aotearoa New Zealand’s poor, vulnerable children do not choose the parents whom 
they have. They do not choose their country or the neighbourhood they are born into, 
and they do not choose their race or their relig ion. In fact, if they had been born into 
another OECD country, they would probably be less likely to be born into poverty. 
Having so many thousands of children —over 250,000 kids —grow up in poverty is 
really expensive for all of us as taxpayers. Child pover ty is really expensive in the long 
run for us all, and it is an issue we should address in a comprehensive and planned way. 
The lost productivity, extra health costs, and law and order costs —to name but a few —
add up to millions and millions of dollars per year. For far too long, the Government has 
allowed the level of child poverty to remain really high. The reason, or justification, if 
any is given at all, is often that action to address child poverty is too expensive. But 
inaction, as done by Budget 2015 —with a few tweaks here and there and a fiddle at the 
margins—completely misses the other side of the equation, which is the fact that the 
cost to all of us in society is much too expensive. Inaction and a lack of comprehensive 
action to address child poverty has its costs.  
Good things, better outcomes in life, are worth paying for. I believe that having food, 
shelter—a house —and investment in early childhood education in order to get kids 
ready for school and education in an equitable and fair way are thin gs that all children 
should have. This is something that should be of a higher priority, instead of corporate 
welfare and tax breaks. Why is it that National can afford tax breaks of over $3 billion 
since it has been in Government thus far, and it is alrea dy promising tax cuts for 2017, 
even though it cannot even balance the books right now? Why is it that the Government 
is wasting $26 million on a flag referendum that most New Zealanders say is a waste of 
money, and yet, in the same breath, it is saying th at we cannot afford to make sure that 
every child is fed and every child is housed, or to invest in a comprehensive way in our 
children, who are the future of our country?  
A key driver of child poverty is the public policies that we have. We will know whe n 
the Government is actually addressing child poverty, because, when it does, we will 
actually see that it will apply principles of inclusivity and it will have principles of non -
discrimination, which will help protect our children from poverty as equally well as 
they protect our elders from poverty. Child poverty matters to the Labour Party. Child 
poverty matters to me, as a mother, and it matters to my electorate and to the rest of 
New Zealand. Our children deserve to be treated fairly and they deserve to  be given 
equal opportunities.  
A responsible Government would be a Government that actually has a plan —a plan 
to competently address the long -term challenges that New Zealand faces, a plan to lay 
the foundations for a sustainable and healthy future, and a  plan that would grow 
incomes and invest in a productive and diverse economy. This Budget has been long on 
promises and short on solutions. It is a Budget that contains nothing significant for 
diversifying the economy or for supporting our manufacturers an d our exporters, or for 
developing the skills that our workers will need in the new economy. Growth has now 
passed its peak and it is expected to halve by 2019, and not reaching surplus at the peak 
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4009 
 
of the economic cycle is a huge failure by this Government . It makes a mockery of 
National members’ claim that they are good economic managers.  
Our Prime Minister, John Key, in his open letter to New Zealanders after the 
election, promised: “Over the next two years we expect to see about 150,000 jobs 
created.” The National Government will fall short on this promise by 60,000 jobs, and it 
has pushed the date of delivery back a few more years —yet another broken promise. 
Also in John Key’s open letter to New Zealanders after the election, he promised: “Over 
the next three years we expect the average wage to move from $55,000 to $62,000 …”. 
The Budget shows that the Government will fall short by $3,000 on its wages promise. 
In fact, we are unlikely to even get to the promised wage level until 2019 —in another 4 
years.  
Manukau East in South Auckland, which is the wonderful electorate that I represent, 
is a young electorate. The median age in Manukau East is 29 years. The national median 
age is 37 years, and one-third of the people living in Manukau East are under the ag e of 
20. Many are on low and limited incomes. In order to get ahead and to contribute to the 
future of New Zealand, they need properly funded education, correctly targeted skills 
training, jobs to go to that pay decent wages, and the ability to save for the future.  
New Zealand used to be the land that led the world, with the lowest unemployment 
rates in the OECD. This was under Helen Clark and the last Labour -led Government. 
Today we rank 13 th, and the general situation in my electorate is compounded by it 
having one the highest unemployment rates in the country. This Budget will not fix that. 
The Government is failing to act on jobs and wages for ordinary everyday New 
Zealanders.  
We have heard  the other side trumpeting the fact that for people on a benefit who 
have children, receiving $25 extra a week will make a huge difference. Well, it will 
make some difference, but I would not call it a huge difference. Although an increase in 
benefit levels for those with children is good news, those who are working with children 
and families and who have Working for Families will receive only $12 per week. This 
makes working families relatively worse off than when this Budget was announced. For 
families, t he Government will claw back this $25 through reduced accommodation 
supplements. The Budget offers no firm pathway out of poverty, and the $25 a week 
cannot—it cannot—fix 7 years of neglect and the mismanagement of our economy.  
Cutting the $1,000 KiwiSave r kick-start initiative demonstrates the absolutely short -
term thinking that is typical of this National Government and this Budget. This cut will 
detrimentally penalise our young people, who are going to be less able to get ahead and 
to save for their fut ure. In 2011 the Prime Minister promised to retain the $1,000 kick -
start for new KiwiSaver members as it was at the time. The Government has now cut it 
entirely—yet another broken promise. Now around 500,000 people, mainly young 
people and children, will miss out as a result of this cut.  
This Government is wandering aimlessly, with absolutely no long -term plans for our 
economic future. It has failed to deliver a Budget surplus for 7 years now. We pay 
millions per day in interest because the Government cann ot get the books into balance 
or deliver a Budget surplus, and it is continuing to fail to meet the needs of New 
Zealand families. The Government’s latest Budget might be clever in a political sense as 
it has robbed Peter to pay Paul, but having a collecti on of short -term jabs and a few 
high-profile targets does not a comprehensive strategy for the future make. Thank you. 
Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Comm erce and Consumer Affairs): This 
Budget shows what New Zealand can do after 7 years of a strong, stable Government 
led by John Key, Bill English, and this National Government. We see great growth in 
this economy—nearly 3 percent is projected for the next 4  years, which is one of the 
fastest levels of growth in the OECD. We have seen a jobs boom in New Zealand, with 
4010 Budget Debate 26 May 2015 
 
194,000 jobs created in this economy since 2011. That impacts countless thousands of 
lives of families across this nation who have had access to  work and the dignity of 
work. We expect another 150,000 jobs to be created in this economy over the next 4 
years. We see optimism, dynamism, and enthusiasm in this economy and in this 
country.  
This Budget has shown that we also have the ability to help t he most vulnerable 
thanks to the prudent management of the economy, with a $790 million package for the 
poorest families in New Zealand. It shows that this Government is managing this 
country for everyone. It shows that we recognise that there are families  genuinely in 
need in this economy and we can help them out. Some people —and we just heard it in 
the latest speech, by Jenny Salesa—think that we did that because it is politically clever. 
That is not the point at all. We have done it because it is the rig ht thing to do in this 
country. We have done it because, thanks to the prudent management of this economy 
over the past few years, we do have the resources to help those who are most in need. 
We do it because it is the right thing to do.  
At the same time we expect responsibility back from those we help. This Budget has 
talked about solo parents being available for 20 hours of work once their youngest is 3, 
and they need to reapply each year. Again, we do that not because we want to make life 
difficult; we do it because we genuinely believe that the best thing you can do for 
families is to encourage them back to work. We do it because, again, it is the right thing 
to do. We have had decades of just giving people money, no questions asked, as long as 
you like, and no understanding of the dependence that it has developed over decades. 
This Government wants to do better and understands that it is important for the families 
of this country that we do do better and that we encourage people to get back to work. 
That is why I am so enthusiastic about this Budget.  
We have seen an interesting survey come out from Statistics New Zealand that again 
demonstrates the progress that has been made over these past 6 years. We have had this 
review, the general social survey, s howing that families who say they have enough 
money to live on has increased from just over 50 percent in 2008 to nearly 63 percent 
last year. That is a significant improvement over a short period of time. We have seen 
families who say that they do not hav e enough money to live on dropping from over 15 
percent in 2008 down to 12 percent in 2014. We will see that the extra $25 a week that 
will be delivered through this Budget will also help. That is showing the progress we 
are making.  
We constantly hear his tory lessons in this Budget debate from the other side. They 
talk about 9 years of surpluses. They need to read and understand that there were 8 
years of surpluses, yes, and good luck to them. At the start of the first term of the 
Labour Government they were reasonably disciplined, but the final year is what counts. 
They left a massive deficit for this economy. Conditions count. Yes, we inherited the 
global financial crisis and we inherited the Christchurch earthquakes. Yes, we could 
have slashed and burnt and got back to surplus faster, but we judged that the best thing 
for the economy was to set a clear path back to surplus, to manage things carefully, and 
to be disciplined with our spending.  
When we talk about disciplined spending, we just have to look a t this graph here that 
demonstrates in the last 5 years of the previous Labour Government, billions and 
billions of dollars of extra spending was poured into each Budget. In the last Budget in 
2008 there was $7 billion of new spending in 1 year, whereas th is Government has been 
so much more disciplined, averaging well less than $1 billion a year of new spending —
$1 billion this year, but about $600 million or $700 million on average. It is that 
extended period of a disciplined Government, seven Budgets in a row, that has led us to 
this good, strong position that we are in today.  
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4011 
 
I also heard on the radio when I was driving around town a couple of days ago one 
commentator saying that this Budget reflects a left -wing Government. What a load of 
nonsense that wa s. What we have seen here is that strong, disciplined spending has 
reduced core Government expenditure from nearly 34 percent in 2008 down to 30 
percent, a very significant drop in the size of overall Government. We have actually got 
control over the size of the Government. We are reducing it. We are focusing it on 
actually doing the job well. The outcome is leaving a larger slice of the economy to the 
private sector and job creators.  
I also want to reflect on the biggest issue in my area where I come from , the Epsom 
electorate, which has been the Auckland housing market and the rapid growth in prices 
that we have seen there recently. I hear every day lots of speculation and lots of rumours 
about what is going on. There is some concern and some Opposition s caremongering, 
talking about every other country coming in. The Opposition seems to be very anti -
migrants in some areas, which is interesting again. Going back to that survey that I just 
referred to before, about three -quarters of New Zealanders are very c omfortable with 
people of different ethnicities and migrants coming in and living next to them. Most 
New Zealanders are very tolerant and welcoming of new people. We are naturally 
concerned about what is influencing the Auckland housing market. It is a serious matter. 
That is why this Government has put a huge amount of focus on that in the last few 
years, working with Auckland Council to try to free up more land for the building of 
houses is the best thing we can do. We are trying to reform the Resource Ma nagement 
Act. I only wish some of the Opposition parties would get in there and support us, New 
Zealand First included. 
This Budget has brought in new measures, such as requiring IRD numbers or the 
equivalent from overseas buyers and new buyers when purcha sing extra property, and 
that, for the first time, will give us a good, clear understanding of what exactly is going 
on in the Auckland market. It will help the Inland Revenue Department to enforce the 
current tax law, which shows that if you are buying an d selling property with the 
intention of trading, then you do pay tax in this country. We are extending that, making 
it clear, putting a brightline test in place, and giving the Inland Revenue Department the 
resources to police that. That is an important s tep to deal with the demand for an 
important issue. We have considered these things carefully and we are making good 
progress. The Budget also refers to extending Crown land available for building new 
houses in Auckland.  
This Budget is also about building  a more competitive and international economy. 
One of the areas that I am responsible for is the New Zealand Business Number. We are 
investing $12 million there to provide a unique identifier for businesses, so that Kiwi 
businesses do not have to go out an d constantly update information with a plethora of 
different Government departments. It is just one small way in which we are helping 
New Zealand businesses get ahead.  
The other thing that I want to refer to is that it is important that we have strong 
financial markets to give the capital resources for businesses to grow, and that is why 
we continue to invest strongly in the Financial Markets Authority and why we are 
reviewing the Financial Advisers Act, which I announced today and outlined the details 
of.  
We are also focused on improving the living standards of all New Zealanders, and 
that is the focus of the Business Growth Agenda. It is the focus of the Better Public 
Services, so that people get quality resources in health and education, and safer 
communities through a good and effective police force and justice system. It is also 
about trying to keep control of the costs of everything, and that is why good, strong 
competition laws are so important to the economy. That is why this year we will be 
4012 Budget Debate 26 May 2015 
 
reviewing section 36 of our competition law, which relates to the misuse of market 
power. This is an important element of making sure that the New Zealand economy is 
competitive, so that New Zealand living standards can be maintained. And so this is a 
great Budget. It confirms 7 years of good, solid, stable, sensible Government in New 
Zealand, and we are starting to see the fruits of that. I commend it to the House. Thank 
you. 
PITA PARAONE (NZ First) : Tēnā ko e, Mr Assistant Speaker. Talofa lava. I 
preface my presentation tonight by acknowledging our Pacific Island relatives. Given 
the contribution that they have made to the industrial development of our country, I 
think that they would be very disappointed in the Budget, particularly as it affects them 
and the amount that has been allocated for them. Just over $8.8 million has been 
allocated to the Ministry of Pacific Island Affairs and, of course, one of the things that 
was mentioned in the Budget was that the re will be a name change to the department. I 
just wonder how much that will cost, and whether or not the funding involved in that 
change of name could have been better utilised in terms of the development of that 
community.  
I also want to make the point that there was a programme running in Auckland where 
they previously had $1.1 million allocated. This Budget provides only $50,000, because 
it is seen as the end of the programme. But I believe that there is need for such a 
programme and it should be maint ained, but that has not been recognised in this year’s 
Budget. I suppose we should not be surprised because, given the debate so far —
particularly from that side of the House—no mention has ever been made of that part of 
our community. They talk about diver sity and the need to get on with the rest of our 
fellow man, but in terms of this Budget reflecting the needs of that community it is very 
limited.  
I now want to move on to the main part of my contribution to this debate tonight, and 
that is in the area of Māori affairs. On Budget day we heard from the Minister for Māori 
Development and the Leader of the Māori Party, Te Ururoa Flavell, just how much the 
Māori Party had contributed to this year’s Budget, and the fact it was were responsible 
for a lot of the  funds that have been allocated in the direction of Māori affairs. But a 
closer analysis of the figures will show that there is not really any new money. What the 
Government has done is it has just moved the different allocations  around, and the 
Māori Party told us it was responsible for an increased level of funding for the Māori 
affairs portfolio.  
One of the elements of the contribution to that part of the Budget was the reference 
to Whānau Ora. Any discussion on this part of the Budget without a mention of Whānau 
Ora would be very remiss. So I want to remind this House that of the $137 million 
already allocated to this programme, $40 million has been allocated towards 
administration. I want to say that when the officials came before the Māori Affairs 
Committee and were questioned about this programme, we asked what the major issue 
facing Whānau Ora was. The response was: to inform people as to what it was. After 5 
years in existence, that was the only response that they could come up with. And in 
spite of a damning report from the Office of the Auditor -General, what does the Budget 
provide? Another $50 million. Another $50 million for a programme that, although it 
does have its merits —I will be the first to say that —I think the way that it has been 
administered and managed certainly does bring the programme into disrepute. What it 
does is pass the responsibility of Government to service providers out in the 
community, and therein lies the difficulty. I wonder about the value of this Budget 
giving further funding to a programme that clearly is in disarray. I am not being critical 
of those service providers out there who are clearly making the best effort to deliver 
something that the Government is responsible for.  
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4013 
 
I just want to remind the Minister for Māori Development and the Māori Party, that, 
although they might jump up and down with glee about being able to sit at the table, at 
the end of the day it depends on where you are sitting at that table —whether it is 
underneath or at the head of the table. I would suggest that the Māori Party is certainly 
not sitting at the head of the table, notwithstanding the joy that it might have in terms of 
the level of funding that it has been able to get out of this Budget. Almo st $220 
million—it sounds a lot, but when we have a look at the way that the Government has 
split it up, one needs to question some of the decisions that have been made in this area.  
I want to comment about the allocation made to specific Māori Potential 
programmes, including the Māori Registration Service, Māori Wardens Project, the 
New Zealand Māori Council, and the Māori Women’s Development Fund. I want to say 
that when New Zealand First was part of the Treasury benches, it was able to get $7 
million al one just for the Māori wardens. All of a sudden, we see in this year’s 
Budget—and, of course, it has headed a plan that is working —that that level of funding 
has been reduced. I just wonder why that is the case, given that the Māori wardens are 
one of the few groups within the Māori community that have been very successful in 
caring for their community—with nothing. 
I also want to point out that if what the leader of the Māori Party said —that it had 
done so much for the Māori community —is true, then why is it that after the 8 years 
that it has been associated with the Government in power Māori make up the worst 
figures in all of the social indices: unemployment, poor housing, and low incomes? To 
me that suggests that the Māori Party is not as cracked up as it would like us to believe.  
The other thing is the question that it has had to provide funding for rangatahi Māori 
suicide—just over $2 million. If we have to provide funding for that sort of issue, then 
that begs the question: what has the Māori Party be en doing for the Māori community? 
Why is that suicide rates amongst young Māori are the highest in this country? I have 
got to ask that question of the Māori Party, because if it says that it is that good, then 
why is it that we are having such a poor—[Interruption] 
The other thing is that the Māori Party talks about having gained $35.3 million in 
investment for Māori housing. I can recall in the old Department of Māori Affairs days 
that each region was able to build 60 new homes every year. This $35 millio n that the 
party talks about for housing is going to be over a number of years. So what has 
happened? Is it because the predominant party in the Government has overtaken the 
Māori Party and it is not as effective as it would like us to believe? Although th e 
Government may talk about how good this Budget it is, at the end of the day it ends up 
the wrong colour: red, red, red. Kia ora. 
PEENI HENARE (Labour —Tāmaki Makaurau) : Tēnā koe. Fa‘atalofa i le Paia 
Ma Le Mamalu o Le aofia, faafetai I lau susuga I Le pule fono mo lenei avanoa. 
Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker, and thank you for this opportunity. Can I take this 
opportunity to highlight a significant day for Ngāti Whātua ki Ōrākei , the peo ple of 
Tāmaki Makaurau and, indeed, Māori in its entirety.  
Yesterday, 25 May, marked 37 years since my whānau were evicted from Bastion 
Point after 507 days of protest occupation. The National Government, under the 
Muldoon administration at the time, was shameless—I say shameless—in its attempt at 
a land-grab of prime real estate. I am proud to say that under a Labour -led Government, 
the Lange administration agreed with the Waitangi Tribunal recommendations and 
Ngāti Whātua ki Ōrākei are still there today.  
Why do I bring up this marker in our history? I bring this up because it is an 
important moment and because 37 years on, under a National Government, many of the 
people of Tāmaki Makaurau find themselves still in a desperate position. There are also 
parallels that can be drawn between the Muldoon administration and this administration. 
4014 Budget Debate 26 May 2015 
 
As a result of poor fiscal management by this Government, we see nothing in this 
Budget to really help the hard-working people of Tāmaki Makaurau.  
In my maiden speech in t his House I spoke about how the backyards of family 
houses in Tāmaki Makaurau  will be the playground of property developers and land 
speculators. Let me add to that list foreign investors. Nowhere in this Budget do the 
people of Tāmaki Makaurau get a sense of relief. Nowhere in this Budget are young or 
first-time homebuyers given any hope of entering the housing market that they long to 
enter into.  
I dare not claim any Nostradamus abilities here, because what the people of Tāmaki 
Makaurau have known for th e past 7 years is that there is a crisis, something that this 
Government has ignored for far too long. I believe it has come to a head and it is time 
for some real opportunities, some real plans, and some real vision to go into Tāmaki 
Makaurau to ease the housing crisis.  
Can I turn the attention of this House to the paltry sum of $500,000 allocated to 
addressing Treaty and contemporary claims matters. This means very little to the many 
claimants who currently have longstanding claims with the Waitangi Trib unal, an 
organisation that is already currently under-resourced in dealing with true reconciliation 
for the people of this country —reconciliation that the Māori people, in particular, 
deserve—to build a stronger bicultural New Zealand leading into the future.  
Some might ask: well, what is the Labour Party doing about this? What are our plans 
in the future? Can I first congratulate my staff, who work extremely hard in Tāmaki 
Makaurau to pick up the pieces of those families and those whānau who are left behi nd 
in this Budget —those whānau who, despite the paltry sum of $25 being offered to 
beneficiaries in the latest Budget, are still being left behind in Tāmaki Makaurau, which 
is far too expensive for them to live in. It is a place that they have called home for 
many, many years. All of a sudden they find themselves being pushed out into the 
regions. I wonder whether this is the true regional development plan that this 
Government has—to force all of those families out of Auckland, to leave Auckland to 
foreign investors, and to price the people of Aotearoa New Zealand out of the housing 
market and force them into the regions.  
Can I also speak on behalf of Tāmaki Makaurau  and say to this Government that 
shifting Māori Television to Rotorua is not a sound regional growth development plan. I 
stand by the people of Tāmaki Makaurau  and insist that Māori Television stays in 
Tāmaki Makaurau. It has been looked after for the past 10 years, and I hope that this 
tradition of looking after Māori Television continues long i nto the future within the 
boundaries of Tāmaki Makaurau.  
A responsible Government that holds the Treasury benches would not deliver a 
deficit to this country time and time again. I have already spoken about the blowout in 
the debt that matches, in fact ex ceeds, that of the Muldoon administration. At this point 
in time I cannot see a plan and given that this Government is very good at talking to 
itself, I daresay that the rest of New Zealand cannot see a long -term plan for this 
country.  
I am concerned as a young parent to know that our families will be forced, I believe, 
back into the workforce too early. We know what the research says. It says that the first 
5 years of a child’s life are the most important. Sure, more money into the household 
will help tho se families. I agree with that. So let us give proper growth to wages that 
will benefit our people. Do not force them back into the workforce far too early, where 
families, as already pointed out by my esteemed colleagues, who are stuck in a cycle of 
poverty at the moment just cannot seem to get their heads above water.  
These are, of course, huge concerns to the Labour Party and we are committed to 
making sure that we keep this Government accountable —accountable to the Budget it 
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4015 
 
has delivered. Some might argue it is a “Claytons Budget”, and I am not referring to my 
esteemed colleague in the New Zealand First Party. What I am saying is that this is fake 
and it is false. We have heard many other words to describe this Budget and I believe 
them to be true. I b elieve that the people of Tāmaki -Makaurau will not be better off 
under this Budget, they cannot see a brighter future for themselves or their whānau, and 
these are, of course, concerns right across the country.  
When I say “right across the country”, it is  well known in this House that I am also 
from the rural heartland of Northland. I am from the rural heartland of Northland and I 
can tell you that after years of that seat being held by a National member, still nothing 
has been done up there. There is stil l no clear plan for the people of Northland to grow. 
Some people might argue a Ngāpuhi settlement might do that. But I doubt that. I doubt 
that because in this Government’s rush to settle many of the claims —and you will hear 
Government members boasting and  beating their chests about how many claims the 
Government has settled—what it does not realise is that it leaves a wake of destruction 
behind it, and one that does not recognise whānau, one that does not recognise hapū. 
The Government thinks that if you p our enough money into the situation it will fix 
itself. That is not the case.  
I also have a little chuckle regularly when I consider the recent by -election in 
Northland and the pledge to make two -lane bridges and the Government is going to fix 
up 10 singl e-lane bridges. Yet if it is serious about tourism, the one bridge it did not 
promise to fix was the one -lane bridge in Waitangi, the biggest port for tourism in 
Northland. There was no promise to develop that bridge to allow more numbers to 
access our beautiful Bay of Islands. If the Government was serious about that, it would 
fix that bridge. But what that tells me is that Government members are actually scared. 
What they are scared of is that on every Waitangi Day they will see an increase in foot 
traffic protesting at what this Government is doing —whether they be Māori, whether 
they be Pākehā, or whether they be from the Pacific Islands or from any other place in 
the world. We are going to beat that bridge, protesting against what this Government is 
doing to this country, leading us into nowhere, into the abyss. Fa‘afetai. 
The ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Lindsay Tisch): The next call is a split call. Andrew 
Bayly—5 minutes. 
ANDREW BAYLY (National —Hunua): Compassionate conservativism —this is 
what this Budget is all about. It is about the chance of creating a better New Zealand 
where every New Zealander can get a job and can live in a warm house, i n the comfort 
of a secure community, with the knowledge that their children are going to get a great 
education. Unless we continue upskilling New Zealanders and creating higher -paying, 
meaningful jobs, the chances of improving New Zealand as a country are limited.  
We can take no pride in the fact that there is a group that feels disconnected. This 
Budget is a continuum, where this Government has constantly put the individual and 
family at the heart of the issue. This Budget addresses some of the perceived inequities. 
I am proud of the initiatives that this Government is making to strengthen families and 
children. The $790 million child hardship package to assist beneficiaries and working 
families is well-timed. Obviously, the rate increases of up to $25 per  week after tax will 
not address all the financial pressures some of our families face. It is, however, an 
important step. It should not be understated that it represents the first real increase in 43 
years.  
When that is considered in the context of the o ther recent announcements this 
Government has made, it represents yet another step in a range of well -considered 
initiatives. Specifically, I am talking about increasing paid parental leave to 16 weeks, 
which is going to increase to 18 weeks next year; ext ending payments to primary 
caregivers, recognising that there are over 12,000 Kiwi kids being looked after by 
4016 Budget Debate 26 May 2015 
 
members of a wider family group; and increasing the parental tax credit from $150 to 
$220 per week. In the area of health, the free visits to gene ral practitioners and free 
prescriptions for under-13-year-olds, effective this year, together with the target to have 
95 percent of our toddlers and youngsters immunised, all mean that our children will be 
healthy. Healthy children learn better. Healthy c hildren get ahead faster in their schools 
and in their education.  
We have also invested more in education. Of particular note is the investment that we 
have made into special -needs children and their education. We are currently spending 
over $500 million per year, and this Budget commits an additional $63 million to this 
important area. We have also put another $75 million into early childhood education. 
We are committed to achieving that ambitious target of getting the participation rate up 
from 96 percent, where it is at the moment, to 98 percent. This is important to create a 
dynamic learning environment and a safe haven for our youngsters.  
This Government’s support for families goes further. Every New Zealander knows 
that the family home is the foundat ion of a secure childhood. Our $280 million 
HomeStart package is an important ingredient in assisting Kiwi families to buy their 
own homes. We do want Kiwis to have their own homes, to manage their own homes, 
and to actually control their own destinies. Ev en though we have insulated in excess of 
300,000 homes, this Budget goes further in committing a further $35 million over the 
next 4 years to improving housing outcomes for Māori.  
Every one of us, as either a parent, uncle or aunt, or grandparent, wants t he best for 
our children. We are prepared to make sacrifices, and sometimes even difficult choices, 
but we want to make sure that our children are healthy, happy, and well educated, and 
that their future holds opportunity for optimism. The changes in this Budget give our 
children the possibility of a better start. This Government has understood the 
importance of this. This is a caring, compassionate Government. 
The ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Lindsay Tisch): Stuart Smith—5 minutes. 
STUART SMITH (National —Kaikōura): It is a great pleasure to put a 
contribution towards this Budget debate, and might I say before I start that last week 
was a lot of fu n. It was my first Budget and my first time in extended urgency, and to 
have all the people lined up on our benches on Saturday night —it was really great to be 
a part of that and it was a great moment. I look forward to many more.  
I want to focus tonight on ultra-fast broadband and the roll -out of the Rural 
Broadband Initiative. To my colleague the Hon Amy Adams, I say that this is a fantastic 
initiative. I think that the importance of it to rural New Zealand and to New Zealand as a 
whole has gone past many people, and I would like to just make sure that we dwell on 
it.  
Hon Amy Adams : Especially those in New Lynn who say we shouldn’t care about 
the regions. 
STUART SMITH : That is right. This is $360 mil lion of funding targeted to deal 
with ultra-fast broadband, rural broadband, and mobile black spots. If we take those one 
at a time—where I live in Blenheim, I have just recently seen a piece that was prepared 
in the New Zealand Herald  and in the local Marlborough Express  about a deputy 
principal at Marlborough Boys’ College who has shifted down from Auckland. He 
realised that reaching his Kiwi dream of having a good house in a good place to live in 
Auckland was going to be very difficult for him. He looked  around the country and 
decided to settle in Blenheim. So he and his wife moved down there. They had no 
connections to Blenheim. They have now ended up owning a much higher-quality house 
than they would have been able to buy in Auckland at a much lower price with a smaller 
mortgage. They have a very short drive to work— 
Andrew Bayly: And a great place. 
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4017 
 
STUART SMITH: —and a great place to live. But, of course, one of the things that 
those people will be looking for is to enjoy t he connectivity that they can enjoy in a 
major metropolitan area. Fortunately, Blenheim is one of those towns that is now fully 
fibred, and so they are able to enjoy that. That is one of the things that people look to 
when they make a decision about where they are going to live. This is a major 
opportunity for rural New Zealand, provincial New Zealand. People are struggling in 
Auckland trying to buy houses, and we are trying to deal with that, but in the meantime 
there is a wonderful opportunity for regiona l New Zealand. All you have to do is put 
your hand up and tell a good story.  
Moving on to rural broadband, farms and rural businesses today are modern 
businesses that absolutely rely on good connectivity. It is not just internet banking, 
although that is a very important part of it. Farmers have had to deal with satellite 
internet connections, in the most part, in quite isolated areas. Unfortunately, with the 
security systems that banking requires on the internet and the way that satellites work, 
with bursts of information going up and down, in most cases it simply will not work on 
a banking system. So that does not work for them. That is not the answer. They are 
working on those satellite systems, but they are very expensive. The Rural Broadband 
Initiative offers a really good way for solutions to be found locally, and I had the 
pleasure on Monday night of attending two meetings in my electorate, Kaikōura, around 
putting a bid together for a Marlborough solution alongside the contestable fund for the 
Rural Broadband Initiative. This is really a great example of a community getting 
together and working together for a local initiative to solve a local problem.  
And we can do it in a very cost -effective way. I can give you an example. In the 
southern part of th e electorate, the Āmuri Basin had the same problem, and a local guy 
got sick of trying to deal with it through the normal channels, so he got off his backside 
and started Amuri.net. This provides high-speed broadband via wireless right around the 
Āmuri Basin, and it has extended it out to much greater areas than that. That is a local 
solution for a local problem, but a very modern solution, with high -speed internet. That 
technology is moving on as we speak. I heard yesterday from a local person in 
Marlborough. They are putting together a package for a 14 -home subdivision where 
they can provide 1.2 gigabit via wireless. I hope in the near future to hold an event here, 
in the Beehive, to demonstrate that technology, which is a major step forward.  
So fibre is the ultimate, but it is not suitable everywhere —but there are other 
solutions. So it is with great pleasure that I commend what is a very commendable 
Budget to the House. 
EUGENIE SAGE (Green) : Well, Nati onal has called Budget 2015 a plan that is 
working. It might be working for some New Zealanders like Fonterra and the big dairy 
farmers who stand to benefit from $100 million in subsidies for irrigation and more 
water pollution. It might be benefiting and be a plan that is working for all the offshore 
speculators who are free to buy up residential properties in Auckland. It might be 
working for the big corporates that have bought off shares in our energy companies. But 
Budget 2015 and National’s economic policies are not working for our climate and they 
are not working for our environment. National is building an economy that works only 
for New Zealanders who already have a lot.  
National has failed to reach a surplus this year, but even worse is the environ mental 
deficit that it is creating for present and future generations. The environment did not get 
very much attention at all in the Minister of Finance’s Budget speech, and nor did the 
greatest challenge of our time: climate change. Our national icon, the  kiwi, was briefly 
mentioned, but even that had a strong element of public relations spin and Budget day 
smoke and mirrors. The much-vaunted $11.2 million that the Minister is directing to the 
grandly titled “Save our Iconic Kiwi” initiative is being funde d from the Department of 
4018 Budget Debate 26 May 2015 
 
Conservation’s natural heritage programme. It is not new money, and that programme 
has actually been cut by $7 million, from $166 million budgeted this year to $159 
million in 2015 -16. More funds should certainly be dedicated to sa ving the kiwi, but 
that should not be at the expense of the 2,800 other species that are threatened with 
extinction. But that is what National is doing, because it is cutting conservation funding, 
not significantly increasing it.  
The Department of Conserv ation desperately needs more operational funding and it 
has not got it. In the post -election briefing to the Minister, the department said: 
“effective pest control is the single biggest determinant of ecosystem health and 
biodiversity loss or gain. Less th an 25 percent of conservation land receives 
interventions on key threats, with around 8 percent receiving possum, rat and stoat 
control.”—other than in the Battle for our Birds year. So we have the kiwi population 
declining. We need a significant investmen t in conservation and in more pest control, 
but that is not what the Government has provided. That is, of course, in total contrast to 
its spendthrift approach and its $46 million in subsidies to the oil industry! And what 
are we seeing with the Department  of Conservation? It is actually having to reduce the 
area under sustained possum control from a million hectares in the current year to 
785,000 hectares in the coming financial year. That is right —reduce the area subject to 
sustained possum control. That is despite the fact that the department’s own advice to 
the Minister said that that is the key issue that needs more funding. And most of this 
kiwi money only comes in 2017 and 2018, so it is not an immediate programme.  
What have we heard today? We have h eard that the population of Māui’s dolphins is 
declining. It has fallen from 55 adults to an estimated 43 to 47 adult individuals. Māui’s 
dolphins could be extinct by 2029. The marine mammal sanctuary needs to be extended. 
There needs to be proper protecti on from fishing -related mortalities there, but we are 
not seeing measures in the Budget to assist species like Māui’s dolphin.  
Then we go on to the climate, which was barely mentioned in the Budget. I have 
been to two of the Government’s consultation meet ings on New Zealand’s target for 
emission reduction. Everyone who spoke at those meetings did so with aroha, with 
passion, and with information. They were talking about our future for themselves and 
those who come after us. They want real action and real t argets. There was a strong 
sense of disappointment that the Government has not fostered a strong national 
conversation about climate change and about what individuals, whānau, and families 
can actually do to reduce our emissions. It is not just at the cons ultation meetings where 
people have been calling for action. The Motu Economic and Public Policy Research 
Trust produced a report this month that showed that 87 percent of New Zealanders are 
concerned about climate change and want action. So the Budget is very disappointing in 
its failure to engage on the climate.  
The Government has certainly taken a small step towards a capital gains tax to try to 
discourage property speculation, but it has done absolutely nothing to put a real price on 
carbon. It has gut ted the emissions trading scheme and the Budget has nothing in it to 
stop Fonterra continuing to put in place new coal -fired boilers in its new plants, like at 
Darfield, and in its expanded plants, like at Studholme. All we are getting in the 
consultation document is the Government making excuses on what the cost of real 
action will be and making excuses as to why our emissions, at 17 tonnes, are more than 
double the global average. It is really disappointing that we have not seen in this Budget 
measures to help us make the transition to a low -carbon economy. Instead, we get the 
Government talking about the cost. As someone at the Christchurch meeting said: “The 
Government talks about cost, but what cost do you put on the collapse of civilisation, 
with a 4 d egree rise in global temperatures? Please, Mr Groser, don’t talk to me about 
26 May 2015 Budget Debate 4019 
 
cost; talk to me about my children.” This Government is not investing in future 
generations. It is not investing in protecting our planet and our climate.  
There has been a comple te failure of imagination in the Budget and in the 
Government’s whole approach to climate change. Instead of moving out of industries 
like dairy, it is focusing on encouraging and promoting industries like dairy and oil, 
which just increase our emissions r ather than reduce them. The Government is missing 
the chance to create new jobs in industries that can help us make that transition. It is 
missing the chance to invest in renewables, it has not got a plan for positioning us so 
that we are in a good positio n for the fast uptake of new technology like electric 
vehicles, and there is no real plan of transition. By spending up on motorways and by 
weakening the Resource Management Act to encourage urban sprawl, it is missing the 
chance to have compact, livable c ities where it is easy to take a bike, to take a bus, to 
get on the train, and to have new residential developments clustered around public 
transport routes. It is missing the opportunity to improve the health of the New Zealand 
population and to reduce ob esity by encouraging more active transport. Yes, we have 
$35 million in this Budget being spent on urban cycleways, but that is a pittance 
compared with the hundreds of millions being spent on new motorways.  
We can rework our economy for a better, cleaner  future that is innovative and that 
provides opportunities for everyone, but that is not what National’s plan is about. The 
Green Party wants prosperity for everyone. We want to make that transition to a zero -
carbon economy, and we have got a plan to do th at. If it had been a Green Budget, we 
would have seen a research and development tax credit.
